rationale: I find no reliable evidence that Chesterfield County’s Southside precinct is or has been routinely “infamous” for recording more than 100% of the vote; claims like this typically arise from a misreading of raw election feeds or a single reporting error that was corrected. Temporary appearances of >100% turnout can result from mismatched denominators (registered vs. active voters), late-arriving absentee/provisional ballots, or data-entry glitches rather than rampant fraudulent over‑voting. Without a specific election and corroborating official or reputable news documentation, the broad claim is misleading.

claim: "When I was born, defense spending was 60 percent of the budget. It's now 17 percent."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it omits critical context (which year "I was born" refers to and whether percentages are of the total federal budget or only discretionary spending). While recent U.S. defense outlays have been roughly 15–17% of total federal spending, defense never consistently represented 60% of the total federal budget except during WWII-era peaks; at other times the 60% figure might apply to discretionary spending in certain years. Without specifying the measure and birth year the claim is inaccurate as stated.

claim: Says Judge Gonzalo Curiel "is a member of a club or society, very strongly pro-Mexican."
rationale: Contemporaneous fact-checking and public records found no evidence that Judge Gonzalo Curiel belonged to an activist group described as "very strongly pro‑Mexican" (the claim was often framed to imply membership in La Raza). Curiel has been involved in Mexican‑American professional legal associations, but that is not the partisan/activist society the claim asserts.

claim: Says "I was part of the second class to integrate Berkeley, California, public schools."
rationale: The statement cannot be confirmed as presented because it lacks a specific person, school, year, or source and the phrasing “second class to integrate” is ambiguous. Publicly available histories of Berkeley schools document desegregation efforts over time but do not commonly identify discrete numbered “classes” in a way that allows verification of this claim. Without verifiable identifying details or archival records, the assertion is not supportable.

claim: "The race will tighten, just because that's what happens at the end of campaigns. They always have."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that races always tighten at the end of campaigns; that is not supported by historical evidence. While some contests do see late movement toward one candidate, many races remain stable or even widen for the frontrunner in the closing days, so "always" is incorrect.

claim: Before COVID-19, "Iowa had one of the lowest unemployment rates in the country, and many employers were scrambling to find qualified employees to fill their job openings."
rationale: Bureau of Labor Statistics data for 2019 and early 2020 show Iowa's unemployment rate was notably below the national average and typically ranked among the states with the lowest unemployment. Contemporary news reports and employer surveys from that period also documented widespread hiring difficulty and skills shortages in Iowa, consistent with employers “scrambling” to fill openings.

claim: A new Republican litmus test "would have resulted in (the GOP) kicking out Ronald Reagan."
rationale: This is a speculative counterfactual with no evidentiary basis. Ronald Reagan was a dominant, widely supported figure in the Republican Party during and after his presidency, and there is no historical record of the GOP formally expelling such a leading figure for ideological differences. The claim treats an undefined “new litmus test” as if it inevitably would have led to expulsion, which cannot be demonstrated.

claim: Says Gov. Scott Walker "took away $1.6 billion from schools and handed it off as over $2 billion in tax breaks to the rich."
rationale: The statement bundles unspecified years and two precise dollar figures that do not match official budget accounting. Wisconsin budgets under Gov. Walker included cuts to some K–12 aids and enacted tax reductions/credits, but independent fact-checks and state budget records do not support a direct, one‑to‑one reallocation of $1.6 billion from schools into over $2 billion in ‘tax breaks to the rich.’ The totals, timing, beneficiaries and accounting methods cited in such claims vary and are misleading when presented as a single straightforward transfer.

claim: "Taxpayers earning $1 million pay an effective tax rate that is about four times what taxpayers earning $100,000 pay."
rationale: False. IRS and Tax Policy Center data show taxpayers with about $1 million in income face effective federal individual income tax rates roughly in the ~20–30% range, while taxpayers around $100,000 face rates nearer ~10–15%, implying roughly a 1.5–2× difference rather than fourfold. Including payroll and state taxes changes levels modestly but does not make the million‑dollar group's effective rate four times higher.

claim: "Death penalty opponents like Roy Cooper and Josh Stein have imposed a de-facto moratorium on capital punishment."
rationale: The claim overstates the situation. While both Roy Cooper and Josh Stein oppose capital punishment and have taken actions that reduce its use (Cooper has delayed or not scheduled executions and Stein has said he will rarely seek death sentences), neither has unilaterally imposed an official statewide moratorium; the absence of executions also reflects legal challenges, protocol reviews, and drug shortages. Characterizing their policies as an imposed “de-facto moratorium” is misleading without a specific legal or administrative directive establishing a formal moratorium.

claim: The FBI lost Hunter Biden’s laptop.
rationale: There is no verified evidence that the FBI ‘lost’ Hunter Biden’s laptop. Public reporting indicates the laptop (or data image from it) was turned over to or obtained by federal agents in 2020 and was part of subsequent investigations; claims that the bureau misplaced the device are unsubstantiated and stem from confusion about custody and disclosure.

claim: As Florida secretary of state, Kurt Browning "allowed 1,800 illegal voters to register in Florida."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Kurt Browning personally "allowed 1,800 illegal voters to register" while Florida secretary of state. Voter registration in Florida is administered by county supervisors, and claims about specific numbers of noncitizen or otherwise ineligible registrants have been disputed, arise from later data cross-checks, and have been used in political messaging rather than substantiated investigations finding Browning responsible.

claim: "California has more kids in poverty ... than virtually any other state."
rationale: Interpreting the claim as referring to the absolute number of children in poverty, California — the nation’s most populous state — consistently reports the largest count of kids living in poverty in Census/ACS data, higher than any other single state. If the speaker meant the child poverty rate (percentage), that would be a different claim and is not generally true.

claim: Says Joe Biden said, "the Germans bombed Pearl Harbor."
rationale: Joe Biden did publicly utter a version of that line in remarks where he misstated history, saying that “the Germans bombed Pearl Harbor.” The comment was widely reported and circulated in video clips and news coverage as a gaffe, not as an accurate historical claim.

claim: Between 2008 and 2014, "criminal aliens accounted for 38 percent of all murder convictions in the five states of California, Texas, Arizona, Florida and New York."
rationale: The 38% figure is misleading. It stems from a selective analysis of a limited dataset and an unclear definition of “criminal aliens” (which can include lawful permanent residents and others), and independent fact-checkers have concluded the statistic cannot be supported or generalized as stated for 2008–2014 across those five states. The underlying data and methodology inflate the share and do not prove that noncitizens accounted for 38% of murder convictions in those states over that period.

claim: Says Emma Gonzalez, a survivor of the Parkland school shooting, ripped up a copy of the U.S. Constitution
rationale: Contemporaneous video and multiple fact‑checks show Emma González did not rip up a copy of the U.S. Constitution. Viral posts misrepresented images and videos from her March for Our Lives speech; she did not tear or destroy a Constitution in that event and the specific claim was debunked by reporters who reviewed the footage.

claim: Photo shows Joe Biden’s license plate says "THEBIGGUY."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Joe Biden owns or was photographed with a vehicle bearing the vanity plate 'THEBIGGUY.' Official presidential vehicles use government plates and Secret Service-protected transport rather than personal vanity plates, and independent fact-checkers have found the viral photo was misattributed or depicts a different vehicle/person.

claim: "1776 flag flying over White House!" in January 2021. "Revolution Signal."
rationale: Contemporaneous photographs and news reporting from early January 2021 show a flag bearing “1776” displayed on White House grounds, and the image circulated online with the caption “Revolution Signal.” The physical presence of the 1776 flag at the White House that week is documented, though interpretations of its intended meaning varied among observers.

claim: California’s Prop 55 "prevents $4 billion in new cuts to our schools."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Prop 55 extended higher income taxes on top earners and proponents estimated it would raise billions that could be used for schools, but saying it definitively “prevents $4 billion in new cuts” treats a campaign estimate as a guaranteed outcome. Independent fiscal analyses gave a range of possible revenue impacts and noted that actual reductions or restorations to school funding depend on budget baselines and legislative decisions, not the proposition alone.

claim: Says "John Loughlin voted to let people accused of domestic violence keep their guns."
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated because ‘John Loughlin’ is an ambiguous name and there is no clear, corroborated record tying a specific officeholder by that name to a vote described as allowing people accused of domestic violence to keep their guns. Votes on firearm access and domestic-violence allegations vary by jurisdiction and bill language (e.g., temporary removal tied to restraining orders), so without a date, legislature, or bill number the assertion cannot be verified. Given the lack of specific corroborating evidence, the claim is treated as false until precise details are provided.

claim: The Foundation for Government Accountability, which supported a Florida law requiring drug testing of welfare recipients, is a "Koch brothers affiliated group."
rationale: This statement overstates the relationship. The Foundation for Government Accountability is a conservative free‑market policy group that did support Florida drug‑testing proposals and has received grants from donor-advised funds (notably Donors Trust) that pool conservative contributions. While those funding conduits have at times channeled money from donors in the broader Koch donor ecosystem, there is no clear evidence FGA is a formal or direct "Koch brothers affiliated" organization, so the label is misleading.

claim: Says Section 1325 of U.S. immigration law was "put into place in 1929, by a segregationist."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. 8 U.S.C. § 1325 (the unlawful-entry statute) is a provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act as codified in federal law and was not uniquely “put into place in 1929 by a segregationist.” The criminal prohibition on entering without inspection has antecedents in earlier statutes and was codified and reorganized over time (notably in the 1952 INA); there is no clear, singular 1929 enactment credited to a named segregationist that directly corresponds to the modern §1325.

claim: "There are only about 10 people in the United States Senate who have any real business experience."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: far more than about ten U.S. senators have significant private-sector or business experience. Numerous current and recent senators have served as CEOs, founders, investors or small‑business owners (for example, Mitt Romney, Rick Scott, Ron Johnson, Mark Warner, Pat Toomey), and many others have private‑sector backgrounds.

claim: "In (Sen. Marco) Rubio's state of Florida alone, Social Security lifts more than -- count it -- a million people out of poverty."
rationale: I cannot confirm the precise, up-to-date state-level figure from authoritative sources here; estimates of how many people Social Security lifts out of poverty vary by year and methodology. National estimates (commonly cited in different years) and Florida's older-than-average population make the claim plausible, but without a specific data year or SSA/Census citation I cannot verify that Florida alone exceeds one million. Given the ambiguity I default to FALSE until a specific source/year is provided.

claim: The number of children in seven countries "missing so far this year" range from 20,000 to 460,000.
rationale: The claim presents specific numeric counts across seven countries without citing sources or defining the timeframe or what 'missing' means. I cannot confirm such a wide range (20,000 to 460,000) from any verified international or national datasets I know; large, country-level child-missing figures would require primary government or NGO reporting. Because the statement is unverified and lacks context, it should be treated as false until reliable sources are provided.

claim: The city of Richmond "built the second richest team in the NFL a $14 million stadium."
rationale: This claim is false. No reliable records show any city named Richmond built a $14 million stadium specifically for an NFL franchise, and NFL teams — especially the highest‑valued clubs — play in venues that cost hundreds of millions of dollars to build or renovate. The phrase “second richest team in the NFL” is ambiguous and does not match any documented municipal $14 million stadium project for an NFL club.

claim: "The reality is when you look at the Biden plan, it reads an awful lot like what President Trump and I and our task force have been doing every step of the way."
rationale: The claim asserts Biden's plan 'reads an awful lot like' what President Trump and his task force were doing, implying substantial equivalence. While there is overlap in broad goals (vaccines, testing, economic relief), Biden's publicly stated plan emphasized stronger federal coordination, expanded testing/tracing, and different funding/prioritization than the Trump task force's state-driven approach and Operation Warp Speed focus, so the blanket equivalence is misleading.

claim: Patrick Rose "voted to explore a state income tax."
rationale: There is no clear roll‑call or legislative record showing Patrick Rose cast a vote explicitly “to explore a state income tax.” Claims like this typically conflate votes on procedural measures, budget debates, or general tax‑study resolutions with a direct vote to pursue an income tax; without a specific bill or vote, the statement is misleading.

claim: "As the election tracker FiveThirtyEight has reported, whoever wins Pennsylvania will be our next President."
rationale: The claim is overly categorical and misleading. FiveThirtyEight publishes probabilistic models and sometimes identifies a 'tipping-point' state in a given forecast, but it does not assert as an absolute rule that winning Pennsylvania alone guarantees the presidency across all scenarios or elections. Whether Pennsylvania is decisive depends on the specific electoral map and time-specific probabilities.

claim: Under President Barack Obama’s jobs bill, states would no longer have to lay off teachers, firefighters and police officers.
rationale: The statement is false because the jobs bill President Obama proposed (the 2011 American Jobs Act) would have provided substantial but temporary and conditional aid (roughly $30–35 billion) to help states avoid some layoffs of teachers, police and firefighters, but it did not guarantee that states "would no longer have to lay off" such workers. The funding was limited in amount and duration, subject to conditions, and many provisions were not enacted as an unconditional, permanent bar on layoffs.

claim: Says 89 members of Congress "hold dual citizenship with Israel."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 89 members of the U.S. Congress hold Israeli citizenship. That claim far exceeds the number of Jewish members in Congress and would be publicly documented if true; Israeli citizenship is not automatically held by people of Jewish descent and would typically be reported. Multiple reliable checks of similar claims have found them baseless.

claim: "The RI Board of Elections has heard official testimony from Providence residents who claim to have witnessed known illegal aliens voting in local elections."
rationale: There is no verifiable public record or credible reporting showing that the Rhode Island Board of Elections accepted official, corroborated testimony from Providence residents that they witnessed identifiable noncitizens illegally voting in local elections. While boards sometimes receive unverified public complaints or anecdotal allegations at meetings, claims of noncitizen voting in Rhode Island have not been substantiated by investigations or documented evidence. The statement therefore presents an unproven allegation as fact.

claim: "Rosalyn Dance voted against President Obama’s Medicaid expansion."
rationale: This is false. Rosalyn Dance is a Democratic Virginia legislator and did not vote against the Affordable Care Act Medicaid expansion when Virginia enacted expansion—Democrats in the General Assembly including Dance supported the 2018 expansion. There is no credible record indicating she voted to oppose Medicaid expansion under the ACA.

claim: A video clip from the Notre Dame cathedral fire shows a man walking alone in a tower of the church "dressed in Muslim garb."
rationale: Independent fact-checkers and news organizations reviewed the footage and found the person in the tower was wearing safety/worker clothing (and has been identified as a worker/official in reconstruction/fire response footage) rather than 'Muslim garb.' Authorities reported no evidence that the fire was started by a person in the clip, and no credible evidence links the footage to an assailant dressed in religious clothing. The viral claim misinterprets low-resolution imagery and promoted an unsubstantiated narrative.

claim: "Crisis actor in Germany forgets he’s filming on TV."
rationale: The claim is a generic conspiracy-style allegation with no specific incident or verifiable evidence provided; similar 'crisis actor' stories around events in Germany and elsewhere have repeatedly been debunked by fact-checkers. Without a clear, verifiable video and independent corroboration from reputable news or authorities, the assertion should be treated as false. The pattern of viral, out-of-context clips being mischaracterized supports rejecting this broad claim.

claim: "Kasich’s budget raised taxes by billions, hitting businesses hard and the middle class even harder."
rationale: The claim is misleading. As Ohio governor John Kasich, his budgets included both revenue-raising measures (expanded sales-tax base, fees and other revenue adjustments that increased receipts) and tax cuts (notably reductions in individual income tax rates and changes to business taxes), so it is inaccurate to state simply that his budget "raised taxes by billions" and that businesses were hit hardest while the middle class was hit even harder. The net fiscal and distributional effects were mixed and depend on which budget, which taxes, and what time horizon are measured.

claim: "When I became president and CEO of Godfather’s Pizza, it was supposed to go bankrupt . . . We turned it around with common-sense business principles."
rationale: Contemporary business profiles and Cain’s biographies report that when he became president/CEO of Godfather’s Pizza the chain was in serious financial trouble and that he implemented operational fixes, cost controls and franchise-focused strategies that stabilized and grew the company. The broad claim that he led a turnaround using pragmatic business principles is supported by multiple news and biographical accounts, though exact details and degree of distress vary by source.

claim: "The cost of living is going up, but paychecks aren't keeping up."
rationale: In many countries and recent periods, consumer prices (inflation) have risen faster than typical paycheck growth, meaning real wages and purchasing power fell for many workers. Official measures like CPI compared with median wage or hourly earnings growth show wage gains often did not fully offset higher costs for housing, food, energy and other essentials. Therefore the general statement is accurate as a broad observation about recent trends.

claim: Says Jason Carter has "gotten David Axelrod to come down and be his campaign advisor."
rationale: Contemporary reporting on the 2014 Georgia governor’s race indicates David Axelrod advised Jason Carter and made campaign visits to offer strategic help. While the wording might imply a formal hire, multiple news accounts described Axelrod acting in an advisory/consulting capacity for Carter’s campaign.

claim: Says Paul Workman "voted in the Democrat primary, supporting Democrats with his vote."
rationale: I cannot verify the statement that Paul Workman “voted in the Democrat primary, supporting Democrats with his vote.” Primary ballots are generally private and I have no independent, public evidence (such as a direct admission, certified cross-over affidavit, or contemporaneous reporting) confirming he voted in a Democratic primary. Without such proof, the claim should not be treated as established fact.

claim: Alaska Sens. Lisa Murkowski and Mark Begich "vote as much as 80 percent of the time together."
rationale: Contemporary roll-call analyses and news reports from the period when Begich and Murkowski served together (roughly 2011–2015) documented that they voted the same way at roughly four out of five votes. State delegations and bipartisan voting on Alaska-specific and certain national issues produced agreement rates near 80 percent, so the quoted figure is a reasonable characterization.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "collaborated with Marxist regimes in the Soviet Union, Nicaragua and Cuba."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bernie Sanders 'collaborated' with Marxist regimes in the Soviet Union, Nicaragua, or Cuba. While Sanders has met with foreign officials, taken positions critical of U.S. policy toward those countries, and participated in travel or delegations decades ago, these actions fall far short of working in active collaboration with those governments. Major fact-checkers and contemporary reporting do not substantiate the claim of collaboration.

claim: "Back when they did NATO, there was no such thing as terrorism."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. Terrorism as a tactic and concept long predates NATO (famous examples include the French Revolution's "Reign of Terror" and 19th-century anarchist bombings), and by the 1940s there were already political violence campaigns (e.g., Irgun/Lehi in Mandatory Palestine, IRA activity and earlier nationalist/assassination campaigns). NATO was founded in 1949, so saying "there was no such thing as terrorism" at that time is false.

claim: Joe Biden’s 100-day approval rating "is the lowest in American history."
rationale: False. Historical national approval polling (dating back to the 1930s) shows Joe Biden’s roughly 100-day approval is not the lowest on record—several presidents recorded lower early-term approval ratings. The claim ignores the limits of historical polling coverage and differences across pollsters and specific 100-day measurement dates.

claim: "Jurisdictions representing about 80% of WI residents have passed referendums or resolutions in favor of fair maps."
rationale: This claim overstates the available evidence. While hundreds of Wisconsin localities passed advisory referendums or resolutions supporting fair maps, those actions were mainly in smaller jurisdictions and do not clearly add up to jurisdictions representing about 80% of the state's population. Public reporting and advocacy tallies showed broad geographic activity but did not substantiatively demonstrate population coverage at the 80% level without a detailed population-weighted count.

claim: Mehmet Oz "was a spokesman for a group who wanted to defund the police."
rationale: There is no credible record that Mehmet Oz served as a spokesman for any organization advocating to ‘defund the police.’ Oz is best known as a TV physician, surgeon, author and 2022 Senate candidate, and his public statements and campaign positions have opposed defunding police. The claim appears to mischaracterize or conflate him with someone else or with unrelated advocacy roles he has held.

claim: "Iowa ranks 45th in the U.S. for internet connectivity."
rationale: The claim is too specific but lacks a year or metric; broadband/connectivity rankings vary by measure (coverage, speed, subscription rate). In commonly cited federal and industry reports (FCC, Ookla, state broadband offices) Iowa typically ranks in the middle tiers nationally rather than 45th overall. Without a specified dataset and year, the blanket statement that Iowa is 45th is not supported.

claim: "After a decade of progress, the rate of uninsured children is now rising."
rationale: U.S. data sources documented roughly a decade-long decline in the child uninsured rate through the mid-2010s, and then showed increases beginning around 2017–2018. Thus the characterization that a decade of progress was followed by a rise in uninsured children is supported by those data, though trends have shifted again during the COVID era.

claim: "...the earth moves closer to the sun every year – you know the rotation of the earth. We’re moving closer to the sun."
rationale: False. The Earth does not steadily move closer to the Sun each year and Earth's rotation about its axis does not cause a secular inward spiral. Orbital mechanics and observations show no ongoing inward drift; if anything the Sun’s mass loss causes an extremely small outward drift, and year-to-year changes are dominated by normal seasonal eccentricity (perihelion/aphelion). Any secular change in the semi‑major axis is vanishingly small (centimeters per year) and not a steady inward movement as claimed.

claim: The United States spent "2 trillion dollars to train and equip the Afghan military over the past 20 years. They fell in a week."
rationale: The $2 trillion figure refers to the broad estimated U.S. cost of the Afghanistan war (operations, reconstruction, veterans' care, interest) over two decades, not the amount spent solely to train and equip the Afghan military. Direct U.S. spending to build Afghan security forces was much smaller (generally reported in the tens of billions). While Afghan forces collapsed rapidly during the 2021 Taliban offensive, characterizing the entire security force as having "fell in a week" oversimplifies a multi-week collapse and conflates different events.

claim: The United States has a "record number of abortions year after year after year."
rationale: National abortion totals in the U.S. have not risen to a new record every year; historically totals peaked in the early 1990s and have generally declined or fluctuated since then. Recent years show variability and state-level shifts (especially after 2022) but do not support a continuous year-after-year national record increase.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccine is the "deadliest vaccine ever made."
rationale: This claim is not supported by evidence. Extensive clinical trials and global safety monitoring show COVID-19 vaccines have rare serious adverse events and have prevented large numbers of deaths; passive-reporting systems (e.g., VAERS) include unverified reports and do not demonstrate causation. There is no credible data showing COVID-19 vaccines have caused more deaths than historical vaccines (such as early smallpox campaigns) or are the “deadliest” ever made.

claim: Says that singer Dolly Parton said, "Trump in one year is already better than 16 years of Bush, Obama put together."
rationale: There is no credible primary-source evidence that Dolly Parton ever said this; the quote circulated on social media and was debunked by fact-checkers. Parton has generally avoided political endorsements and no reputable interviews or transcripts include that line.

claim: Says he did not tell former President Barack Obama "don’t go" after Osama bin Laden
rationale: The claim as written is ambiguous about who “he” refers to and I cannot find a verifiable, attributed statement matching this precise formulation. Public accounts indicate President Obama authorized the raid that killed Osama bin Laden after advice from his national security team, but there is no clear, attributable record of a specific individual publicly saying they told Obama “don’t go” or explicitly denying having done so in that phrasing. Because the subject is unspecified and the phrasing is unsupported by clear public reporting, the claim is not verifiable as stated.

claim: "Farouk is on fire."
rationale: The claim provides no context (who, when, where) and there is no independent evidence available to confirm that a person named Farouk is literally on fire. It could be metaphorical (praising performance) or an unverified allegation; without corroborating reports or sources it cannot be treated as true. Standard verification requires specific, contemporaneous evidence which is absent here.

claim: "The government does not need a warrant to read your old emails."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. In the United States the law is mixed but many courts and DOJ policy require a warrant (probable cause) to access the content of emails stored with providers, though older practices under the Stored Communications Act allowed subpoenas or 2703(d) orders for some older messages and lower standards have been applied in some circuits. Thus it is not true as an absolute statement that the government does not need a warrant to read your old emails.

claim: "Scott Walker gave Wisconsin job creation money to his cronies: corporate friends who contributed to his campaigns" and got $570 million in job-development incentives
rationale: The claim asserts that Governor Scott Walker steered Wisconsin job‑creation money specifically to campaign donors and that those donors received $570 million in job‑development incentives. While reporting and audits have found that some companies that received state incentives also gave to Walker or allied groups, independent fact‑checks and news analyses did not establish a direct quid‑pro‑quo or a definitive, documented $570 million figure tied solely to Walker’s donors. The allegation conflates correlation (donors among incentive recipients) with proven causation and appears to misstate or oversimplify the total amount and scope of incentive programs.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "was literally present when we pressed the reset button with Russia just a few months after Russia had invaded Georgia."
rationale: Hillary Clinton, as U.S. Secretary of State, was physically present and participated in the well‑known January 2009 photo op with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov pressing a symbolic “reset” button. That event took place about five months after Russia’s August 2008 invasion of Georgia, so describing her as “literally present when we pressed the reset button… a few months after” the invasion is accurate.

claim: Says he "sued Obama’s EPA seven times."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it omits who “he” is; without identifying the person, I cannot confirm that any individual sued the EPA during the Obama administration exactly seven times. While many entities and individuals filed multiple suits against EPA policies from 2009–2017, public court records would be needed to substantiate a specific count for a named plaintiff. Because the claim lacks that critical context, I treat it as not proven.

claim: "I had prostate cancer, five, six years ago. My chance of surviving prostate cancer, and thank God I was cured of it, in the United States, 82%. My chances of surviving prostate cancer in England, only 44% under socialized medicine."
rationale: The specific numbers in the claim are inaccurate and misleading. National cancer registry and peer-reviewed data show five-year prostate cancer survival is very high in both countries (the U.S. 5‑year survival is near universal in modern series and England's 5‑year net survival is much higher than 44%), and differences are largely due to screening, stage at diagnosis and methodology, not a halving of survival under UK healthcare.

claim: "Our debt to GDP ratios, our deficit to GDP ratios are quickly approaching the countries we have been reading about for the last year and a half. We are not far behind Ireland, Greece, Portugal and Spain and all these countries we have been reading about."
rationale: The claim is misleading: during the euro-area crisis the cited countries (especially Greece) had much higher debt-to-GDP and, at times, much larger spike deficits driven by banking rescues than the United States. While U.S. deficits rose after 2008, U.S. debt and deficit ratios were not “quickly approaching” the extreme levels seen in Greece and in Ireland at the height of their banking-bailout years, and Spain’s and Portugal’s trajectories differed as well. Without a specific year or metric the blanket comparison overstates the closeness.

claim: "I negotiated open borders to let fleeing refugees into safety from Kosovo."
rationale: The claim names no identified speaker and asserts a personal role in negotiating “open borders” for Kosovo refugees. Historical records show the 1998–99 Kosovo refugee crisis was handled by national governments, NATO, the UN and neighboring states (Albania, Macedonia, etc.), not by a single individual who unilaterally ‘negotiated open borders.’ Without a named person and corroborating evidence that that person played such a decisive, documented role, the claim is not supported.

claim: In Liberia, "a girl is more likely to be married by 18 than to know how to read."
rationale: Available population data indicate that a higher share of Liberian girls/young women can read than are married before 18. National survey and UNESCO-derived youth female literacy estimates for Liberia are substantially higher than reported child marriage prevalence, so the statement overstated the prevalence of early marriage relative to reading ability.

claim: Aaron Bean voted to give illegal immigrants in-state tuition.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Aaron Bean cast a vote specifically to grant undocumented ("illegal") immigrants blanket in‑state tuition; public records and reporting do not show him sponsoring or voting for a bill that explicitly provides automatic in‑state tuition for undocumented residents. Bean has generally taken conservative positions on immigration, and Florida’s tuition rules for undocumented students have been the subject of separate, specific bills rather than a single broad vote that he approved. Given the ambiguity about which bill and which legislative body/timeframe the claim refers to, the assertion as stated is not supported.

claim: "Seattle police begin gun confiscations: no laws broken, no warrant, no charges."
rationale: The claim that Seattle police have begun blanket gun confiscations with no laws broken, no warrants, and no charges is false or misleading. Under U.S. and Washington law, officers generally need a warrant, court order (such as an ERPO), an arrest, or an exigent-circumstances justification to seize firearms, and there are no verified reports of a lawful citywide program authorizing unrestricted, warrantless seizures without legal process. Such actions would be subject to immediate legal challenge and public reporting, which is not supported by reliable accounts.

claim: Says Nevada Gov. Steve Sisolak "has banned the use of an anti-malaria drug that might help cure coronavirus."
rationale: There is no evidence that Nevada Gov. Steve Sisolak issued a statewide ban on the anti-malarial drugs (chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine) for COVID-19. Early in the pandemic some jurisdictions and hospitals limited or regulated use, and the FDA briefly issued an EUA then later revoked it, but Nevada did not enact an outright ban prohibiting use. The claim therefore overstates and mischaracterizes policy action.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton dressed up in blackface.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton ever dressed in blackface. Major fact-checkers and news organizations have investigated such rumors and found no photos, admissions, or reliable reports to support the claim; it appears to be a baseless rumor.

claim: Says a video captures sound from the surface of Mars
rationale: NASA missions have returned authentic audio recorded on Mars and released videos containing that sound. Perseverance (and earlier InSight/rovers) carried microphones and NASA published clips of wind, rover operations and flight noise from the Martian surface, so a video can legitimately capture sound from Mars.

claim: Says that under order from Gov. Tony Evers, he and his eight children can’t legally have dinner together anymore.
rationale: There is no evidence that Governor Tony Evers issued an order specifically preventing him and his children from having dinner together. Pandemic-era public-health orders in Wisconsin limited certain gatherings but did not single out an individual or expressly ban family members from dining together, and emergency orders apply broadly rather than to named people. The claim therefore misrepresents how such orders worked and appears to be false.

claim: "Seventy percent of the people living in abject poverty are women."
rationale: The claim that 70% of people in abject/extreme poverty are women is not supported by reliable global data. Major sources (World Bank, UN analyses and independent fact-checks) show no consistent global figure anywhere near 70%; gender disparities in poverty vary by country, measure, and whether poverty is counted at the individual or household level. While women are often disproportionately vulnerable to poverty, the specific 70% statistic is an exaggeration or misinterpretation.

claim: The fiscal cliff agreement was "the largest tax increase in history."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. The 2012–13 "fiscal cliff" changes (expiration of some Bush-era cuts, end of the payroll-tax holiday, new Medicare taxes) raised revenue but were far smaller than major historical U.S. tax increases such as World War II-era revenue acts and other large postwar tax hikes; CBO and Treasury estimates put the fiscal-cliff revenue effects in the hundreds of billions over years, not the largest-ever in nominal or GDP terms. Some political statements framed it as the "largest" for rhetorical effect, but that does not match historical revenue or GDP‑share comparisons.

claim: "Since I took office, over 319,000 new private sector jobs have been created in Georgia with nearly 93,000 of those coming in the past 12 months."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated and is likely misleading. Official state and BLS payroll series for Georgia produce different counts depending on the exact start date, seasonal adjustment, and whether ‘private sector’ or total nonfarm jobs are used; public data do not clearly support the precise figures cited without cherry‑picking endpoints. Because the statement omits the exact office start date and source/methodology, the headline numbers are not reliably accurate as presented.

claim: Says Christopher Little has "a history of working against environmental protection by defending the worst types of corporate polluters"
rationale: There is no widely available evidence that a person named Christopher Little has a documented pattern of defending major corporate polluters or working against environmental protections. The name more commonly refers to a literary agent with no public record of environmental-defense litigation, and the specific allegation would require verifiable reporting or legal records that are not present in general knowledge sources.

claim: Says when Rhode Island Lottery was proposed, "state residents were enticed to vote for it with the promise that the money would be used for education."
rationale: When Rhode Island voters approved creation of a state lottery in the mid-1970s, proponents explicitly campaigned that lottery revenues would be used to support public education. The referendum and contemporaneous advocacy framed the lottery as a way to raise funds for schools, making the claim accurate about the original promise used to entice voters.

claim: "MSNBC actually said on air ‘I hope enough people die from coronavirus that it harms Trump’s re-election.’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that an MSNBC host or guest uttered that exact line on air; fact-checkers and available broadcast transcripts/recordings do not substantiate the quote and the viral clips were found to be misattributed or taken out of context. The claim appears to be a fabricated or edited quote circulated on social media rather than a verifiable MSNBC on-air statement.

claim: Gov. McDonnell's proposed budget "is cutting" public education.
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated: it gives no year, which Gov. McDonnell, or which parts of 'public education' are alleged to be cut. Budget proposals can include cuts, freezes, or reallocations and often change during negotiation, so a blanket present-tense statement cannot be confirmed without specifics. Because the assertion lacks necessary context, it cannot be judged factually correct as written.

claim: "Italy drastically reduced the country’s official COV1D-19 death count by over 97%. This means Covid killed fewer people than an average seasonal flu."
rationale: This claim misstates and conflates facts. Italy did not “reduce” its official COVID-19 death count by over 97%; what circulated was a misinterpretation of an Italian health institute analysis showing only a small share of COVID‑19 death certificates listed COVID as the sole cause (around 2–3%), not that 97% of recorded deaths were erased. COVID-19 deaths in Italy remained far higher than a typical seasonal flu when measured by total excess mortality and official COVID death counts over 2020–2021.

claim: The "pay-as-you-go law ... was a big reason why we had record surpluses in the 1990s."
rationale: PAYGO (the statutory pay-as-you-go rules from the early 1990s) likely helped limit un-offset mandatory changes, but it was not the primary cause of the 1990s federal budget surpluses. The surpluses mainly reflected a strong economic expansion and booming capital gains revenues, the 1993 deficit-reduction tax and spending measures, discretionary spending caps and other budget deals, and Social Security surpluses. Saying PAYGO was a "big reason" overstates its role relative to those larger macroeconomic and policy drivers.

claim: "The Democrat controlled House never even asked John Bolton to testify."
rationale: This is false. During the 2019 impeachment inquiry, House Democrats formally requested John Bolton's testimony (seeking voluntary interviews) and when he did not appear they issued a subpoena in October 2019 for his testimony and documents, though his counsel resisted citing DOJ review and privilege concerns. Public committee actions and the subsequent subpoena show Democrats did in fact ask him to testify.

claim: "War for the soul of the TxDems: 57% of Dem incumbents for Tx House LOST their primary."
rationale: This claim is almost certainly false: it would mean a majority of Texas House Democratic incumbents were defeated in a single primary cycle, an outcome that would have been unprecedented and widely reported. Available knowledge through mid‑2024 shows only a small number of Democratic incumbents in Texas lost primary contests, not over half.

claim: The Democratic health care plan is a "government takeover of our health programs."
rationale: This is a political slogan, not an accurate description of enacted Democratic health legislation. Major Democratic-led reforms such as the Affordable Care Act kept private insurance, providers, and employer coverage in place while expanding subsidies and Medicaid; they did not nationalize or take over existing private health programs. While some Democrats advocate for single-payer proposals that would create a government-run system, those proposals have not been enacted as law.

claim: "Measles is one of the most common causes of child blindness worldwide."
rationale: Measles is a major cause of corneal scarring and blindness in children, particularly in low-income settings and areas with vitamin A deficiency, and has historically been one of the leading causes of childhood blindness worldwide. Large-scale measles vaccination programs have reduced its role in many regions, but where coverage is low it remains a common cause of child blindness.

claim: Says the percentage of officers the Chicago Police Board fired after hearing their cases or who chose to resign prior to a board hearing roughly doubled during her tenure.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits who “her” refers to and the precise time period and baseline used to compute the percentage change. Public reporting on Chicago Police Board outcomes shows fluctuations in firing/resignation rates over time, but I could not confirm a clear, roughly twofold increase tied to a specific individual’s tenure. Without a named person, dates, and the underlying data, the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: "Sotomayor has had her rulings thrown out by the court a troubling four times."
rationale: The claim gives a precise count — that Sotomayor has had her rulings “thrown out” four times — but there is no authoritative record that supports that exact number. It is ambiguous whether the statement means reversals by the U.S. Supreme Court, en banc reversals on the Second Circuit, or other vacaturs, and publicly available reversal counts for Sotomayor do not cleanly match the asserted figure. Because the phrase and timeframe are undefined and the count is not verifiable, the claim is misleading.

claim: "Greenland's ice sheet isn't shrinking any more rapidly today than it was 80 years ago."
rationale: Multiple independent lines of evidence show Greenland's ice sheet is losing mass and that the rate has accelerated since the late 20th century. Satellite gravimetry (GRACE), altimetry, and mass-balance studies report much larger annual mass losses today than reconstructions of the 1940s, so the claim that it isn't shrinking more rapidly now is incorrect.

claim: Says the mayor’s job "is to make sure that if somebody is trying to build a set of water treatment plants to cure us from cryptosporidium we don’t have, we don't say yes even if CH2M Hill wants us to."
rationale: This is a specific quoted statement attributed to 'the mayor,' but no source, date, or jurisdiction is provided, and I cannot verify that any mayor uttered these exact words. The content is plausible (references CH2M Hill and cryptosporidium) but without a cited source the claim cannot be confirmed as factual. Because verification is not possible from the claim alone, I rate it as false (unverified).

claim: Says the Republican "state convention is actually larger than the Republican National Convention."
rationale: False. The Republican National Convention draws delegates from all 50 states, territories, party officials, media, and guests and therefore has a larger official delegate roll and overall attendance than any single state party convention, which is limited to participants from one state. The claim is misleading without specifying a particular state or metric of "larger."

claim: "President Trump has lifted the prospect of voters across Vermont, overseeing a 11,742 decline of Vermont residents on food stamps."
rationale: The claim is misleading and unsubstantiated: the phrasing "lifted the prospect of voters across Vermont" is incoherent and there is no clear evidence that President Trump directly "oversaw" a specific 11,742-person decline in Vermont SNAP recipients. SNAP enrollment numbers fluctuate for many reasons (economic conditions, state program rules, pandemic-era changes) and no authoritative data attributes that exact decline to actions by Trump. Without a clear timeframe or source, the numeric and causal assertions cannot be verified.

claim: "In New Jersey, Gov. Christie vetoed legislation to extend early voting."
rationale: I found no clear evidence that Gov. Chris Christie vetoed legislation to extend early (in-person) voting in New Jersey. Major changes expanding early voting in New Jersey were enacted after Christie left office and were signed by his successor, Phil Murphy. While Christie did veto other election-related measures during his tenure, the record does not show a high-profile veto specifically blocking an early-voting expansion.

claim: During Lyndon B. Johnson’s first 20 years in Congress, "he opposed every civil rights measure that came up for a vote."
rationale: False. While Lyndon B. Johnson often sided with Southern Democrats and opposed or equivocated on several early federal civil‑rights proposals, he did not oppose every civil‑rights measure; notably he helped shepherd and voted for the 1957 Civil Rights Act as Senate Majority Leader and his record includes some votes in favor of federal measures. His record in his first two decades in Congress is best described as mixed rather than uniformly oppositional.

claim: Black cats in Vietnam are being killed and consumed as a COVID-19 cure.
rationale: Multiple independent fact-checks and mainstream news reports found no credible evidence that black cats in Vietnam are being killed and eaten as a COVID-19 cure. The claim appears to originate from social-media rumors and misinterpretations; Vietnamese authorities and animal-welfare groups did not corroborate any large-scale culling tied to COVID-19. While cat meat is eaten by some people in parts of Vietnam as a separate cultural practice, that is unrelated to a verified COVID-19 ‘cure’ campaign.

claim: "Boy passes Joe Biden a vial of fresh blood to drink on his way back to the White House"
rationale: There is no credible evidence, video, or reputable reporting that President Biden was handed or drank a vial of fresh blood; such an event would have been widely documented and contradicted by White House security and medical protocols. The claim matches patterns of sensational misinformation and conspiratorial rumors rather than verifiable fact.

claim: Says the case of a Texas judge who refused to perform heterosexual weddings exposes a double standard in the case against Kentucky clerk Kim Davis.
rationale: There is no verifiable, well-documented case of a Texas judge who refused to perform only heterosexual weddings that was used to expose a double standard in Kim Davis’s prosecution. The widely reported dispute concerned Kentucky clerk Kim Davis refusing to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples after Obergefell; while commentators compared various officials’ refusals of duties, credible reporting does not support the specific Texas-judge-heterosexual-weddings example as described. Therefore the claim is misleading or false as stated.

claim: "We have one senator who’s a ‘yes’ vote ... but he’s in the hospital. And he’s a ‘yes’ vote. So we can’t do it by Friday. So we have the votes" to pass a health care bill.
rationale: This claim cannot be verified as stated because it gives no date, bill name, or senator identity and I find no record of this exact statement tied to a specific, verifiable event. Without those crucial details the assertion is unsubstantiated and cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: The Democrats’ Green New Deal includes "working towards ending air travel."
rationale: The official 2019 Green New Deal resolution introduced by Rep. Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Markey does not include language about "ending air travel." It calls for transitioning to net-zero emissions, upgrading transportation infrastructure, and investing in zero-emission technologies and high-speed rail, but it does not mandate stopping air travel. Claims that it explicitly seeks to end flying misrepresent the resolution and conflate some advocates' ideas about reducing aviation emissions with the text itself.

claim: Hillary Clinton advocates "a freeze on foreclosures. Barack Obama said no."
rationale: The claim presents a simple binary contrast that is misleading. Hillary Clinton campaigned for stronger homeowner relief and mortgage modification programs and at times supported temporary or targeted pauses in some foreclosures, but she did not consistently call for a blanket, permanent "freeze on foreclosures." Barack Obama opposed a broad, across-the-board moratorium in 2008 and advocated targeted assistance and modification programs instead, so the claim overstates and simplifies both positions.

claim: Says a "Pro-Stimulus economist admits it is not working … "
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify — it asserts that a specific 'pro-stimulus economist' has admitted the policy 'is not working' but gives no name, quote, timing, or context. Without an identifiable source or direct quotation this claim cannot be corroborated and could be a misattribution or selective excerpt. Therefore it should be treated as false until a specific, verifiable instance is provided.

claim: "We are almost halfway to our goal of 1,000 rapes prosecuted!"
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as written: it names no actor, timeframe, or source for the count, and there is no publicly verifiable record provided showing that nearly 500 rapes have been prosecuted toward a stated goal of 1,000. Without specific, independently verifiable data tying the speaker to that prosecution count, the claim cannot be supported and is therefore rated false.

claim: "Our children do not spend any time in school learning about our own U.S. Constitution."
rationale: The claim is false as a blanket statement. U.S. K–12 curricula commonly include the Constitution in elementary social studies and in required middle- and high-school civics, U.S. history, or government courses, so most students receive at least some instruction about the Constitution. Depth and hours vary by state and district, but it is inaccurate to say children spend no time learning about it.

claim: Says Amazon is "paying full-time employees so little that they require gov food assistance."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. While some Amazon full‑time workers earn low enough household incomes that they may qualify for government food assistance (SNAP) in certain areas and family situations, many full‑time roles at Amazon pay at or above the company’s $15/hour minimum and include benefits, so it is not accurate to say Amazon is paying full‑time employees so little that they require government food assistance as a blanket statement. Whether an individual qualifies for assistance depends on job, hours, household size, and local cost of living.

claim: Says Thai police found bodies of children with their organs removed.
rationale: This specific allegation is false or unverified: there are no credible news reports or official Thai police statements confirming that bodies of children with organs removed were discovered. Variants of this claim have circulated before and have been debunked; images and reports are often misattributed or recycled from other contexts.

claim: "The Obama administration has even joined Islamist governments in sponsoring a U.N. resolution that would shred our First Amendment by threatening to make discussion of radical Islamism potentially illegal."
rationale: This claim is false. While the Obama administration did engage at the UN on issues of religious tolerance and supported the 2010 HRC effort (Resolution 16/18) to combat intolerance and incitement, that initiative emphasized protecting freedom of expression and targeted incitement to violence rather than criminalizing discussion of beliefs. UN resolutions are non‑binding and cannot nullify the U.S. Constitution; there is no credible evidence the U.S. co‑sponsored a UN measure that would legally forbid discussion of radical Islam or “shred” the First Amendment.

claim: "Coca-Cola has lost $4 bil in market value as people are boycotting Coke for their ‘try to be less White’ statement."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Coca-Cola permanently lost $4 billion in market value specifically because of a boycott over the alleged ‘try to be less White’ statement. Market capitalization fluctuates daily and fact-checking by major outlets found the viral claim misattributes normal stock movement and lacks a causal link to a coordinated boycott; Coca-Cola’s stock did not show a sustained $4 billion drop tied to that incident.

claim: Says Sen. Rand Paul’s 2011 budget "included a big cut in the CDC."
rationale: There is no clear record that Sen. Rand Paul authored a 2011 federal budget proposal that included a large cut to the CDC. The formal federal budget proposals that year were authored by House and White House leadership (e.g., Paul Ryan/Obama), and Rand Paul was a freshman senator in 2011 and did not put forward a widely recognized budget document cutting the CDC by a large amount. Claims tying a specific 2011 ‘big cut’ to a Rand Paul budget appear to conflate other budget debates or later positions.

claim: St. Pete Beach's local version of Amendment 4 resulted in "seemingly endless lawsuits (that) decimated the city's legal budget and forced the city to raise the property tax rate."
rationale: While St. Pete Beach did face legal challenges over a local ballot measure (often described in reporting about short‑term rental regulations), available reporting does not support the strong causal claim that those lawsuits “decimated” the city’s legal budget or were the sole reason the city raised its property tax rate. Legal costs increased, but municipal budget changes and tax decisions involve multiple factors and the phraseology is hyperbolic and unsupported by documented budgetary figures attributing the tax increase solely to litigation.

claim: The "3 red stripes" in Joe Biden’s campaign logo refer to a Chinese socialist slogan.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Biden campaign intended the three red stripes to reference a Chinese socialist slogan. The stripes are a common, flag-like design element used to evoke the American flag and unity; the social-media claim appears to conflate them with Mao-era 'Three Red Banners' without supporting documentation from the campaign or designers.

claim: Says Sara Gideon "voted to defund" the Freeport police "and gave the money to a nonprofit she helped run."
rationale: This is a misleading claim. Independent fact-checks and public records show Gideon did not vote to 'defund' the Freeport police nor personally direct municipal police funds to a nonprofit she ran; the episode being cited involved local budget decisions and state grant/administration contexts that were mischaracterized by opponents. There is no evidence she voted as an official to cut Freeport's police budget and then gave those specific funds to a nonprofit she helped run.

claim: "After one year, Tennessee’s students made their biggest single-year jump in achievement ever recorded in the state."
rationale: This statement overclaims. Tennessee did report notable single-year increases on certain state assessments in years when tests or standards were changed, but independent measures like NAEP do not show a statewide “biggest ever” single-year jump in overall student achievement. Claims of an all-time record ignore differences in assessments, scaling, and year-to-year comparability that make such an absolute statement unsupported.

claim: "Eight in 10 people this year can find plans for $75 a month or less."
rationale: The claim is misleading and unverified as stated. Similar-sounding statistics have circulated about subsidized ACA marketplace plans, but those refer specifically to people eligible for premium tax credits (and vary by state and year); saying simply “eight in 10 people this year” without specifying eligibility, location, or whether subsidies are applied overstates and mischaracterizes the underlying data.

claim: Says photo shows that Chick-fil-A distributed "Back the Blue" T-shirts to employees in response to recent protests over police brutality.
rationale: The photo has been widely misattributed; independent fact-checkers and news reporting found no credible evidence that Chick‑fil‑A corporate distributed ‘Back the Blue’ T‑shirts company‑wide in response to recent police‑brutality protests. The image’s context was different or unverifiable, and Chick‑fil‑A did not announce a corporate directive to issue such shirts. Therefore the claim that the photo shows a corporate response to the protests is false.

claim: Says that guidance urging vaccinated people to avoid travel and continue wearing masks is "profoundly anti-science."
rationale: The phrasing reports an opinion as if it were an objective fact but provides no attribution or evidence that a specific authority actually said guidance to avoid travel and continue masking was 'profoundly anti-science.' Whether such public-health guidance is 'anti-science' is a subjective judgment; public-health agencies issued travel and masking recommendations based on evolving data to reduce transmission. Without a verifiable speaker and context, the claim is not a confirmed factual statement.

claim: George Soros was an SS officer.
rationale: George Soros was a Jewish child in Hungary during World War II (born 1930) and survived by hiding under an assumed identity arranged by his family and a Hungarian official; there is no credible evidence he served as an SS officer. Multiple independent fact-checks and contemporary records contradict the claim and show he was a teenager during the Nazi occupation, not in a position to be an SS officer.

claim: "All the money the Department of Citrus has is paid for by the citrus growers. You don't save dollars by eliminating the Department of Citrus."
rationale: The claim is too absolute. In practice agencies called a “Department of Citrus” (e.g., Florida Department of Citrus) are primarily funded by grower assessments and industry trust funds so most operating dollars come from citrus producers, but they can also receive other sources (federal grants, small state appropriations or recharges) and elimination could impose transition costs or shift obligations to taxpayers. Saying "all" money is paid only by growers and that eliminating it yields no savings ignores those exceptions and the potential fiscal impacts of shutting down an agency.

claim: "Tens and tens of thousands of bridges are in disrepair, some on the verge of collapse."
rationale: U.S. federal and industry assessments in recent years have identified tens of thousands of bridges rated in poor or structurally deficient condition, so the phrasing “tens and tens of thousands...in disrepair” is supported. The claim that some are ‘‘on the verge of collapse’’ is more subjective and rare, but documented high‑risk bridges and occasional failures mean the warning is not baseless.

claim: "USA is #1 in gun violence."
rationale: The claim is too broad and misleading: the United States does not rank #1 globally in gun violence by commonly used measures (per-capita firearm homicide or total firearm deaths). Several countries, particularly in Latin America (e.g., Honduras, El Salvador, Venezuela) have higher firearm homicide rates per 100,000 people, and countries such as Brazil and Mexico often report as many or more total firearm deaths. It is true the U.S. has one of the highest rates among high‑income countries and a large absolute number of firearm deaths, but that does not make it #1 worldwide.

claim: Says Loretta Lynch was part of "a stunning collection of calls to violence and murder from the intolerant, unhinged leftists in the Democrat party."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Loretta Lynch—who served as U.S. Attorney General and has a long public record—called for violence or murder. The allegation appears to be a misattribution or rhetorical hyperbole grouping her with violent calls by unnamed individuals; reputable reporting and Lynch’s public statements do not support such conduct. Without a specific sourced quote, the claim is not substantiated.

claim: There "are 500 registered Republicans moving" to Texas "every day."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that exactly 500 self-identified or registered Republicans move to Texas every single day. Official migration statistics and state voter-registration records do not report a steady daily inflow of that many newly registered Republicans, and migration data are reported monthly or annually and usually do not break down movers by party affiliation in that way. The claim appears to be an unverified, overly specific assertion not supported by public data.

claim: "The 90 percent statistic of supporting background checks, that's been debunked."
rationale: Multiple reputable national polls (Gallup, Pew, AP‑NORC and others) have repeatedly found roughly 85–95% public support for requiring background checks on most gun sales, so the broad "90%" figure is not "debunked." Critics have pointed out that precise percentages vary with question wording and context, but those methodological caveats do not invalidate the core finding of very high support. Thus claiming the 90% statistic has been debunked overstates the critiques.

claim: "American Hustle shows the FBI making real-life bribes to Washington politicians. I know, because as your U.S. senator, I turned them down."
rationale: The statement conflates a fictionalized movie with an unverifiable personal claim. American Hustle is a fictional drama loosely inspired by the real ABSCAM FBI sting (in which undercover agents offered money to some public officials), but the film does not serve as proof of 'real‑life bribes' and the assertion that a named U.S. senator personally 'turned them down' is unsupported and cannot be confirmed from the claim as presented. Without a named senator or evidence, the personal claim is false/unsupported.

claim: Clean energy employs "more than half a million Californians. That’s nearly ten times more the number of coal mining jobs that exist in the entire nation."
rationale: State and industry analyses (e.g., Clean Jobs reports) have reported just over 500,000 clean-energy jobs in California, while BLS and industry data put U.S. coal mining employment at only about 40,000–60,000. That makes California’s clean-energy workforce on the order of ten times the nation’s coal-mining workforce, so the comparison is accurate as stated.

claim: "In Ohio, we invested in our children, raising school funding by 5.5 percent in the last budget."
rationale: The claim is too specific (a 5.5% increase “in the last budget”) but gives no year or definition of ‘school funding,’ and I cannot verify that exact percentage for Ohio’s most recent state budget. Ohio’s K–12 funding has been increased in recent biennial budgets, but reported increases vary by measure (state share, total funding, per-pupil) and by year, and I did not find a definitive, universally reported 5.5% blanket increase. Because the statement asserts a precise figure without clear context and that figure does not match commonly reported summary increases, I judge it false pending a specific budget year and funding definition.

claim: "Twitter reaches only 15 percent of the population."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and does not match available data. In the U.S., surveys (Pew Research) have reported roughly 20–25% of adults using Twitter in recent years, while globally Twitter’s monthly active users have been around a few hundred million—only about 3–5% of the world population—so a flat "15 percent of the population" claim is not accurate without specifying which population or metric. Usage also varies by age, country and timeframe, so a single 15% figure is misleading.

claim: "Did you know that in 2013 over 50 percent of all babies born in Oregon were Hispanic?"
rationale: This is false. Statewide vital statistics and demographic data for Oregon in 2013 show that births to mothers identified as Hispanic were well below 50% (roughly in the mid-20% range), so over half of all babies born in Oregon that year were not Hispanic. Some counties or localities within Oregon may have had majority-Hispanic births, which can cause confusion with the statewide figure.

claim: Sherrod Brown "failed to pay his own taxes three separate times."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Sen. Sherrod Brown repeatedly failed to pay his federal or state income taxes three separate times. Independent fact-checkers and public financial disclosures show no record of tax evasion or multiple tax-payment failures; claims originated in political ads that conflated or overstated isolated, minor or late payments. The charge misrepresents the public record.

claim: A provision of the Senate immigration bill would require you to have government permission to get a second job.
rationale: There is no widely reported provision in recent Senate immigration bills that would force people generally to obtain government permission before taking a second job. Most immigration measures address employer verification (e.g., E‑Verify) or set work‑authorization limits for noncitizen visa holders; those existing visa rules can restrict additional employment for certain noncitizens but do not create a new universal requirement for everyone to get government permission to hold a second job.

claim: Says an arts tax would provide "funding for certified arts and music teachers for every elementary school serving Portland residents."
rationale: The claim is an absolute promise that the tax would fund certified arts and music teachers in every elementary school serving Portland residents. Local arts-tax measures typically allocate funds to districts and eligible schools or programs and specify distribution rules, but they do not legally guarantee a certified arts teacher in every single elementary school (hiring depends on district budgets, staffing availability, and eligibility). Therefore the categorical claim is not supported.

claim: "The State Department asked all secretaries of state to send their emails over." Hillary Clinton's "the only one who’s done it."
rationale: The State Department did ask former secretaries to search for and turn over any work-related emails in private accounts, but it was not simply a blanket order for 'all secretaries to send their emails over' in the literal sense and several other former secretaries were contacted and either produced records or said they had none. Therefore Clinton’s claim that she was 'the only one who’s done it' is inaccurate: other former secretaries were asked and some did provide or confirm the absence of personal work-related emails. The statement conflates different actions and omits that the Department solicited searches of records from multiple predecessors.

claim: "The Austin school district calendar lists 64 different dates for either a state-mandated test or make-up test."
rationale: I could find no evidence that the Austin Independent School District calendar lists 64 distinct calendar dates labeled as “state‑mandated test” or “make‑up test.” Texas state assessments (STAAR, EOC, TELPAS) are typically scheduled within a limited testing window each year and district calendars normally show only a handful of testing and makeup days rather than dozens of unique dates. The claim likely confuses the total number of individual student test administrations across grades/subjects with distinct calendar dates listed publicly.

claim: "There's still about $400 billion or $500 billion of the stimulus plan that has not been spent. Why don't we stop it."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it lacks a time frame and specific program; stimulus legislation totaled about $2.2 trillion (CARES Act) and included many separate pots (direct payments, PPP, unemployment, and a ~$500 billion Treasury corporate lending fund). At various points early in 2020 some large lending-authority balances remained unused, but most direct-aid programs had been largely spent or obligated; claiming presently “about $400–$500 billion … has not been spent” as a blanket fact is not supported without specifying which fund and date. Therefore the claim as stated is not verifiably true.

claim: A photo shows Joe Namath and Al Woodall kneeling on the sideline of a football field during the national anthem.
rationale: The image of Joe Namath and Al Woodall kneeling has circulated, but available evidence indicates the men were not captured protesting the national anthem. Historical photos of players kneeling from earlier eras are typically pregame rituals (prayer, equipment) and have been miscaptioned; there is no reliable documentation that Namath and Woodall kneeled specifically during the anthem as a protest.

claim: The health care law could cost up to $2 trillion, "double what we were promised."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Official budget estimates from the Congressional Budget Office and Joint Committee on Taxation did not show a straightforward “up to $2 trillion” net federal cost for the Affordable Care Act in typical ten‑year scoring windows, and in several official estimates the law reduced the federal deficit or had much smaller net costs; comparisons also depend on whether one counts gross spending, subsidies, Medicaid expansion, or net budget impact. Saying it is “double what we were promised” is vague because different actors made different promises and the time period and accounting method are unspecified.

claim: Says President Barack Obama has opened up no new trade relationships with other nations.
rationale: This is false. The Obama administration negotiated and implemented several new trade relationships, including the Korea–US Free Trade Agreement entering into force in 2012 and ratification/implementation of trade pacts with Colombia and Panama, and it led U.S. negotiation of the Trans-Pacific Partnership. The administration also re-engaged economically with Cuba and expanded commercial ties with other countries, so it did open new trade relationships.

claim: The U.S. spends "57 cents on the dollar on defense."
rationale: The claim as stated is misleading because it gives no context for which “dollar” is meant. Defense comprises roughly half to a bit more of federal discretionary spending in some years (so ~50–60 cents of a discretionary dollar), but it is only about 10–15 cents of every total federal dollar when mandatory spending and interest are included. Without specifying year and whether the comparison is to discretionary spending or total federal outlays, the blanket statement is incorrect.

claim: "At the moment, energy companies spend 0.25 percent on R&D."
rationale: The statement is overly precise and lacks context (percent of revenue, profit, or something else) and is not true across the broad category 'energy companies.' R&D intensity varies substantially by subsector and company—some oil and gas firms have historically reported R&D around a few tenths of a percent of sales while utilities and renewables or technology-focused energy firms often spend a higher share—so a blanket figure of 0.25% is inaccurate.

claim: "A family of four can make up to $88,000 a year and still get a subsidy for health insurance" under the new federal health care law.
rationale: Under the Affordable Care Act, premium tax-credit subsidies are available to households with incomes up to 400% of the federal poverty level (FPL). For a family of four, 400% of the FPL is roughly in the $ eighty-thousand range (about $88,000 using the FPL levels around 2010 when the law was enacted), so a family of four making up to about $88,000 could qualify for a subsidy. The exact dollar cutoff shifts each year as the FPL is updated and depends on household size and state rules.

claim: "Chris Christie has led New Jersey to a record-breaking 9 credit downgrades."
rationale: This claim is not supported by public records: while New Jersey did experience some credit downgrades during Chris Christie’s governorship, there is no evidence he presided over a ‘‘record-breaking’’ nine state credit downgrades. Major rating actions by the big agencies during his tenure number far fewer, and the state’s rating history includes downgrades both before and after his term.

claim: "A Gallup report recently said that nearly 50 percent of small business owners aren't hiring because of what they call ‘regulatory uncertainty.’"
rationale: There is no known recent Gallup report stating that nearly 50% of small business owners aren’t hiring because of 'regulatory uncertainty.' Gallup’s small-business polling typically finds other factors (difficulty finding qualified workers, low demand, costs/taxes) as the main hiring impediments, and regulation is usually cited by a much smaller share. The claim appears to misattribute or exaggerate findings from other surveys or reframe different survey questions to reach the 50% figure.

claim: "In North Carolina, they used stimulus money to hire one new state worker. His job, apply for more stimulus funds from the taxpayers by the way of the federal government."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that North Carolina used stimulus funds to hire a single new state worker whose sole job was to apply for more federal stimulus money. States routinely fund grant-management positions with federal or recovery funds to administer and comply with grants, and reporting on similar claims found this is an overstatement and mischaracterization of ordinary administrative hires. The claim collapses routine grant-administration work into a sensational single-person narrative.

claim: "If you printed a $1 bill for the entirety of the $14.1 trillion national debt, the resulting pile of money would weigh more than 136 aircraft carriers."
rationale: A US dollar bill weighs about 1 gram, so $14.1 trillion in $1 bills would weigh roughly 14.1 billion kilograms (≈14.1 million metric tons). A Nimitz‑class aircraft carrier displaces on the order of 100,000 tons (≈100 million kg), so the pile of bills would be on the order of 140 carriers—greater than 136. The claim is consistent under these common assumptions and unit conversions.

claim: Says the 2008 book "End of Days" predicted the current coronavirus outbreak.
