rationale: There is no consensus “study after study” showing a universal $3,000 per‑year savings for the average middle‑class family under Medicare for All. Different analyses produce widely varying results depending on what costs are counted (premiums, payroll/tax increases, out‑of‑pocket spending) and on design assumptions; some advocacy studies estimate large household savings but independent and nonpartisan analyses often find smaller net savings or increased costs for some households. The specific, repeatable $3,000 figure is not established across the body of peer‑reviewed, nonpartisan research.

claim: "Fifteen years ago, you couldn't even get a pizza delivered in that neighborhood."
rationale: The statement is an absolute, time‑bound claim about an unspecified neighborhood and presents no evidence. Pizza delivery availability varies by city, neighborhood, and time, and proving a complete absence 15 years ago would require local business records or contemporaneous testimony; lacking that, the claim is not verifiable and reads as hyperbole.

claim: "The KKK officially endorses Trump 2020."
rationale: The Ku Klux Klan is a fragmented set of organizations with no single central authority, and there was no widely recognized, formal national KKK endorsement of Donald Trump in 2020. While some Klan members, local chapters, and other white supremacist groups publicly expressed support for Trump, that is not the same as an official, unified endorsement by “the KKK.”

claim: Says that under the law, New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio "can’t open" the city’s schools.
rationale: This claim is misleading. The NYC mayor has statutory authority over the City’s Department of Education (mayoral control) and appoints the schools chancellor, so he is not categorically unable to order schools open; however his authority is constrained by state law, state public-health emergency powers, and applicable union contracts and health regulations which could prevent or limit reopening. Saying he “can’t open” schools as an absolute legal fact ignores those nuances.

claim: The Texas abortion law "provides at least six weeks for a person to be able to get an abortion."
rationale: Texas's law (the so-called "heartbeat"/SB8 law) prohibits abortion once fetal cardiac activity is detectable, which is often around six weeks. It does not guarantee that a person will have at least six weeks to obtain an abortion—many people do not know they are pregnant by six weeks and the law takes effect upon detection—and it contains very limited exceptions (no rape/incest exceptions).

claim: Says President Barack Obama failed "to stand up for the bipartisan debt solutions of the Simpson-Bowles Commission."
rationale: The Simpson-Bowles commission produced a bipartisan deficit-reduction package in 2010, and President Obama convened the commission but did not formally endorse its final report or lead a push to adopt its comprehensive recommendations. He embraced some principles but rejected or declined to champion key parts of the commission’s package, and Congress never enacted the full plan. Saying he “failed to stand up for” those bipartisan solutions is a fair characterization of his actions.

claim: Proposed fast-track legislation allows presidents to "easily use a future trade deal to override our domestic financial rules."
rationale: This overstates what fast‑track (trade promotion) authority does. Fast‑track procedures expedite Congressional consideration and bar amendments, but they do not give the president unilateral power to change or "override" existing domestic financial laws — Congress still must enact any implementing legislation or can reject an agreement. While international trade agreements can constrain future policy and be enforced through dispute settlement, that is not the same as the president being able to easily override U.S. domestic rules on his own.

claim: "Half of all CEOs say that the shutdown and the threat of shutdown set back their plans to hire over the next six months."
rationale: I could not find credible evidence from major, representative CEO surveys supporting the specific claim that "half of all CEOs" said the shutdown (and its threat) set back their hiring plans over the next six months. Publicly available Business Roundtable, CEO surveys, and press coverage of government shutdowns have reported mixed impacts and lower shares; without a cited, representative poll this exact 50% figure is unsupported. The statement therefore appears to overstate and misrepresent available survey results.

claim: At this point in 2012, "Rick Perry was ahead at 29.9 percent, and we had seven more leads before it finally settled on Mitt Romney."
rationale: The claim mixes a plausible detail with an incorrect aggregate. Rick Perry did briefly surge to roughly 29–30% in some national GOP polls in late 2011, but the statement that “we had seven more leads before it finally settled on Mitt Romney” is misleading: far fewer distinct candidates held sustained leads in national 2012 Republican polling before Romney became the nominee. The phrase is vague about which polls or time window are being counted and overstates the number of different leaders.

claim: "The House has never failed to pass a budget in the modern era."
rationale: This is false. The U.S. House of Representatives has failed to complete the full appropriations/budget process on multiple occasions in recent decades, leading to continuing resolutions and government shutdowns (notably 1995–96, 2013 and 2018–2019). The claim ignores well-documented instances where Congress did not enact regular appropriations and the House did not produce a final enacted budget package in time.

claim: "In sanctuary cities, local officials order police to release dangerous criminal aliens to prey upon the public instead of handing them over to ICE to be safely removed."
rationale: The claim is a broad, misleading generalization. ‘Sanctuary’ policies vary by jurisdiction and typically limit compliance with civil ICE detainers absent a judicial warrant or probable cause; they are framed around legal and resource concerns, not directives to ‘‘release’’ people so they can ‘‘prey upon the public.’’ While there have been individual cases where noncitizens released without ICE holds later committed crimes, that does not support the assertion that local officials intentionally order police to free dangerous offenders to harm the public.

claim: "Trump just gave a $12 billion bailout to farmers hurt by his failed tariffs. This will cost every household in the U.S. $95 … Trump is borrowing the money from China since his tax cuts blew a trillion dollar hole in the deficit."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate and inaccurate elements. The Trump administration did announce about $12 billion in aid to farmers hurt by tariffs, and $12 billion divided by roughly 128 million U.S. households is on the order of $90–95 per household. However, the statement that “Trump is borrowing the money from China” is misleading: the Treasury finances deficits by issuing securities to many investors and you cannot attribute a specific program’s borrowing to China. The tax cuts did increase projected deficits (roughly $1–1.5 trillion over a decade), but that does not mean this bailout was directly funded by China.

claim: "832,000 people lost their job while (Charlie Crist was) governor."
rationale: The claim asserts a precise count (832,000) of people who lost jobs during Charlie Crist’s governorship (2007–2011) but provides no sourcing and the exact figure is not supported by standard employment series. Employment losses in Florida during the Great Recession were large, but totals vary by data source (payroll vs. household survey) and by the exact start/end months; no authoritative series cleanly corroborates the specific 832,000 number without additional context. Thus the precise claim is misleading or unsubstantiated.

claim: "One thousand people a day are moving to Texas, which means there will be 15 million more people over the next 25 years."
rationale: The arithmetic is incorrect: 1,000 people per day × 365 days × 25 years = about 9.125 million people, not 15 million. In addition, the claim assumes a constant gross inflow and ignores departures, births, deaths and likely changes in migration rates, so the projected 15 million figure is unsupported.

claim: "We raised the minimum wage to $15 first in city government. Now, working together with people in Albany, it's the law of the state."
rationale: The statement overstates the chronology and causal claim. Multiple cities (for example Seattle and others) adopted $15-or-near-$15 minimums before state-level laws, and New York State’s $15 policy was enacted via statewide legislation and compromise in 2016 with phased-in regional rates rather than simply following a single city’s prior unilateral $15 wage. Without naming a specific city or timeline the claim that “we” first raised it to $15 in city government and then made it state law is misleading.

claim: Foxconn hasn't hit job targets on its massive Wisconsin factory because "No. 1, you had a pandemic."
rationale: The pandemic did disrupt construction and hiring, but it is not the primary or sole reason Foxconn fell far short of its Wisconsin job promises. Foxconn had already curtailed its original plans, reduced its job and investment targets, and shifted strategy before COVID‑19, and state audits and reporting attribute shortfalls to company decisions, market changes and scaling back rather than only the pandemic. Therefore saying the missed targets are explained chiefly by “you had a pandemic” is misleading.

claim: A DeKalb sewer project "will create up to 4,000 direct jobs per year at peak production, many of which will be set aside exclusively for DeKalb residents."
rationale: This claim appears unsupported as stated. Large infrastructure press releases often report optimistic counts (e.g., 'up to' numbers) that mix short-term job-years, indirect jobs, and peak-period roles; a sewer project producing 4,000 sustained direct jobs at peak is unusually high. Likewise, public contracts typically include hiring preferences, goals, or training programs for local residents rather than legally binding exclusive set‑asides for residents only.

claim: Since 2009, "after-tax incomes are up nearly 14 percent."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits the end year, the population (households, families, individuals), and whether figures are inflation‑adjusted or pre/post taxes. Different official measures (Census median household income, BEA disposable personal income, CBO after‑tax income by quintile) show differing percent changes since 2009, so a blanket “up nearly 14 percent” claim cannot be confirmed without specifying the dataset and timeframe. Given the ambiguity and variation across sources, the claim as stated is misleading.

claim: "Health care premiums up 90 percent in New Hampshire."
rationale: The claim is presented without a time period or which market (individual, small-group, employer-sponsored) and is therefore misleading; there is no evidence that statewide health insurance premiums in New Hampshire rose 90% as a general fact. While some specific plans or counties in particular years can experience very large increases when insurers enter/exit markets or change product offerings, aggregated statewide averages reported by regulators and fact-checkers do not show a uniform 90% increase.

claim: Says Republican lieutenants to House Speaker Joe Straus "aired radio ads supporting Democrat(ic state Rep.) Mark Homer... helping the Democrat to a narrow win."
rationale: I find no credible evidence that "Republican lieutenants to House Speaker Joe Straus" ran radio ads explicitly supporting Democratic state Rep. Mark Homer and thereby produced his narrow win. While Straus-aligned Republicans have intervened in Texas House contests, contemporary reporting does not document radio ads by his lieutenants that aided Homer. The claim appears to conflate general intervention by Straus allies with a specific, unverified ad campaign for Homer.

claim: "We haven’t seen a single American megachurch offer anything to help Ukrainians."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement but is contradicted by public reporting: multiple large U.S. churches and their leaders have organized fundraisers, issued public appeals, and partnered with relief organizations to assist Ukrainians since the invasion. While not every megachurch acted, it is incorrect to say that not a single one offered any help.

claim: Says "Ammar Campa-Najjar is working to infiltrate Congress" and "is being supported by CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood."
rationale: The claim mixes a conspiratorial framing (“working to infiltrate Congress”) with an attribution of support that lacks credible evidence. Ammar Campa‑Najjar is a public political candidate who has run for Congress; portraying that as “infiltration” is a misleading characterization. There are no verified records showing organizational direction or operational support from the Muslim Brotherhood, and allegations tying U.S. candidates to the Muslim Brotherhood have repeatedly been debunked; any ties to CAIR are not established as coordinated backing by a foreign organization.

claim: "Sixteen [federal] programs exist to fight homelessness" and some of them are duplicative.
rationale: Federal reviews (notably by the U.S. Interagency Council on Homelessness and the Government Accountability Office) identify on the order of 16 distinct federal programs that directly support people experiencing homelessness, and those reviews have documented overlap and fragmentation among programs that can create duplicative efforts. Therefore the two-part claim — that about sixteen programs exist and that some are duplicative — is broadly accurate, though exact counts depend on definitional choices and timing.

claim: "We've seen six months of positive job growth by the private sector."
rationale: The statement gives no timeframe or data source, so it cannot be verified as a factual, current claim. Whether there have been six consecutive months of private‑sector job growth depends on the specific months and which series (BLS private payrolls, household survey, or private payroll providers) are used; without that context the assertion is unsubstantiated. Therefore I rate the claim as false/unsupported as presented.

claim: If sea levels rise six feet due to climate change, Waterplace Park in Providence and Wickford village would be swamped
rationale: Both Waterplace Park in downtown Providence and Wickford village sit at very low elevations adjacent to the Providence River and Narragansett Bay, respectively. A permanent sea-level rise of about six feet (≈1.8 m) would place large portions of those waterfront areas below typical high-tide levels and therefore inundated without major protective measures or elevation changes.

claim: "My mask will keep someone else safe and their mask will keep me safe."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. Masks do reduce transmission — primarily by source control (your mask lowers how much you expel) and some masks/proper fit (e.g., respirators) protect the wearer — but they do not make others or you completely safe in all circumstances.

claim: "Three years ago, a newly elected President Obama told America that if Congress approved his plan to borrow nearly a trillion dollars, he would hold unemployment below 8 percent."
rationale: There is no authoritative record that President Obama explicitly promised that Congress’ passage of his roughly $787 billion stimulus would keep unemployment below 8 percent. He argued the Recovery Act would blunt job losses and create/save jobs, but analysts and fact-checkers say the claim misstates his comments; unemployment climbed above 8% in 2009 despite the stimulus.

claim: Says there is a report "that showed that, should we move to cover more people to a Medicare for All system, we could actually save the system trillions over an extended period of time."
rationale: The claim only asserts that a report exists showing that expanding Medicare to cover more people could save the system trillions over time. Multiple published analyses (notably analyses commissioned by proponents of single-payer plans) have produced multi-trillion-dollar net savings estimates over multi-year periods, so the existence of such a report is correct. This does not validate the accuracy of those estimates, which are contested.

claim: The Senate seat won in a special election by a Democrat had been "held for more than thirty years by Republicans."
rationale: The statement is unverified because it does not identify which Senate seat or special election is meant; without that specific context the claim cannot be confirmed. Party control of individual Senate seats varies widely over time—some have been in Republican hands for decades, others have not—so asserting a >30-year Republican hold requires a named seat and timeline. Because the claim as written is ambiguous and unsupported, it is treated as false.

claim: "Sen. Obama's chair in New Hampshire is a lobbyist. He lobbies for the drug companies."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the person who served as Barack Obama’s New Hampshire campaign chair was a pharmaceutical industry lobbyist. Reporting and public records about Obama’s New Hampshire campaign leadership do not identify a drug-company lobbyist in that role, and the claim appears to conflate or misidentify someone. Without a specific name and supporting sources the allegation is unsubstantiated.

claim: The departments of Commerce, Education and Energy and the EPA saw their spending increase by between 130 percent and 219 percent between 2008 and 2010.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. While some agencies (notably Commerce because of the 2010 Census and Energy and Education because of Recovery Act funding) did see large year-to-year spikes, the EPA’s spending did not uniformly rise by 130–219% over 2008–2010 and official budget/obligation data show varying increases well below that range for at least one of the named agencies. The broad uniform range across all four agencies therefore overstates and misrepresents the actual budget changes.

claim: "Donald Trump would receive $17 million for three hotels closed for four days under Republican bill! How in the hell is this right?!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any recent Republican bill would pay Donald Trump $17 million specifically for three hotels being closed for four days. Major federal relief and liability proposals (e.g., CARES Act, liability-shield proposals) did not include targeted payments of that form, and such a large, specific payment to the former president’s businesses would have been widely reported and legally problematic. The claim appears to conflate or misstate provisions and lacks verifiable sourcing.

claim: In Ohio, "each year an estimated 1,000 children become victims of human trafficking, and over 3,000 more are at risk."
rationale: The specific figures appear in advocacy materials but are not supported by reproducible, statewide empirical data; Ohio does not publish a validated annual count showing exactly 1,000 child victims and 3,000 at-risk children. Estimates of trafficking prevalence are typically extrapolations from hotline reports, service agency caseloads, or modeled projections and vary widely, so the precise numbers in the claim are not reliably verified. Because methodology and year are not specified, the claim overstates certainty.

claim: The Department of Energy’s "Billion Ton Study" has shown that wind and solar energy combined "could at best provide only 5 percent of our total energy needs."
rationale: The DOE's "Billion Ton Study" is a biomass resource assessment and did not conclude that wind and solar combined could provide only 5% of U.S. energy. The 5% figure is a misattribution or misinterpretation; DOE and NREL analyses of wind and solar resource potential show they could supply a far larger share of U.S. energy than 5%.

claim: "Kenosha car dealer kills himself after insurance won’t cover … damages caused by the riots."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official confirmation that a Kenosha car dealer killed himself because insurance wouldn’t cover riot damages. Major news outlets and fact‑checkers investigated similar viral posts and found no evidence of such a suicide or police reports supporting the claim. The story appears to be a rumor amplified on social media without substantiation.

claim: Georgia’s HOPE scholarship is "still the richest scholarship program in America."
rationale: HOPE was historically very generous but its benefits have been reduced and it does not unambiguously rank as the nation's most generous scholarship program today. Other state and private programs provide larger per-student awards or broader coverage (e.g., full tuition plus living costs), and ‘‘richest’’ is vague without a specific metric or year.

claim: "As Ohio treasurer, Josh Mandel loaned your money to Chinese business interests, and Mandel opposed a bill holding Communist China accountable when they cheated and stole American jobs."
rationale: The claim mixes and exaggerates facts. While Josh Mandel was Ohio Treasurer and the office invests state funds in diversified instruments, there is no clear, documented evidence that he directly 'loaned your money to Chinese business interests' as the statement asserts; at most critics pointed to investments in funds with international exposure. The second part is vague about which bill is meant and there is no definitive record that Mandel singularly 'opposed a bill holding Communist China accountable' in the sweeping way claimed — the language appears to be a partisan simplification rather than an accurate account of specific votes or actions.

claim: "Grandparents must pickup up all their grandchildren every weekend no matter what or they will be fined $5,000."
rationale: There is no universal law requiring grandparents to pick up all their grandchildren every weekend or imposing a blanket $5,000 fine for failure. Child custody and visitation are decided case-by-case by courts, and any obligations or penalties would be set by specific court orders or state statutes, not a general rule applying to all grandparents. Thus the categorical claim is false.

claim: "West Virginia is near last in the U.S." rankings of education, clean drinking water, and child mortality.
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. West Virginia does rank near the bottom on many education measures (test scores and attainment) and has higher-than-average infant/child mortality, but it is not uniformly “near last” across all possible national water-quality rankings—water safety rankings vary by metric and time and WV is not consistently the absolute worst on drinking-water indicators. The statement lacks specificity and mixes different metrics, so as phrased it is inaccurate.

claim: Says the Obama administration approved a major disaster declaration for Oklahoma in 2009, when nine of the state’s 77 counties burned for "about three days," while Texas wildfires have been burning for longer without such a declaration.
rationale: The claim mixes events and is misleading. While the Obama administration did approve a major disaster declaration for Oklahoma wildfires in 2009, Texas experienced large, longer-running wildfire outbreaks (notably in 2011) that also received federal disaster assistance under the Obama administration. Saying Texas wildfires burned longer without a similar declaration ignores later federal actions and conflates different events and timelines.

claim: "There's no evidence that white supremacists were responsible for what happened on Jan. 6. That's a lie."
rationale: Multiple law-enforcement investigations, prosecutions, and reporting have documented participation by white supremacist-aligned individuals and groups in the Jan. 6 attack (including convictions of Proud Boys members and other extremists), so the claim that “there’s no evidence” is incorrect. While not the only actors involved, white supremacist-linked actors were present and implicated by evidence and charges.

claim: Wisconsin’s middle class is the "most diminished" in the United States.
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated: major analyses of middle‑class trends (by sources using Census data, Pew Research, Brookings, etc.) do not identify Wisconsin as having the single most diminished middle class nationwide. Results vary by how “diminished” is measured (share of households in the middle-income band, median income erosion, mobility), and other states show equal or larger declines depending on the metric and period. Without a cited metric or timeframe, the claim cannot be verified and appears false.

claim: "Three of five detainees swapped (for Bowe Bergdahl) are now ISIS leaders."
rationale: Contemporary fact-checking and news reporting found no credible evidence that three of the five Gitmo detainees exchanged for Bowe Bergdahl became ISIS leaders. Public tracking showed at most isolated reports or allegations about one individual's later associations, while others were reported to have rejoined Taliban elements, remained in Qatar under monitoring, or had unclear status. The claim overstates and misattributes affiliation and leadership roles.

claim: "U.S. military at the White House arresting Congress."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that U.S. military personnel are at the White House arresting members of Congress. Such an action would be unprecedented and illegal without due process and would have been widely and immediately reported by major news outlets and official sources.

claim: Says Joe Biden said: "If Haiti just quietly sunk into the Caribbean, or rose up 300 feet, it wouldn’t matter a whole lot in terms of our interests."
rationale: There is no credible record or contemporaneous reporting showing Joe Biden uttered that line; major fact-checkers and news archives do not document him saying it. The quotation appears to be a fabricated or misattributed statement circulating online rather than a verifiable Biden remark.

claim: "We've got to find 2 billion gallons (of water per day) between now and 2025."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it provides no region, agency, or source for the target of 'finding 2 billion gallons per day by 2025.' Water-supply shortfall figures and recovery goals are set regionally and vary widely; there is no universally recognized or widely reported mandate to find that exact volume by 2025. Without specific context or a cited plan, the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: "Corporate income has increased as a share of" gross domestic product.
rationale: The claim is too general and the trend depends on country, timeframe and how “corporate income” is measured. In the U.S., corporate profits as a share of GDP have fluctuated substantially (rising in some periods and falling in others) and are not a monotonic increase. Without specifying the measure (pre‑tax vs after‑tax, domestic vs national accounts) or period, the assertion is not reliably true.

claim: "Pelosi’s $1.9 trillion bailout gives EVERY federal employee a $21,000 bonus check… they never lost their job!"
rationale: The $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan did not include a $21,000 bonus for every federal employee. The law provided $1,400 direct payments to eligible individuals, unemployment and state/local relief, vaccine and public-health funding, and targeted programs, but no provision sending every federal worker a $21,000 check.

claim: Quotes Alexandria-Ocasio Cortez as saying private truck drivers are "destroying America" and should be "government regulated and drivers should be on full-time camera until we can figure out how to automate our shipping and do away with them altogether."
rationale: The specific quoted language is not supported by any credible reporting, public record, or AOC social media posts and has been circulated as a fabricated/misattributed quote. The sentiments ascribed (calling private truck drivers "destroying America" and advocating constant cameras and eliminating them) conflict with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's well-documented pro-labor and worker-protection positions and there is no evidence she made such statements.

claim: Says Mike Pence was arrested.
rationale: As of my last verified information through June 2024, there were no credible reports or official records indicating that former Vice President Mike Pence was arrested. I have no confirmation of an arrest after that date and the claim lacks supporting reliable sources in the timeframe I can verify. Because I may not have updates beyond my cutoff, I cannot definitively rule out later developments.

claim: A Georgia law has not "criminalized giving people bottles of water." It pertains to political organizations.
rationale: Georgia's 2021 election law (SB 202) includes a prohibition on giving ‘anything of value’ to voters within certain distances of polling places, and that definition explicitly can include food and water. The restriction is not limited to political organizations — it applies to 'any person' other than poll workers/election officials and therefore can criminalize giving water to voters in line in those zones. There are limited exemptions, so saying the law categorically 'has not criminalized giving people bottles of water' or that it only pertains to political organizations is misleading.

claim: Says Sen. Kay Hagan "has missed half of the (Senate Armed Services) Committee's hearings in 2014."
rationale: This specific claim is misleading — publicly available committee attendance records and contemporaneous fact-checks did not support that Sen. Kay Hagan missed half of Senate Armed Services Committee hearings in 2014. The assertion appears to overstate absences, likely by counting a narrow subset of sessions or misreporting the timeframe. Without a clear, authoritative roll call showing a 50% absence rate, the claim is not supported.

claim: The United States is "the only advanced country on Earth" that doesn’t guarantee "paid maternity leave to our workers."
rationale: Interpreting “advanced country” as developed/OECD-level countries, the United States is the only one that lacks a national statutory paid maternity (or parental) leave program. Other wealthy nations guarantee at least some weeks of paid maternity/parental leave; the U.S. federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides unpaid leave but no universal paid benefit.

claim: "The Congressional Budget Office has this economic model where they measure the economy going forward, and they are now telling us that the entire economy crashes in the year 2037 because their computer simulation can't conceive of any way in which the U.S. economy can continue."
rationale: This claim misrepresents CBO work. The Congressional Budget Office produces baseline and alternative budget/economic projections showing rising deficits and debt over coming decades and warns of fiscal challenges, but it does not state that the "entire economy crashes in 2037" nor that its models "can’t conceive" of any continuation. CBO projections are scenario-based and depend on assumptions; they do not output a single deterministic collapse date for the whole U.S. economy.

claim: "‘TrumpCare’ would allow insurance execs to personally make millions off your health care."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While bills labeled “TrumpCare” (various Republican health proposals) could change regulations and funding in ways that might increase insurer profits, the legislation does not directly authorize or guarantee that insurance executives will personally pocket millions. Executive compensation is determined by private corporations and market outcomes, making any personal windfall speculative rather than a direct feature of the law.

claim: "Black Lives Matter is a terrorist organization."
rationale: The label is false: Black Lives Matter is a decentralized social movement and there is no designation by the U.S. government or other major governments that the movement or the Black Lives Matter Global Network is a terrorist organization. While some protests associated with the movement have involved violence or property damage by individuals, that does not meet the legal standard or formal designation of a terrorist organization.

claim: "We are within the margin of error."
rationale: The statement is unverified as presented because it does not identify which poll or measurement, the reported point estimates, sample size, or the stated margin of error and confidence level. Without those specifics one cannot determine whether results actually lie within any given margin of error, so the claim cannot be substantiated and is classified as FALSE.

claim: 7 million people the Congressional Budget Office says won't have health insurance coverage under the Senate health care bill "don't exist."
rationale: This is false: the CBO's estimate of 7 million refers to the projected number of people who would be uninsured under a particular Senate bill relative to current law, not a claim that individual people literally do not exist. CBO estimates are statistical projections based on enrollment, eligibility and coverage models; they describe real people who would lack coverage under the policy, not an invented population.

claim: "Florida is now the No. 1 state in the country for automobile accident fraud."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported by a single, current authoritative ranking. Florida has frequently been cited among states with high levels of staged-collision and PIP-related automobile fraud, but national rankings vary by metric (number of suspicious claims, paid losses, per-capita rates) and by year, and there is no universally accepted, up-to-date source that definitively names Florida as the No. 1 state across the board.

claim: "California won’t let law enforcement officers like you and your people transfer prisoners to ICE custody or even to communicate with ICE that you’re about to release them from your custody — people that ICE is looking for."
rationale: California law (principally the California Values Act, SB54) generally bars state and local law enforcement from honoring ICE civil immigration detainers or using resources to transfer people to ICE custody and restricts sharing release-date information with ICE. However the prohibition is not absolute—there are explicit exceptions such as when ICE presents a judicial warrant, a court order, the individual consents, or other narrowly defined circumstances. The claim is accurate as a general statement of California policy but omits those exceptions.

claim: Says "I’ve been proven right" about "Hillary Clinton's radical call for open borders, meaning anyone in the world can enter the United States without any limit at all."
rationale: This is false: Hillary Clinton’s public positions and campaign proposals consistently supported comprehensive immigration reform and measures to secure the border, not an unconditional “anyone in the world can enter” open-borders policy. Major fact-checkers and her own policy statements have rejected the characterization that she called for no limits on immigration, so claiming one has been “proven right” about that framing misstates her record.

claim: "House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said this week that the Democrats have to pass their terrible health care bill so that the American people can actually find out what's in it."
rationale: This mixes and misstates Pelosi's remarks. Pelosi did famously say in 2010 about the Affordable Care Act, 'we have to pass the bill so that you can find out what is in it,' but she did not call it 'their terrible health care bill' and there is no evidence she made that pejorative phrasing 'this week.' The claim combines an old quote with inaccurate wording and timing.

claim: "Mitt Romney’s platform ...won't protect the mortgage interest (tax) deduction for middle-class families."
rationale: Romney’s 2012 tax blueprint and repeated campaign statements said he would preserve the mortgage interest deduction for ordinary homeowners (often framed as protecting middle‑class homeowners) while seeking to eliminate or limit some other deductions. Opponents sometimes argued his broader tax‑reform proposals could indirectly affect who benefits, but his stated platform did not say it would abolish the mortgage interest deduction for middle‑class families.

claim: "One of the most troubling aspects of the Rubio-Schumer Gang of Eight bill was that it gave President Obama blanket authority to admit refugees, including Syrian refugees, without mandating any background checks whatsoever."
rationale: The claim is false. The 2013 'Gang of Eight' bill (S.744) did not give President Obama a new blanket power to admit refugees without background checks; refugee admissions are governed by the Immigration and Nationality Act and long-standing interagency vetting (State, DHS, FBI, biometric checks) which S.744 did not abolish. Critics conflated executive discretion over refugee admissions with eliminating security screening, but the bill did not remove statutory vetting requirements.

claim: "Kyle Rittenhouse files $400 million suit against CNN!"
rationale: There are no credible news reports or public court filings showing Kyle Rittenhouse filed a $400 million lawsuit specifically against CNN. While Rittenhouse has pursued or threatened legal action and has been involved in defamation-related claims, the $400 million figure against CNN is not supported by reliable sources. Therefore the claim as stated is false.

claim: "I’ve never supported legislation that invades people’s choices about contraception."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as presented because it is a universal "never" about an unspecified speaker; proving a universal negative requires a complete legislative and public-record review. Many politicians have supported laws or policies that limit access to contraception or allow exemptions (for example, employer exemptions to contraceptive coverage), so absent a full, documented record for the speaker the assertion is unlikely to be reliable.

claim: The book Little Red Riding Hood is something "that’s been banned in America," but not assault weapons.
rationale: The claim is misleading. While variants of Little Red Riding Hood have occasionally been challenged or removed by local schools or libraries, it has not been universally banned nationwide; conversely, assault weapons are in fact banned or heavily restricted in multiple U.S. states and were subject to a federal ban from 1994–2004. Saying Little Red Riding Hood is "banned in America" but assault weapons are not is therefore inaccurate.

claim: Wisconsin sold fresh water to California, helping that state's dairy industry, and "lost a bunch of jobs (and) a bunch of farmland."
rationale: There is no evidence that the State of Wisconsin sold bulk fresh water to California in a way that materially supplied California's dairy industry or caused widespread job and farmland losses in Wisconsin. Large interstate transfers/diversions out of the Great Lakes basin are tightly restricted (Great Lakes Compact), and what limited bottled-water withdrawals from Wisconsin exist are small commercial operations and not linked to California dairies. Wisconsin's farm losses are better explained by long-term economic trends in agriculture, consolidation, and market factors, not a state water sale to California.

claim: "As a city, we currently use about 4 percent less electricity today than we used in 1989."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not identify which city or what exact metric (total vs. per-capita electricity use) and timepoint “today” refers to. Electricity consumption trends vary widely across cities due to population change, efficiency improvements, and electrification, so a general claim that a city now uses about 4% less than in 1989 cannot be confirmed without specific utility or municipal data. Given the ambiguity and lack of supporting data, the claim is treated as false.

claim: Says Donald Trump "doesn't make a thing in America."
rationale: The absolute statement that Donald Trump "doesn't make a thing in America" is incorrect. The Trump Organization owns and operates numerous U.S.-based businesses (hotels, golf courses, real-estate developments) that produce services and economic activity in the United States, so it is not true that he makes nothing in America.

claim: "The latest evidence of Republican success is that since the beginning of the current legislative term, state unemployment has gone down almost 20% to 5% adjusted."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated and is likely false because it fails to identify which state or the exact legislative term and mixes percent-change language with an absolute unemployment rate. Unemployment data are reported as rates or percentage-point changes; saying 'down almost 20% to 5% adjusted' is ambiguous without a baseline and timeframe and does not match typical published state series. Without a specific state and dates, the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "The National Academy of Medicine points to a significant correlation between marijuana and psychosis, schizophrenia, and other psychotic disorders, particularly in teenagers where the risk of developing schizophrenia increases three fold."
rationale: The National Academies (formerly National Academy of Medicine/NASEM) has concluded there is substantial evidence of an association between cannabis use and increased risk of schizophrenia and other psychoses, especially with early and frequent use. However, the Academy did not categorically state a specific “threefold” increased risk for teenagers; that numeric magnitude comes from some individual studies and meta-analyses and varies by study design, frequency of use, and age of onset. Thus the claim mixes a correct general finding with an unsupported attribution of a precise 3× figure to the Academy.

claim: "Violent crime is now going down for the first time in a long while."
rationale: The statement is too sweeping and not supported as a general fact. Violent-crime trends vary by country, city, and offense, and in the U.S. there were substantial declines across the 2010s, a spike around 2020–2021, and only mixed declines afterward — so it is incorrect to say violent crime is "now going down for the first time in a long while."

claim: "Maybe (the COVID-19 vaccine) doesn't work, and they're simply not telling you that."
rationale: Extensive randomized trials and large-scale real-world studies have demonstrated that authorized COVID-19 vaccines substantially reduce symptomatic infection, severe illness, hospitalization, and death. National and international public-health agencies publish surveillance and study data on vaccine effectiveness, waning immunity, and variant impact, so the blanket claim that vaccines “don't work” and that this is being concealed is contradicted by abundant public evidence. While vaccines are not 100% protective and effectiveness can wane or vary by variant, the core assertion is false.

claim: The novel coronavirus was "man-made."
rationale: This is false: the consensus of virologists and multiple independent genomic analyses find SARS-CoV-2’s sequence is consistent with natural zoonotic evolution and lacks signatures of deliberate genetic engineering. Closely related coronaviruses have been identified in wild bat (and related) populations, and no credible evidence has been produced showing the virus was man‑made.

claim: The federal government "reviewed and verified" his administration’s numbers showing Wisconsin added 23,608 jobs in 2011.
rationale: This is false because although the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics reviews state employment-estimation methods and publishes official state job series, it does not simply 'review and verify' a governor’s political claim about a specific jobs number. The 23,608 figure was a state-reported number and the federal role is methodological review and production of official estimates, not endorsement of an administration's headline claim; fact-checkers found the wording misleading.

claim: A second impeachment means Donald Trump loses his lifetime pension, travel allowance, Secret Service detail, and his ability to run for public office.
rationale: This is false. A House impeachment alone does not strip a former president of pensions, travel allowances, Secret Service protection, or bar him from future office — those penalties would require conviction by the Senate, and disqualification from future office requires a separate Senate vote. Whether statutory benefits would be eliminated following a Senate conviction/ removal is governed by law and is legally unsettled.

claim: When Terry McAuliffe was governor, "Unemployment went down in every single county, including rural Virginia by nearly 50%.
rationale: This is inaccurate: while Virginia's overall unemployment rate declined during Terry McAuliffe's 2014–2018 term, the statement that unemployment fell in every single county and that rural Virginia fell “by nearly 50%” is unsupported. County-level BLS and state labor data show wide variation—many localities saw sizable declines but not universally, and the “nearly 50%” figure appears to be an exaggerated or ambiguous percent-change rather than a documented uniform outcome. Media and data reviews of that period treat the claim as an overstatement.

claim: Says Gov. Scott Walker’s proposed budget "would sell off Wisconsin’s state parks."
rationale: That phrasing is misleading. Walker’s budgets included provisions to reduce state funding for parks and to allow the sale or transfer of certain Department of Natural Resources properties or to enable local/private management of some sites, but they did not propose an across‑the‑board sale of Wisconsin’s entire state park system. Critics summarized those measures as a “sell‑off,” which overstates the policy as a blanket disposal of all state parks.

claim: "Hedge fund managers and others in private equity pay much lower (tax) rates on their income than do truck drivers and teachers and nurses."
rationale: Many hedge fund and private equity managers receive a large share of pay as carried interest or long‑term capital gains, which are taxed at preferential federal rates (about 20% plus 3.8% NIIT) and generally avoid payroll taxes, while truck drivers, teachers and nurses earn ordinary wages taxed at ordinary income rates (up to 37%) and subject to payroll taxes. Empirical analyses of effective tax rates show that top investment managers often end up with substantially lower effective tax rates than many middle‑class wage earners, though outcomes vary by individual income mix and state taxes.

claim: Says "Donald Trump himself contributed $100,000" to the Clinton Foundation.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or Clinton Foundation donor record showing that Donald J. Trump personally gave $100,000 to the Clinton Foundation. Contemporary fact-checks and public records do not document such a personal donation; the claim appears to conflate or misattribute donations by other entities or individuals.

claim: "The CBO, the Congressional Budget Office has said that Obamacare will kill 800,000 jobs."
rationale: This is false. The CBO did not say the Affordable Care Act would "kill 800,000 jobs"; CBO reports discussed a modest reduction in labor supply (measured as fewer hours worked or in full‑time‑equivalent terms) attributable to some people choosing to work less once they had access to subsidized coverage. Those analyses framed the effect as a reduction in hours or labor force participation, not as government‑caused job destruction of 800,000 positions.

claim: "Corona is so bad, this guy died twice!"
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: there are no verifiable reports showing a person literally died twice from COVID-19. While patients can be clinically dead (no pulse) and later resuscitated, that is different from the sensational phrasing “died twice” and requires specific, verifiable details which are not provided, making the claim misleading.

claim: Israel's per capita income "is greater than probably three-fourths of the rest of the world."
rationale: Israel is classified as a high‑income economy and, in common international datasets (World Bank/IMF/CIA), its GDP per capita typically ranks within the top quartile of countries, meaning it is higher than roughly three‑quarters of other countries. Exact placement can shift with the year and whether nominal or PPP measures are used, but the general claim is accurate.

claim: Opposition to having a fully elected Chicago Board of Education is in the "super minority."
rationale: The claim is unverified and ambiguous: there is no clear, public evidence that opposition to a fully elected Chicago Board of Education is confined to a tiny or “super” minority. Public debate and legislative actions around Chicago school-board elections have shown mixed support and opposition among politicians, community groups, and voters at different times, so labeling opposition as a super-minority is not substantiated. Without specific poll or vote figures tied to a timeframe, the statement cannot be treated as fact.

claim: Text from someone "connected" to Raleigh police: "antifa may be heading into the wealthy neighborhoods tonight to take what should be theirs."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that a person connected to Raleigh police sent that message or that organized “antifa” units were heading into wealthy neighborhoods to loot. The claim matches a common pattern of unverified, sensational social-media rumors during protests and was not corroborated by official Raleigh Police statements or independent reporting. Without attribution or confirmation, the statement should be treated as false.

claim: The Obama administration "spent more money on the Cash for Clunkers program than the space program."
rationale: The Cash for Clunkers (CARS) program was funded at roughly $3 billion total in 2009. By contrast NASA’s annual budget in the Obama years was on the order of $17–19 billion per year (and cumulatively many tens of billions over the administration). Therefore the administration spent far more on the federal space program than on Cash for Clunkers.

claim: A CNN chyron said, "Antifa has just taken responsibility for storming Capital Hill."
rationale: This claim is false. Multiple independent fact-checkers and CNN itself have confirmed that no CNN chyron stating “Antifa has just taken responsibility for storming Capital Hill” ran; the image/video circulating was fabricated and does not appear in archived CNN broadcasts. While there was speculation about who was responsible for the Capitol attack, that speculation was not presented on-screen by CNN in the quoted chyron form.

claim: "New Jersey today has fewer employees in state government than it had when Christie Whitman left office in January of 2001, and I think that’s good. And we did it without any layoffs. We did it through attrition."
rationale: The claim is not reliably supported as stated. It uses an unspecified “today” and does not define which categories of employees are being counted; New Jersey payroll and personnel reports vary by category and year and do not consistently show a clear net decline from January 2001 to recent years. The additional assertion that reductions were achieved entirely by attrition with no layoffs is likewise unverifiable without precise timeframe and personnel records and conflicts with documented workforce actions and reorganizations in some years.

claim: Says a photo shows a man wearing a "government issue Saint Laurent hazardous materials suit."
rationale: The claim conflates a luxury fashion brand (Saint Laurent) with government-issued hazardous-materials protective gear, which are distinct product categories. Governments procure certified protective suits from industrial/safety manufacturers (e.g., Tychem, Dupont) rather than high-fashion houses, and there is no evidence Saint Laurent produces an official “government issue” hazmat suit. Without provenance or manufacturer labeling in the photo, the assertion is not supported.

claim: "Eliminating earmarks does not reduce spending."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that cannot be generally supported. Empirical evidence and budget practice show that banning congressional earmarks typically eliminates or reduces targeted project outlays and can lower discretionary spending, although in some cases funds are reallocated elsewhere so total spending effects vary. Therefore it is incorrect to assert categorically that eliminating earmarks does not reduce spending.

claim: A campaign poster for New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern with the slogan, "No jab. No job, no refunds."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Jacinda Ardern or the New Zealand Labour Party produced a campaign poster reading 'No jab. No job, no refunds.' The phrase appears to be a viral or doctored meme conflating public discussion of vaccine mandates with campaign advertising rather than an actual official poster.

claim: "We’ve got 600-plus police and fire pensions Downstate that are on the cusp of insolvency because they don’t have the revenues that they need to be able to keep those pensions going."
rationale: The statement overstates and is unsupported as phrased. It is true that Illinois (outside Chicago) has roughly six hundred or more local police and fire pension funds and many are underfunded, but there is no clear evidence that 600+ of those funds are currently ‘on the cusp of insolvency’ for lack of revenues—the fiscal condition varies by fund and depends on specific funding metrics and timing. Calling all or more than 600 ‘on the cusp’ is therefore an exaggeration without supporting data.

claim: "Twice as much (federal) money is going back to Hawaii, Virginia and Alaska than is coming home to Oregon."
rationale: The claim gives a precise proportional comparison but provides no year or definition of “federal money” (gross outlays, net transfers, or tax burden). Federal spending and receipts by state fluctuate year-to-year and by category; while Hawaii, Virginia, and Alaska can receive large federal outlays for military, veterans, and energy programs, there is no general rule that their combined federal receipts are exactly double Oregon’s. Because the statement is underspecified and unlikely to hold universally without a specified timeframe and metric, I judge it false as stated.

claim: Video shows a Ukrainian fighter pilot shooting down a Russian plane.
rationale: No specific video, source, metadata, or corroborating official confirmation was provided, so the claim cannot be independently verified. Videos online are frequently misattributed, recycled from other conflicts, or lack verifiable geolocation and timing; without OSINT verification and authoritative confirmation, asserting it shows a Ukrainian pilot shooting down a Russian plane is unsupported.

claim: Says John F. Kennedy "smoked cannabis in the White House, while president, because he suffered from severe back pain and Addison's disease."
rationale: There is no credible historical or medical evidence that John F. Kennedy smoked cannabis in the White House while president. Detailed biographies and his medical records document extensive treatment for chronic back pain with prescription medications and other therapies, but contemporary physician notes and reputable histories do not report presidential cannabis use or a well‑substantiated diagnosis of Addison's disease causing such use.

claim: A photograph shows Joe Biden with a Grand Wizard of the Ku Klux Klan.
rationale: There is no credible evidence of a photograph showing Joe Biden with a Ku Klux Klan ‘Grand Wizard.’ Photos that are circulated usually show Biden with the late Senator Robert Byrd, who was a one-time, low-level KKK member in the 1940s and later renounced the organization; Byrd was not a Grand Wizard. Thus the claim that a photo shows Biden with a Grand Wizard is false or a mischaracterization.

claim: "The bill also provides full federal funding for abortions…"
rationale: The statement is too general and cannot be verified without naming the specific bill; most federal law and appropriations include the Hyde Amendment or similar restrictions that prevent full federal funding of elective abortions. Unless a specific bill explicitly and unambiguously repeals those restrictions and authorizes unrestricted federal payment for abortions, the claim is incorrect. Given typical legislative practice, a blanket claim of 'full federal funding' is unlikely to be accurate.

claim: "Our economy is so much stronger than when (Barack Obama and Joe Biden) took office. Nearly 15 million new private-sector jobs."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it gives no timeframe and the specific figure is not supported by official payroll data for the obvious comparison periods. BLS series for private‑sector employment show roughly 11–12 million private‑sector jobs added during Obama’s two terms (2009–2017); depending on endpoints through 2019–early 2020 cumulative gains vary, but the unqualified claim of “nearly 15 million” is not a reliably supported, time‑bound fact. The broad claim that the economy is “so much stronger” is subjective and depends on metrics beyond a single rounded jobs figure.

claim: "If the shot actually saved lives, they’d be priced so high that you literally could not afford them, you know like insulin."
rationale: This asserts a universal market rule that any life-saving shot would be priced unaffordably like insulin; that is incorrect. Many life‑saving vaccines are inexpensive or provided free through public programs, bulk procurement, subsidies, or nonprofit supply, whereas high insulin prices are due to specific patent, market, and regulatory factors rather than an inevitable outcome for all lifesaving treatments.

claim: The Democratic health care plan is a "government takeover of nearly 20 percent of our economy."
rationale: This statement conflates the share of the economy accounted for by health care (about 17–18% of U.S. GDP) with a claim that Democrats planned to nationalize that share. The major Democratic plan commonly referenced (the Affordable Care Act) expanded subsidies and Medicaid but left private insurers and providers intact rather than instituting a government takeover; other Democratic proposals (e.g., single‑payer) differ and would be a different claim.

claim: "When people enter the service, there’s not a mental health evaluation."
rationale: The claim is a categorical statement without specifying which “service” it refers to, and many services routinely perform mental health screenings or evaluations at intake (e.g., healthcare, military enlistment, substance use treatment, homelessness and social services). Because practices vary by program and jurisdiction, the universal negative (“there’s not a mental health evaluation”) is unsupported and therefore false as a general claim.

claim: Says most of Austin’s biggest parks have recycling though as "many as 293 out of 300" Austin city "parks have no recycling, including almost every neighborhood park."
rationale: The statement is internally inconsistent and implausible: it asserts that most of Austin’s biggest parks have recycling while also claiming "as many as 293 out of 300" city parks have no recycling (leaving only ~7 parks with recycling). Public information about Austin Parks & Recreation shows targeted recycling at many major sites and ongoing city recycling initiatives, not a near-total absence at 293 of ~300 parks. The 293/300 figure appears exaggerated or taken out of context and conflicts with available municipal recycling program descriptions.

claim: "We have about six school districts that are in school 140 to 150 days this year."
rationale: The statement is unverified and likely incorrect as presented because it gives no jurisdiction or school year. In the United States most school districts operate roughly 170–180 instructional days due to state minimums and common practice, so claiming “about six” districts are in school only 140–150 days this year is implausible without specific local data. Without a named state or year the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: "I have cut taxes 63 times, including a 2006 property tax reduction that ranks as the largest in state history."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated and likely misleading: it lacks the identity of “I,” the state, and what counts as a separate “tax cut.” Public records typically do not support a single official universally documenting 63 distinct tax cuts nor a universally agreed 2006 property tax reduction that is the largest in any state’s history without specifying the state. Because the assertion is specific but missing crucial context and corroboration, it should be treated as false unless specific, verifiable details are provided.

claim: If Joe Biden can’t serve his full term, Kamala Harris "cannot by constitutional law become president."
rationale: The U.S. Constitution and its 25th Amendment explicitly provide that the Vice President becomes President if the President dies, resigns, or is removed from office. Historical practice (e.g., John Tyler in 1841, Lyndon Johnson in 1963, Gerald Ford in 1974) and the Presidential Succession Act confirm that a Vice President can and does assume the presidency. The claim that Kamala Harris "cannot by constitutional law become president" is therefore incorrect.

claim: Newt Gingrich "co-sponsored a bill with Nancy Pelosi that would have given $60 million a year to a U.N. program supporting China’s brutal one-child policy."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. While Congress has debated funding for the U.N. Population Fund (UNFPA) and $60 million has been cited as an annual cap in some appropriations contexts, Newt Gingrich did not co-sponsor a bill with Nancy Pelosi that specifically ‘‘would have given $60 million a year to a U.N. program supporting China’s one‑child policy.’’ The statement conflates authorization/appropriation language, misattributes co‑sponsorship, and implies UNFPA explicitly backed coercive Chinese policy (which UNFPA and fact‑checks have denied).

claim: ICE está en Uvalde, Texas, "entonces los padres indocumentados tienen que temer la deportación antes de verificar si sus hijos están vivos".
rationale: La afirmación mezcla hechos y suposiciones. Si bien hubo presencia de agencias federales ligadas a inmigración (como personal de la patrulla fronteriza/CBP y otros componentes del DHS) en Uvalde tras la masacre, no hay evidencia clara de que ICE estuviera realizando redadas o detenciones masivas en el lugar ni de que padres fueran efectivamente deportados antes de confirmar el estado de sus hijos. Presentarlo como que “ICE está en Uvalde” con la consecuencia directa de que padres indocumentados deben temer la deportación antes de verificar a sus hijos es engañoso y no está comprobado.

claim: "US Capitol raided 2/2/21."
rationale: This is false. The widely reported breach/attack on the U.S. Capitol occurred on January 6, 2021, not February 2, 2021. There are no credible records or mainstream reports identifying a separate raid of the Capitol on 2/2/21. The claim appears to misstate or confuse the date of the January 6 incident.

claim: Says Target installed urinals in a women’s bathroom to "accommodate the ones who have giblets."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Target installed urinals in women’s restrooms for the reason claimed. Target adopted gender-inclusive policies and added single-occupancy restrooms, but fact-checkers and news reports have debunked viral posts alleging urinals were put in women’s bathrooms — those posts were miscaptioned or fabricated. The quoted phrase appears to be inflammatory social-media rhetoric rather than a documented company action.

claim: Says "over 50 percent of U.S. job growth in June came" from Wisconsin.
rationale: The claim is implausible and inconsistent with typical BLS monthly employment patterns: national nonfarm payroll gains in a single month are usually in the low hundreds of thousands, and Wisconsin—being a mid‑sized state—regularly contributes only a few thousand to several tens of thousands of jobs. For Wisconsin to account for over 50% of U.S. monthly job growth would require it to add more than the combined rest of the country, which does not match historical state-by-state BLS data or typical labor market distributions.

claim: Only Nancy Pelosi is "responsible for what happened at the Capitol" on Jan. 6, "security at the Capitol is her job."
rationale: The claim is false because responsibility for Capitol security is distributed across the U.S. Capitol Police, the Capitol Police Board (including the House and Senate Sergeants at Arms and the Architect of the Capitol), and federal partners such as the Pentagon/National Guard, not solely the Speaker of the House. Multiple official investigations and reporting found failures across agencies and leadership decisions, and both Sergeants at Arms resigned after Jan. 6, indicating shared operational and managerial responsibility rather than sole accountability by Nancy Pelosi.

claim: "I'm the only front-line prosecutor in this race that's actually used the resources of the Wisconsin Crime Lab in the prosecution of cases."
rationale: This is an absolute claim about being the only front-line prosecutor in a particular race to have used the Wisconsin Crime Lab. I cannot verify that no other front-line prosecutor in the race has ever used the lab’s resources, and many prosecutors routinely use state crime lab services. Because the claim is categorical and unsubstantiated here, it should be treated as false absent specific evidence.

claim: Says Charlie Crist "stood there, over 3 African-American prisoners in chains, on their knees, on the side of the road. Saying that it was a great sight. Saying we needed to bring it to Florida. And you did this — whether you know or not — on the eve of Juneteenth, the day the African-American community celebrates the end of slavery."
rationale: There is no credible record or contemporaneous reporting showing Charlie Crist uttered those words praising a display of chained African-American prisoners or saying it should be brought to Florida. Such an inflammatory statement would have been widely documented and fact-checked by major news outlets, but no reliable source attributes this quote to Crist. The phrasing appears to be an allegation or misattribution rather than a verified direct quote.

claim: Says coronavirus is just "the damn flu."
rationale: The claim that coronavirus is "just the damn flu" is false. COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2 (a different virus family than influenza), has led to substantially higher rates of hospitalizations and deaths globally than typical seasonal flu, and can cause distinct complications and long-term effects (long COVID). While symptoms can overlap with influenza, the overall severity, transmissibility, and population impact have been greater for COVID-19.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton won "health care for 8 million children."
rationale: This phrasing is misleading. Hillary Clinton did advocate for expanding children's coverage, but the State Children's Health Insurance Program (SCHIP/CHIP) was enacted by Congress in 1997 and signed by President Bill Clinton; attributing a program 'win' for 8 million children solely to Hillary Clinton is inaccurate. Enrollment figures for CHIP have varied over time and the '8 million' number is a rough, context‑dependent estimate rather than proof of a singular personal victory.

claim: Says "Biden wants a nationwide lockdown to combat a virus that has a 99%+ survival rate."
rationale: This claim misrepresents Biden's publicly stated COVID-19 policy and oversimplifies fatality statistics. Biden called for a national strategy, stronger public-health measures, and targeted restrictions at times, but did not explicitly call for a blanket nationwide lockdown. Also, COVID-19 survival rates vary widely by age, health, time period, and location; overall infection fatality estimates in many settings were higher than a uniform <1% implied by '99%+ survival.'

claim: "Nearly half of African-American children under the age of 6 are living in abject poverty."
rationale: This claim is not supported by U.S. poverty statistics. While Black children have higher poverty rates than the national average, nationally the share of African‑American children under 6 in poverty (and even in "deep" or "extreme" poverty) is substantially below 50%. The term "abject poverty" is also imprecise and could conflate different measures.

claim: The increase in the current state budget was greater than the inflation rate and the rate of population growth in Georgia.
rationale: The statement lacks a specific fiscal year and precise budget measure, so it cannot be verified as written. Whether a state's budget increased more than inflation and population growth depends on the chosen time period and which budget component is compared, and those details are missing here.

claim: In the United States, we’ve had "12 years in a row of wages declining."
rationale: There is no U.S. wage series (nominal average hourly earnings, real average hourly earnings, or median household/weekly earnings) that shows a continuous 12-year decline. Official BLS and Census income series show ups and downs but include multiple years of wage gains during any recent 12-year span, so wages did not fall for twelve straight years. The claim likely conflates long-term stagnation or isolated multi-year declines in specific subgroups with a continuous nationwide 12-year drop.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "wants to go to a single-payer plan" for health care
rationale: This is inaccurate. Hillary Clinton has repeatedly said she does not support a single‑payer 'Medicare for All' plan and instead has advocated building on the Affordable Care Act and pursuing more incremental reforms (and at times a public option). In her 2016 and 2019–2020 campaign statements she explicitly opposed adopting a single‑payer system.

claim: "An 8-year-old Ukrainian girl confronts a Russian soldier telling him to go back to his country."
rationale: I could not confirm a reliable, independently verified account that a specific 8-year-old Ukrainian girl confronted a Russian soldier and told him to go back to his country. While short clips of children confronting soldiers circulated widely, many were reposted with conflicting ages, locations, or context and lacked authoritative sourcing. Because the claim names a precise age and definitive action without verifiable evidence, it cannot be treated as established fact.

claim: "More people now die in Wisconsin from drug overdoses than car crashes."
rationale: I cannot reliably verify the present-tense claim because it lacks a specific year and Wisconsin vital statistics vary by year; while overdose deaths have risen nationally and exceeded motor-vehicle deaths in many states recently, I do not have definitive, up-to-date Wisconsin totals to confirm this statement. Given the ambiguity about “now” and the potential for year-to-year changes, I treat the claim as unproven. To confirm would require the latest Wisconsin Department of Health Services or traffic fatality data for a specific recent year.

claim: "Seventy percent of all Texans are overweight or obese."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and likely incorrect as stated because public health statistics on overweight/obesity are normally reported for adults, not “all Texans” (which would include children). Adult combined overweight-or-obesity estimates for many U.S. states are near 60–75% depending on year and source, but the exact value for Texas varies and nationwide self-reported surveys can under- or over-estimate true prevalence. Because the claim gives a single blanket 70% for “all Texans” without specifying age group, year, or source, it is not reliably supported.

claim: Four (maybe five) Latinos have served on the Austin City Council.
rationale: The claim understates representation: historical records and accounts of Austin city government show more than five Latino individuals have served on the Austin City Council over the city's history. The phrasing is vague and doesn't match the broader record of multiple Latino councilmembers across several decades.

claim: Says Barbara Buono "voted to raise her own pay 40 percent."
rationale: There is no clear record that Barbara Buono cast a vote that directly raised her own legislative salary by 40%. Political ads and opponents have sometimes conflated votes on pension or benefit changes or broader budget items with a direct pay increase for sitting legislators, producing a misleading impression. Without specific bill language showing a 40% salary hike tied to her vote, the claim is not supported as stated.

claim: Says Mitt Romney wants to "get rid of Planned Parenthood."
rationale: Mitt Romney has repeatedly opposed Planned Parenthood and publicly supported cutting off its federal funding and limiting its ability to provide services; his long record includes calls to end taxpayer support and back legislative efforts to defund the organization. While he may not have used the exact words “get rid of Planned Parenthood” in every instance, his stated positions and policy proposals are consistent with wanting the organization’s funding and role eliminated.

claim: Says he "was the only Republican" to vote against creating a House panel to investigate Planned Parenthood.
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because it lacks a specific person and date, and House votes to create investigative panels have sometimes included multiple Republican dissenters rather than a single lone Republican. Without a precise vote, the claim that someone “was the only Republican” is likely inaccurate or at least ambiguous. Historical voting patterns on Planned Parenthood investigations show more than one Republican occasionally opposed procedural moves or specific panels.

claim: Wisconsin has "the fastest-shrinking middle class in the country."
rationale: The statement is misleading because whether a state has the "fastest-shrinking middle class" depends entirely on the definition and time period used, and no authoritative, widely-accepted measure shows Wisconsin topped the nation. Census and research analyses using common metrics (share of households in middle-income brackets or middle three quintiles) show Wisconsin’s middle class has declined in some periods but other states experienced larger drops; fact-checkers have flagged this claim as unsupported without a specific metric/timeframe.

claim: "Some even advocate wiping out 401(k)s entirely and replacing them with government-run accounts."
rationale: True. In U.S. policy debates a number of academics, commentators and some policymakers have argued for eliminating or sharply curtailing private 401(k)-style arrangements in favor of government-managed or universal retirement accounts. While the proposals vary in scope and detail, the existence of advocates pressing for government-run alternatives to 401(k)s is well documented.

claim: "When Rachel Zenzinger was on the Arvada City Council, she voted to spend taxpayer funds for a junket to China."
rationale: I could not find reliable evidence that Rachel Zenzinger, while serving on Arvada City Council, voted to spend taxpayer funds for a ‘‘junket’’ to China. Local records and news reporting do not document a council vote authorizing taxpayer-funded leisure travel to China by Zenzinger; similar sister‑city or trade delegations are often funded by a mix of private sponsors or participant-paid expenses. Given the lack of corroborating public records, the specific claim is not supported.

claim: Barack Obama's church gave a lifetime achievement award to Louis Farrakhan.
rationale: Contemporary fact-checking found no evidence that Trinity United Church of Christ (the church Barack Obama attended) presented a lifetime achievement award to Louis Farrakhan. While Farrakhan has been honored by other groups and has spoken at various Black churches and events, reputable sources concluded the specific claim about Obama’s church giving him a lifetime achievement award is unsupported.

claim: More than 1.5 million people moved into Georgia between the past two Census counts, and a majority consider themselves, African-American, Latino or Asian-American.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. The U.S. Census shows Georgia's population rose from about 9,687,653 in 2010 to about 10,711,908 in 2020—an increase of roughly 1.02 million, which is well under 1.5 million. While Black, Hispanic (Latino), and Asian populations grew and account for much of Georgia's diversity increase, available census totals do not support that a majority of the net gain were specifically African‑American, Latino, or Asian‑American without additional migration breakdowns.

claim: "In 2011, (Debbie) Wasserman Schultz missed 62 congressional votes — one of the worst records of any member of Congress."
rationale: The raw figure that Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz missed 62 roll-call votes in 2011 is broadly consistent with public roll-call records, but the claim that this was “one of the worst records of any member of Congress” is misleading. Several members missed more votes that year and different rankings and exemptions (excused absences, leadership duties) affect attendance comparisons, so calling it among the very worst overstates the case.

claim: Says President Barack Obama initially said the national health-care mandate isn't a tax, but his administration now says it is a tax.
rationale: President Obama and other White House spokespeople publicly described the individual mandate penalty as not being a tax during the political debate over the Affordable Care Act. However, when defending the law in court (notably in the Supreme Court case NFIB v. Sebelius), the Obama administration argued the payment operates as a tax or is within Congress’s taxing power. The Court ultimately upheld the payment as a tax for constitutional purposes, reflecting the administration’s legal position.

claim: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome "is absolutely a side effect of vaccination."
rationale: Extensive epidemiological research and reviews by major health organizations have found no causal link between routine childhood vaccination and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS); some studies report equal or lower SIDS rates among vaccinated infants. The peak age for SIDS coincides with the infant vaccination schedule, which can create a misleading temporal association but does not establish causation.

claim: Says Gov. Andrew Cuomo and Democratic lawmakers are "granting free tuition to illegal immigrants while closing Excelsior Scholarship applications to citizen students."
rationale: This claim misstates and conflates separate policies.
