claim: Says that the "28th Amendment" prohibits Congress from creating laws that apply to U.S. citizens but not to them, and vice-versa.
rationale: There is no ratified 28th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution—27 is the last amendment (ratified in 1992). Because no 28th Amendment exists, it cannot impose any prohibitions on Congress; claims about its text or effects refer to an unratified or nonexistent amendment and are therefore false.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson "voted to cut $700m from Medicare."
rationale: The claim as phrased is inaccurate or misleading. There is no record of Sen. Ron Johnson casting a specific vote that directly and explicitly "cut $700 million from Medicare;" discussions and votes he supported related to budget resolutions and health-care bills were characterized by much larger, longer-term entitlement savings estimates (often cited as hundreds of billions) or changes to Medicaid/ACA rather than a one-time $700 million Medicare cut. The figure and framing therefore misstate the public record.

claim: "After every major conflict ... what happened was that we ultimately hollowed out the force, largely by doing deep, across-the-board cuts."
rationale: The statement overgeneralizes. While many postwar periods (e.g., after World War I, Vietnam, and the post–Cold War drawdown) involved rapid demobilization and budget cuts that harmed readiness, not every major conflict resulted in uniform, deep across-the-board cuts that ‘hollowed out’ forces; some postwar periods led to targeted reforms or rapid rebuilding (and post‑9/11 saw substantial increases in defense spending). Thus the universal claim is inaccurate.

claim: Says Beto O’Rourke is "the only candidate to the U.S. Senate to call for" impeaching President Donald Trump.
rationale: The claim is false. Beto O’Rourke was not uniquely the only U.S. Senate candidate to call for President Trump’s impeachment — other candidates and public officials also publicly supported or called for impeachment at various times, and O’Rourke’s own statements were often conditional on evidence. The statement appears to overstate and ignores other races and candidates who took similar positions.

claim: Says President Barack Obama said that if he doesn’t turn the economy around after three years in office, he’ll be a one-term president.
rationale: There is no reliable record of President Obama making that exact three‑year ultimatum phrased as “if I don’t turn the economy around after three years, I’ll be a one‑term president.” He did acknowledge during his first term that voters would judge his economic performance and that the 2012 election would be a referendum on his stewardship, but the specific quoted threat appears to be a paraphrase rather than a documented statement. Given available public transcripts and fact‑checks, the claim overstates and misattributes a precise quote.

claim: "The Lancet peer-reviewed study confirms vaccine efficacy, not as 95% stated by the vaccine companies, but as: AstraZeneca 1.3%; Moderna 1.2%; J&J 1.2%; Pfizer 0.84%."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Peer‑reviewed randomized trial reports (many published in high‑profile journals including The Lancet and NEJM) show vaccine efficacy as large relative risk reductions (e.g., Pfizer ~94–95%, Moderna ~94%, AstraZeneca ~60–70% depending on dosing, J&J ~66% overall), not the ~0.8–1.3% figures quoted. The tiny percentages in the claim appear to be a miscalculation or confusion with absolute risk differences or different denominators, and no Lancet paper concludes those values as vaccine efficacy.

claim: Says President Barack Obama "spent nearly a trillion dollars on make-work government jobs."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. The largest single stimulus under Obama, the 2009 Recovery Act, totaled about $787 billion and its funds were split among tax cuts, safety-net programs, state fiscal relief, and infrastructure — not nearly $1 trillion spent solely on "make-work" government jobs. Even aggregating multiple budget items across his presidency does not support the specific assertion that nearly $1 trillion was spent on make-work government jobs.

claim: Congressman Robert Hurt has a plan to cut education by 40 percent.
rationale: There is no credible record that Rep. Robert Hurt authored or publicly promoted a specific plan to cut education funding by 40 percent. While Hurt voted with Republican budgets and proposals that sought reductions or restructuring of federal education spending, claims of a 40% across‑the‑board cut are not supported by documented policy proposals tied to him. The statement appears to conflate general partisan budget cuts with a precise, attributable plan.

claim: "Fox News went from 97% reporting to 94% in Virginia. The fraud is so blatant it's not funny anymore."
rationale: The claim mixes an unverified numerical change with an accusation of fraud without evidence. Election reporting percentages (e.g., “% reporting”) can move up or down when data feeds are corrected, precincts are reclassified, or totals are updated, and there is no credible evidence that Fox News shifted from 97% to 94% in Virginia as proof of fraud. Without a timestamp, source image, or corroborating official data, the fraud assertion is unsupported.

claim: The impeachment inquiry hearings "going on behind closed doors over which Congressman Schiff is presiding—they are consistent with the rules" of the U.S. House of Representatives.
rationale: House committees routinely conduct depositions and interviews in closed (executive) session and committee chairs have authority to run such proceedings. The Constitution vests impeachment power in the House and House rules and longstanding practice do not require an initial full-floor vote to begin a committee-led impeachment inquiry, so closed-door depositions overseen by Chairman Schiff were consistent with House rules and precedent.

claim: Says the Steele dossier "was—according to (James Comey's) June 2017 testimony—'salacious and unverified.' "
rationale: In his June 2017 congressional testimony Comey characterized the Steele dossier as unverified and described aspects of it as salacious. Multiple contemporaneous transcripts and news reports record him saying the FBI had not verified much of the dossier and that it contained salacious allegations, so the claim accurately reflects his testimony.

claim: At the State of the Union address, Democrats, "even on positive news … were like death and un-American. Un-American. Somebody said, ‘treasonous.’ I mean, yeah, I guess, why not? Can we call that treason? Why not?"
rationale: This quote matches remarks President Donald Trump made criticizing Democrats' reactions to his State of the Union address. Multiple contemporary news reports and transcript excerpts recorded him saying Democrats were “like death and un-American,” noting someone said “treasonous” and asking “Can we call that treason? Why not?”

claim: "Wages are on the rise — in fact we were the top small-business wage growth state in the nation."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits which state and the time period or data source are referenced; public wage-growth rankings are tied to specific datasets (BLS, ADP, state labor agencies) and I am not aware of evidence that any unspecified state was definitively the national leader for 'small‑business wage growth' without those details. Absent a named state, timeframe, and source, the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: "The Biden Administration is recklessly releasing hundreds of illegal immigrants who have COVID into Texas communities."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Biden Administration has a policy of purposely releasing known COVID-positive migrants en masse into Texas communities. Border and immigration agencies have medical screening, isolation, and transfer protocols for symptomatic or COVID-positive individuals, and while some migrants have been released to sponsors or parole programs after screening, documented instances of hundreds of known COVID-positive people being intentionally released are lacking.

claim: "That’s 5,615 projected coal-powered plants in just 8 countries. The USA has 15 - building 0 more."
rationale: Major public trackers of coal‑plant development do not support the precise figure of 5,615 'projected' coal plants in eight countries, and that number is far higher than commonly reported counts of proposed/planned projects. The United States does have existing coal capacity measured in hundreds of units but essentially no large new coal plants under serious construction or development, so the claim’s comparison and absolute numbers are misleading or incorrect.

claim: Quotes Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as saying "I’m speaking with myself, number one, because I have a very good brain and I’ve said lots of things."
rationale: There is no reliable record or credible sourcing showing Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez ever said that line; it appears to be a viral/misattributed quote. The wording also echoes phrases more commonly associated with other public figures and internet memes, suggesting the attribution is incorrect.

claim: Says "Eric Holder and his group came in and made" the Wisconsin Supreme Court race "highly partisan."
rationale: The claim attributes the transformation of a Wisconsin Supreme Court race into a "highly partisan" contest solely to Eric Holder and an unspecified "group." Contemporary reporting and campaign finance records show many national and local actors, party committees, and outside PACs contributed to the nationalization and partisanship of such races; there is no clear evidence that Holder alone or a single group he led uniquely caused that shift. Saying he "came in and made" the race highly partisan overstates and misattributes a broader, multi-actor process.

claim: "The United States is the No. 1 country in the world for energy resources. … We are the king daddy dogs when it comes to energy."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While the U.S. is among the world's top energy producers (recently leading in oil and natural gas production), it does not have the largest proven oil or natural gas reserves — countries like Venezuela, Saudi Arabia and Russia have larger proven reserves — and leadership varies by resource (coal, uranium, renewables). Saying the U.S. is the unequivocal “No. 1 country … for energy resources” overstates the case without specifying the metric.

claim: "CNN reports DemDebate had 2.3 million viewers. Trump rally had 6.7 million last night!"
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific pair of Nielsen/viewership figures as stated because the claim gives no date or source for either number. CNN does publish audience estimates for specific Democratic debates, but those figures vary by event and whether streaming is included; similarly, reported audience for a Trump rally can differ widely depending on whether it aggregates TV, streaming and social-media views. Without a clear date/source, the precise numbers (2.3M and 6.7M) cannot be verified as CNN-reported and thus the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: Photos prove the Denver light rail system has low ridership.
rationale: Photographs are anecdotal snapshots of particular times and places and cannot demonstrate system-wide or time-averaged ridership. Official ridership requires systematic counts (boardings, passenger miles, automated counters) and must account for peak vs off-peak, line segments, and seasonal variation, so photos alone do not prove low ridership.

claim: "The FBI just confirmed that it was ANTIFA, not Trump supporters, who breached the Capitol."
rationale: This is false. The FBI did not “confirm” that Antifa, rather than Trump supporters, breached the Capitol; DOJ prosecutions and FBI identification of hundreds of suspects tied the attack largely to Trump supporters and allied extremists. The FBI has explicitly said it found no evidence the riot was a coordinated Antifa operation and continues investigating many individual participants.

claim: European allies "pay us $2.5 billion a year to keep our forces there. It would cost us more money to bring the troops home than to keep them in Europe."
rationale: The claim mixes different accounting categories and is misleading. Allies do provide host‑nation support and contribute to NATO common budgets, but they do not collectively pay the U.S. a simple $2.5 billion per year to ‘keep our forces there,’ and reported reimbursements are lower and handled through complex agreements. The assertion that it would cost more to withdraw than to remain is speculative — relocation has up‑front costs but long‑term basing costs and savings depend on accounting choices and time horizon, so presenting it as a settled fact is incorrect.

claim: "We now have more jobs in solar than we do in oil."
rationale: The statement is presented without a timeframe or geography and is misleading as a universal claim. Globally (and in many major producing countries) oil and gas sectors still support as many or more jobs when direct, indirect and downstream employment are counted, while solar employment has grown rapidly but has not clearly surpassed oil/gas worldwide. In specific countries or by narrow definitions (direct, installation-only jobs) solar may outnumber certain oil subsectors, but that does not justify the blanket claim.

claim: "George Floyd’s ‘murder’ filmed before COVID-19."
rationale: The widely seen video of George Floyd’s killing was recorded on May 25, 2020, and his death occurred that day. The COVID-19 pandemic was already ongoing by then (WHO declared a pandemic on March 11, 2020), so the filming did not occur before COVID-19.

claim: "Have the suburbs been inundated with former residents of Atlanta housing projects? Absolutely not."
rationale: Available evidence from Atlanta public-housing redevelopment and relocation programs (e.g., HOPE VI and voucher displacements) shows residents were dispersed across the metropolitan area and many remained in the city rather than producing a large, concentrated influx into suburbs. Scholarly analyses and census/mobility data do not support a widespread ‘inundation’ of suburban jurisdictions by former Atlanta project residents.

claim: Says marijuana is "legal in most states in this country."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it omits what form of legalization is meant. As of mid‑2024 adult‑use (recreational) marijuana is legal in roughly half the states (about 24 states plus DC), not a majority, though medical cannabis is legal in a larger number (around 38 states). Without specifying recreational versus medical use, saying marijuana is "legal in most states" is inaccurate for recreational laws.

claim: "While (women) represent 47 percent of the overall work force, we only make up 23 percent of STEM-related occupations."
rationale: The claim is broadly accurate for common U.S. measures from the mid-2010s: women have made up roughly 46–48% of the civilian labor force while their share of many STEM-occupation measures has been in the low-to-mid-20s. Exact percentages vary by year and by how “STEM-related occupations” are defined, but 23% falls within the range reported by reputable sources for some definitions.

claim: The FEMA health care workers replacing the noncompliant nurses and doctors are NOT required to get vaccinated via the CDC."
rationale: The CDC issues guidance and recommendations but does not itself impose vaccination mandates; vaccination requirements are set by employers, states, or federal policy. Therefore saying FEMA health care workers are not required to be vaccinated “via the CDC” is accurate. However, those workers may still be subject to separate federal or employer vaccination requirements.

claim: "I can send every qualified person to a four-year college in their state for $150 billion."
rationale: The claim is implausible given basic arithmetic and public-college costs. There are millions of students who would qualify for in-state admission, and average annual in-state tuition at four-year public colleges is typically in the several-thousand to low-five-figure range; $150 billion divided across that population would not cover a full year of tuition for all, let alone multi-year degrees or additional costs. The statement also omits a timeframe and definitions (who counts as "qualified"), making the flat $150 billion figure unrealistic as a universal guarantee.

claim: Says Oregonians for Food and Shelter "proudly features board members from Monsanto and Syngenta and the (Oregon) Farm Bureau also receives funding from biotech companies."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and organization disclosures have shown that Oregonians for Food and Shelter has included representatives/affiliates of major seed and crop-chemical firms (commonly listed as Monsanto and Syngenta) on its board or membership lists, and the Oregon Farm Bureau has accepted sponsorships and funding from biotechnology/agrochemical companies. Both types of relationships have been publicly noted in news coverage and organizational materials.

claim: "One out of every two kids who are graduating college right now can't find a job."
rationale: The claim that 50% of current college graduates "can't find a job" is inconsistent with labor statistics and graduate surveys: unemployment rates for recent college graduates are typically in the single digits, and most graduates are employed, in grad school, or in other activities shortly after graduation. While underemployment or job-market mismatches affect some graduates, they do not amount to half of all graduates being jobless.

claim: Says we could have saved ourselves the cost of building the Powell Butte water reservoir.
rationale: The statement asserts that someone said the cost of building the Powell Butte reservoir could have been avoided, but no source, speaker, or supporting analysis is provided. I cannot verify that the quoted claim was actually made or that a credible technical/economic case exists showing the project costs were avoidable, so the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "One would have to go back more than a century to find a scenario where a president’s nominee for the Supreme Court was confirmed by the opposition party in the Senate when the vacancy occurred during an election year."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Historical Senate confirmation records show at least one instance within the past century where a president’s Supreme Court nominee was confirmed by an opposition-party Senate when the vacancy arose in an election year, so it is not true that you must go back more than a century. Whether a particular case qualifies can hinge on timing and how one defines ‘vacancy occurred during an election year.’

claim: "She’s voted for 60 tax increases, hurting the middle class and small businesses."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as written because it does not identify who “she” is and the claim’s numeric precision is not supported by verifiable roll‑call counts. Similar claims about female politicians have been repeatedly rated misleading or false by independent fact‑checkers because they rely on broad definitions of “tax increases,” include procedural or non‑tax votes, or count budgetary offsets. Without a clear target and a specific list of 60 identifiable votes that raise net taxes, the claim cannot be treated as factual.

claim: Repeal of Obamacare would "take away health care for 10.3 million Americans" who have received coverage since Oct. 1, 2013.
rationale: The 10.3 million figure corresponds roughly to early ACA enrollment totals (marketplace selections plus Medicaid expansion enrollments) since Oct 1, 2013, but saying repeal would automatically "take away health care" for all of them is misleading. Some of those people have other coverage sources or could obtain alternative coverage, and the number who would become uninsured depends on the specific repeal details (timing, replacement policies, and state actions).

claim: "Hillary Clinton killed in monster truck mishap."
rationale: This claim is false. There are no credible reports or official statements that Hillary Clinton died in any accident, and such a high-profile death would be widely and promptly reported by major news organizations; instead the item appears to be a viral hoax or satire.

claim: "Why would our president close the embassy to the Vatican? Hopefully, it is not retribution for Catholic organizations opposing Obamacare."
rationale: False. The United States has maintained an embassy to the Holy See (Vatican) since it was established in 1984 and no president has closed it; there is no documented instance of the embassy being shut as retribution. Claims that the embassy was closed or closed in retaliation for Catholic opposition to the Affordable Care Act are not supported by public records or reporting.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Steve Southerland "voted himself health care for life."
rationale: The claim is a misleading characterization. Members of Congress participate in the Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB) program and can continue coverage into retirement if they meet ordinary federal retirement rules and pay premiums; that is not a special "health care for life" giveaway enacted by a single vote. Ads or statements saying Southerland "voted himself health care for life" conflate routine federal employee benefits or votes preserving or continuing FEHB with a new, unilateral lifetime entitlement for members.

claim: Says David Perdue wants to abolish the U.S. Department of Education, which would cost Georgia schools $1 billion a year and eliminate millions in student loans.
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes policy and impacts. While some Republicans have advocated shrinking or eliminating the Department of Education, there is no reliable evidence that Perdue put forward a concrete plan that would directly cause Georgia to lose exactly $1 billion a year or "eliminate millions in student loans." Abolishing the Department would not automatically cancel existing federal student loans and federal K–12/higher‑education funding is distributed through many programs and laws that would require separate legislative changes.

claim: President Joe Biden will "control health care costs by slapping a 95% tax on prescription drugs."
rationale: There is no Biden administration policy or enacted law that imposes a 95% tax on prescription drugs. Biden has proposed and supported measures to lower drug prices (Medicare negotiation, caps, and penalties for excessive price hikes), but none call for a 95% tax; existing penalties in past legislation have been much smaller and/or structured differently. The 95% figure is a mischaracterization or exaggeration of negotiation/penalty proposals.

claim: Says Joe Biden stayed silent about violence at Black Lives Matter protests.
rationale: False — Joe Biden did not stay silent about violence at Black Lives Matter protests. During the 2020 unrest following George Floyd’s killing and in other instances, Biden publicly condemned violence and looting, urged protests remain peaceful, and called for accountability for both police misconduct and criminal acts. Saying he “stayed silent” contradicts widely reported public statements and speeches he made on the topic.

claim: "#GradInsurance debacle is a DIRECT result of #ObamaCare. #MIZZOU has to break the law to do the right thing."
rationale: The claim presents an unsupported causal link and an extreme prescription. While the Affordable Care Act has prompted many institutions to change health-plan administration, there is no clear evidence that a specific "GradInsurance debacle" at Mizzou was a direct and sole result of Obamacare, nor that the university is legally compelled to "break the law" to resolve it. Most campus insurance problems arise from administrative, budgetary, or contractual choices rather than a federal law forcing illegal action.

claim: Student loans from the federal government issued between 2007 and 2012 are on target "to produce $66 billion in profits for the United States government."
rationale: The $66 billion claim is misleading: that specific headline figure reflects a particular accounting choice and a narrow set of loans/years in some analyses, not a single uncontested government forecast. Different official estimators (CBO, Treasury, OMB) and different accounting methods (cash/budgetary vs. fair-value) produce substantially different results for loans issued 2007–2012, so stating a blanket ‘‘on target to produce $66 billion in profits’’ is inaccurate without that context.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson "opposes faster broadband internet in small towns" and "got nearly $90,000 in campaign contributions from the telecom special interests."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not verifiably true as stated. Ron Johnson has opposed certain government-funded or municipal broadband interventions, but that is not the same as flatly opposing "faster broadband" for small towns; the statement conflates policy disagreement with opposing better service. The contribution figure is ambiguous (no timeframe or defined donors) and cannot be confirmed as "nearly $90,000" without specifying the election cycle or which telecom groups are included.

claim: Says Texas U.S. Rep. John Culberson "was caught using campaign cash on collectibles, including Civil War memorabilia and fossils."
rationale: I find no clear, credible public reporting or campaign-finance documentation showing Rep. John Culberson was “caught” using campaign funds to buy collectibles such as Civil War memorabilia and fossils. Major reporting on his campaign expenditures focused on routine items (travel, events, staff) and there are no widely corroborated news accounts or audit findings that substantiate this allegation. Without a specific source or line-item evidence, the claim is not supported by available public knowledge.

claim: That Donald Trump said in 1998 if he were to run for president he would run as a Republican because "They’re the dumbest group of voters in the country. They believe anything on Fox News. I could lie and they’d still eat it up. I bet my numbers would be terrific."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and reliable archives contain no record or verifiable source for Trump making this remark in 1998; the wording first circulated years later on social media and has been flagged by multiple fact‑checkers as unsubstantiated. Major fact‑checking organizations found no primary source (no transcript, recording, or contemporaneous interview) to support the quoted claim.

claim: Says a car driving former University of Missouri System President Tim Wolfe "ran through the students, hit one of them" at the MU Homecoming Parade.
rationale: Contemporary news coverage, eyewitness video, and subsequent fact-checks show that Tim Wolfe drove his vehicle slowly through the MU Homecoming parade crowd but did not 'run through the students' or strike and injure anyone. No credible reports, hospital records, or police statements documented a student being hit by Wolfe's car.

claim: "The stock market does better when you have a Democratic president in the White House."
rationale: This claim is an oversimplification and not universally true. While some historical analyses show higher average stock returns during Democratic presidencies over certain long samples, results vary by time period, index used, and whether you measure price or total returns; correlation does not prove causation. Stock performance is driven by many factors (business cycles, monetary policy, global events) beyond the president's party.

claim: Says President Donald Trump's "effort to roll back regulations means that Big Ag now gets to inspect its own pork" and "they decided to stop testing for E. coli."
rationale: This is a misleading oversimplification. The Trump-era USDA did finalize a new swine inspection system that shifted some routine tasks to plant employees, but FSIS retained inspection authority and federal inspectors remained on site and in oversight roles—it was not a wholesale handover of inspection to industry. Separately, FSIS revised certain E. coli testing protocols (reducing or changing some routine testing programs), but it did not categorically stop all E. coli testing of pork across the board.

claim: Says Ted Cruz’s father "was with Lee Harvey Oswald" before the assassination of President John F. Kennedy.
rationale: Independent fact-checking and historical research have found no credible evidence that Rafael (Ted) Cruz's father was with Lee Harvey Oswald before JFK's assassination. The photo and claims circulating online were misidentified and contradicted by contemporaneous records and reporting, and historians have not corroborated the alleged meeting. The allegation originates from a debunked conspiracy theory rather than verifiable documentation.

claim: This year’s state budget and my spending proposal for Fiscal Year 2016 represent an infusion of more than $1 billion in additional money for K-12 education.
rationale: The claim is unverified because it does not identify the state or the speaker; without the specific state's FY2016 enacted budget and the named official's spending proposal there is no basis to confirm an extra $1 billion for K–12. While some states did increase K–12 funding by amounts on that order in 2015–16, the statement as presented is ambiguous and unsupported by the necessary budget documentation.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on gun control.
rationale: This is supported by the public record: Romney adopted different gun-control stances at different times — as a Massachusetts politician he supported some gun-safety measures, while as a national Republican presidential candidate he moved to more pro-gun, NRA-aligned positions. Those shifts have commonly been described as a flip-flop by fact-checkers and commentators.

claim: "Governor (Perry), you were a Democrat, having worked for Al Gore as his campaign manager..."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. While Texas Governor Rick Perry began his political career as a Democrat before switching to the Republican Party, he never worked as Al Gore’s campaign manager; there is no record of him holding a managerial role in Gore’s presidential campaigns. The statement conflates two separate facts and misattributes a national campaign position to Perry.

claim: The debt ceiling deal will result in "the lowest level of annual domestic spending since Dwight Eisenhower was president."
rationale: This claim is not supported by historical data or the provisions of recent debt‑ceiling agreements. Dwight Eisenhower's 1950s-era domestic spending was far lower in both nominal and inflation‑adjusted terms, and the contemporary debt ceiling deal mainly caps or modestly trims projected discretionary spending rather than cutting annual domestic spending to 1950s levels. Therefore it will not produce "the lowest level of annual domestic spending since Dwight Eisenhower was president."

claim: "45.6 million people watched (the State of the Union), the highest number in history. @FoxNews beat every other Network, for the first time ever, with 11.7 million people tuning in."
rationale: The claim mixes a true-sounding audience figure with incorrect context. While Nielsen reported about 45.6 million viewers for that specific State of the Union telecast, it was not the highest in history — earlier addresses (for example, some Obama-era SOTUs) drew larger audiences. Likewise, although Fox News drew roughly 11.7 million viewers for that telecast and may have been the single most-watched channel that night, it was not the first time Fox had topped other networks for a State of the Union broadcast.

claim: "The violent crime rate has risen, and the homicide rate has risen by more than 20 percent in just two years, really after 30 years of decline in violent crime."
rationale: The claim accurately summarizes U.S. trends: violent crime rates rose in the 2019–2021 period after roughly three decades of lower violent crime since the early 1990s, and homicide counts/rates increased by more than 20% over a two‑year span in federal/CDC data. Exact percentages vary by data source and the precise two‑year window, but the overall characterization is supported by FBI and CDC reporting.

claim: Says taxpayer subsidy for the Oregon Convention Center hotel jumped $100 million in closed-door sessions
rationale: I am not aware of credible reporting or public records through mid‑2024 that corroborate a specific claim that the taxpayer subsidy for the proposed Oregon Convention Center hotel increased by exactly $100 million during closed‑door sessions. Coverage of the project did report increases and complex subsidy calculations and that some negotiations occurred in executive sessions, but no reliable source shows a $100M jump tied to closed‑door meetings. Because the claim ties a precise dollar increase to secret meetings, it requires documentary evidence that is not available in the records I know.

claim: Says "in Katrina, they approved $60 billion within 10 days of the storm on a voice vote."
rationale: This is inaccurate. In the days after Hurricane Katrina Congress approved a much smaller immediate emergency package (on the order of ~$10 billion), while larger supplemental packages totaling roughly $60+ billion were enacted in subsequent weeks and through standard roll-call procedures rather than a single $60 billion voice vote within 10 days. The amount, timing, and procedure in the claim do not match the congressional record.

claim: Says "some people in the Great State of North Carolina have been sent TWO BALLOTS. RIGGED ELECTION in waiting!"
rationale: It is true that some North Carolina voters have received duplicate absentee/mail ballots in isolated, documented administrative errors; election officials and news outlets reported such cases. However, there is no reliable evidence that these incidents represented a coordinated effort to 'rig' the election or that they led to double-counting of votes given established safeguards and procedures.

claim: "74 percent of Republicans support the Affordable Care Act."
rationale: Major public-opinion polling over the last decade shows Republicans generally oppose the Affordable Care Act; overall GOP support has typically been well below 50%, not 74%. While some specific ACA provisions (e.g., protections for preexisting conditions) receive broad bipartisan backing, the claim that 74% of Republicans support the ACA as a whole is inconsistent with major polls from Gallup, Pew, and Kaiser.

claim: "There were 36 states where Republicans who were in charge refused to implement a state (health insurance) exchange."
rationale: This statement overstates and misattributes the situation. While a large number of states ultimately used the federal health insurance marketplace (commonly reported as about 34–36 depending on the date), not all of those states were led by Republicans nor did all “refuse” to implement exchanges for partisan reasons. Control of governors’ offices and legislatures varied across those states and the precise count depends on timing and how one counts state-partnership exchanges.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty advocated lowering the penalty for crimes like strangulation in domestic violence cases because "they just ‘throw more people into the’" jail "‘system."
rationale: I cannot find reliable evidence or credible reporting that Gerald Daugherty made that statement or advocated lowering penalties for strangulation in domestic violence cases. The claim appears unverified and may be a misquote or misattribution. Without a primary source (audio, video, or reputable news citation) the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: Wisconsin is "clearly seeing a decline in COVID infections"
rationale: I cannot verify that Wisconsin is "clearly seeing a decline in COVID infections" without up-to-date, state-level surveillance data. Determining a clear decline requires multi-week decreases in reported cases, test positivity, hospitalizations, and/or wastewater signals; trends have varied over time and by region within the state. Because I lack current data, I cannot confirm the claim as stated.

claim: If Missouri Amendment 1 passes, the auditor's office "could take one district, St. Louis here, and merge it with a district in southwest Missouri, a Republican district, and they don't even have to touch."
rationale: Missouri law and typical redistricting rules require districts to be contiguous and meet population and legal standards; an auditor would not be empowered to unilaterally splice a St. Louis district onto a noncontiguous southwest Missouri district so that the two "don't even have to touch." Amendment language changing who draws maps does not override basic contiguity and legal constraints or give the state auditor carte blanche to create noncontiguous districts. Any maps would also face judicial review and federal requirements.

claim: "The permission to engage was given before the word RPG was ever used."
rationale: The claim makes a precise chronological assertion but provides no context (which event, actors, or sources). Without transcripts, timestamps, or authoritative records proving that the authorization preceded any mention of "RPG," the assertion cannot be verified and should not be accepted as fact. Because this is an absolute statement and lacks supporting evidence, I judge it false for now.

claim: "There are no provisions in here that substantially affect or advantage the big Wall Street bankers."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it refers to an unspecified text (“in here”). Absent the specific bill or document, asserting that it contains no provisions that substantially affect or advantage large Wall Street banks is implausible; many financial and regulatory texts include clauses that have measurable impacts on big banks. A document-specific analysis is required to support such a categorical assertion.

claim: "If you’re a low-wage worker and you’re single and don’t have children, we’re literally taxing you into poverty."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. While low‑wage single workers without children often pay regressive payroll taxes and receive little or no refundable tax credits (unlike parents who qualify for larger EITC/CTC amounts), whether taxes alone push someone below the poverty line depends on their pre‑tax earnings, hours worked, state policies, and benefits. Many low‑wage single workers earn slightly above the federal poverty threshold before taxes, so taxes can reduce but do not universally “literally” drive them into poverty.

claim: "U.S. teenagers have now fallen behind their counterparts in Ireland, Poland and even Vietnam in math and science."
rationale: International assessment results in recent cycles (notably PISA and TIMSS) show U.S. teenagers score below peers in countries such as Ireland and Poland and have been outscored by Vietnam in math and/or science in several administrations. While exact rankings depend on the specific test year and grade, the broad claim that U.S. teens have fallen behind these countries is supported by those assessment trends.

claim: Says a gun bill before the Senate "is proposing the universal registration of all firearms and their owners."
rationale: The claim is not supported by widely known Senate gun proposals; recent federal gun bills have focused on background checks, crisis interventions, safe-storage incentives, and funding rather than creating a universal registry of all firearms and owners. Universal registration is politically contentious and would normally be explicit in bill text; no prominent pending Senate bill contains language requiring universal registration of every firearm and owner.

claim: Says Texas "high school graduation rates are at all-time highs."
rationale: The statement is too general and lacks a timeframe; while Texas reported record or near‑record graduation rates in some recent years, outcomes depend on the specific metric (four‑year cohort rate, extended‑year rates), subgroup, and year. Because the claim asserts a blanket, current "all‑time highs" without specifying which rate or year, it is not verifiably true as stated.

claim: "Two million more people just dropped out of Obamacare. It is in a death spiral."
rationale: The claim that “two million more people just dropped out” is not supported by official enrollment data; recent years showed stable or rising ACA marketplace enrollments after subsidies were expanded, and no credible report documented a sudden 2 million exodus. Calling the law “in a death spiral” is a subjective political claim that requires evidence of sustained premium spikes and mass healthy-person departures, which has not occurred given government subsidy adjustments and enrollment trends.

claim: Says professional football coach Rex Ryan "won championships in New York. The AFC, I think, twice."
rationale: Rex Ryan did coach the New York Jets to two consecutive AFC Championship Game appearances (2009 and 2010) but his teams lost both games, so he did not win the AFC championship twice in New York. The statement misstates appearances as championships won.

claim: "Most of Ted Cruz’s money comes from Washington, from outside the state of Texas."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and likely incorrect as stated. While Ted Cruz has attracted substantial out-of-state donations—especially during his 2016 presidential campaign—there is no clear evidence that a majority of his receipts come specifically from Washington, D.C.; his funding has come from a broad national donor base and significant support within Texas. Financial disclosure and campaign‑finance data show mixed geographic sources rather than a dominant Washington, D.C. share.

claim: President Barack Obama, Nancy Pelosi and Harry Reid support Rick Perry’s "decision to give in-state tuition to illegal immigrants."
rationale: The claim says Obama, Pelosi and Reid supported Rick Perry’s decision to grant in‑state tuition to undocumented students; there is no clear public record that the three national Democratic leaders explicitly endorsed Perry’s specific Texas action. While Democrats including Pelosi and Reid and Barack Obama have historically supported federal measures like the DREAM Act or state policies expanding tuition access for undocumented students, that is not the same as a public endorsement of Perry’s gubernatorial decision and the claim conflates general Democratic positions with direct support for Perry.

claim: "If we keep the minimum wage at the current level, then single-parent families earning the minimum wage at a full-time job will live in poverty in New Jersey."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement but the outcome depends on specifics (wage level, hours, family size, taxes and benefits). For some household sizes and the current New Jersey minimum wage a full-time earner would fall below the federal poverty guideline, but for smaller single‑parent households or with additional tax credits/benefits they could be at or above the poverty line. Because it’s conditional on unspecified parameters, the blanket phrasing “will live in poverty” is not generally true.

claim: Insurance companies have seen their profits soar by more than 400 percent since 2001.
rationale: The statement is overbroad and not verifiable as stated. ‘‘Profits’’ can mean different measures (net income, underwriting profit, after‑tax profits) and outcomes vary by insurer and year; available industry data and prior fact‑checks show large increases for some measures or firms but not a uniform 400%+ rise across the insurance industry since 2001. Without a specified metric and end year the claim is misleading.

claim: "We borrow $4 billion every single day, much of it from China."
rationale: The claim is misleading. U.S. federal borrowing averaged roughly $1–3 billion per day in many recent years (varying by fiscal year) and only in some high-deficit years would it approach $4 billion/day; the exact daily figure depends on the year and how 'borrow' is measured. Also the U.S. finances deficits with a mix of domestic and foreign buyers, and China holds a substantial but minority share of U.S. Treasuries, not 'much' of daily new borrowing.

claim: Figures for September 2014’s job growth in Wisconsin mark the "largest private-sector job creation we've had in the month of September in more than a decade"
rationale: The claim asserts Sept 2014 was the largest September private‑sector job gain in more than a decade, but historical payroll data for Wisconsin show multiple Septembers in the prior ten‑plus years with comparable or larger private‑sector gains. Because the statement is a superlative about a specific month over a long window and available monthly series show variability, the claim overstates 2014’s uniqueness and is not supported as presented.

claim: The Wisconsin state Assembly chambers extend to the bathroom and the parlor, and rules allow members to vote for each other if the member is in the chambers.
rationale: This claim is false. Wisconsin Assembly rules and the state constitution require members to be physically present on the Assembly floor for their vote to count and do not authorize casting votes on behalf of another member; there is no rule that the chamber 'extends' into bathrooms or parlors. The Assembly also has enforcement mechanisms (sergeant-at-arms) to compel attendance rather than allowing remote or proxy voting.

claim: Early morning election results from Michigan and Wisconsin show voter fraud.
rationale: This claim is false as stated: there is no credible evidence that early-morning result patterns in Michigan or Wisconsin constitute voter fraud. Official canvasses, bipartisan audits, recounts and court rulings have not substantiated widespread fraud in those states, and the common explanation for early shifts is the later reporting of absentee/mail ballots and normal reporting delays rather than illicit activity.

claim: "People (are) paying more in taxes than they will for food, housing and clothing combined."
rationale: The statement is a broad, unqualified claim about "people" that is inconsistent with typical household spending patterns. Data on household budgets show housing and food are the largest expense categories and combined with clothing usually exceed the average total tax burden (federal, state and local) for most households; while some very high‑income households could pay more in taxes than they spend on those categories, the blanket claim is misleading and false as stated.

claim: "The average life expectancy for African Americans in Saint Louis and Saint Louis County varies by as much as 18 years compared to the white population, with nearly half of all African-American kids under the age of 18 living in poverty."
rationale: Multiple public-health analyses and local reporting have documented life-expectancy differences on the order of 15–20 years between predominantly Black and predominantly white neighborhoods in St. Louis, and U.S. Census/American Community Survey estimates show Black child poverty in the city approaches about half. Although exact numbers shift by year and by whether one looks at city or county alone, the core claims — an ~18-year life-expectancy gap and nearly half of Black children living in poverty in parts of the St. Louis area — are supported by published local analyses and census-based poverty data.

claim: New York is "leading the nation with the lowest imprisonment rate of any large state"
rationale: The claim lacks a date and a precise definition of “large state,” and available data show New York reduced its incarceration rate but is not clearly the single lowest among all large states. Other high-population states (and some comparably large states like New Jersey, Illinois, or Pennsylvania depending on the year and metric) have had similar or lower imprisonment rates. Because rankings change by year and by how ‘imprisonment rate’ and ‘large’ are defined, the blanket claim is not supported as stated.

claim: Says the Ohio Consumers’ Council office employs 74 lawyers and that the funding them is wasteful duplication.
rationale: The claim that the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel office employs 74 lawyers is inaccurate: the Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel is a relatively small, statutory consumer-advocate agency and its staff count (including attorneys) is far lower than 74. The second part—labeling funding for the office as “wasteful duplication”—is an opinion, not an objective fact; the office has a distinct statutory role representing residential utility customers that is not simply duplicative of other agencies. Because the numeric assertion is wrong and the policy judgment is subjective, the overall claim is false.

claim: Says New Hampshire had the fourth-lowest unemployment rate in the country during Maggie Hassan’s time in the state Senate.
rationale: Maggie Hassan served in the New Hampshire State Senate roughly 2004–2010, and state unemployment rankings change monthly and yearly. New Hampshire did often have low unemployment during that era, but it did not consistently hold the specific position of fourth‑lowest for the entire period; without a precise date the blanket claim is unsupported and therefore misleading.

claim: Supported in-state tuition in Arkansas for illegal immigrants "if you'd sat in our schools from the time you're 5 or 6 years old and you had become an A-plus student," among other things.
rationale: The claim as presented is unverified and lacks an attributed speaker or time; I could not confirm a reliable record that Arkansas formally granted in-state tuition to undocumented immigrants under the quoted condition or that a public official made that exact statement. Arkansas law has generally restricted in-state tuition to residents/citizens, and the quoted phrasing does not match any well-documented policy change or attributed public quote. Because of the missing context and lack of corroboration, the claim is judged false as stated.

claim: Says Ayn Rand said, "The question isn’t who is going to let me; it’s who is going to stop me."
rationale: The line "The question isn’t who is going to let me; it’s who is going to stop me" is widely and reliably attributed to Ayn Rand and appears in her work; it is a well-known Rand quotation. It has been reproduced in many quotation collections and cited as coming from her novel The Fountainhead (and from her public remarks), so attribution to Ayn Rand is correct.

claim: The debt is "nearly $6 trillion more than when President Obama was sworn into office."
rationale: The statement is not accurate as presented. Using standard measures, U.S. federal debt rose by substantially more than $6 trillion from when President Obama was sworn in (January 2009) to the end of his term — roughly $8–10 trillion for total gross federal debt and roughly $6–8 trillion for debt held by the public, so “nearly $6 trillion more” understates the increase or depends on a nonstandard cut. The claim omits which debt measure and which comparison date it uses, making the plain reading misleading.
cited_knowledge: Based on historical U.S. federal debt data (Treasury/CBO measures): total federal debt outstanding was about $10–11 trillion in Jan 2009 and roughly $19–20 trillion by 2017 (and debt held by the public rose from roughly $6 trillion to the low- to mid-teens), so increases were larger than $6 trillion under common measures.
safety_notes: Ambiguity over which debt measure (total debt vs. debt held by the public) and which comparison date can change the arithmetic; if a different start/end date or narrow component is intended the numeric claim could be closer to true.

claim: Insurance companies "have made a fortune with Obamacare."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. While some insurers have earned profits from ACA-related markets in certain years, many insurers lost money on the individual marketplaces early on and profitability has varied widely by company, state, and year. ACA rules (like the medical loss ratio) and the structure of subsidies mean gains are not uniformly large or guaranteed across the industry.

claim: "Most of these killers tend to be 18, 19 years old."
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported: it does not define which category of "killers" or the jurisdiction/timeframe. Broad crime data and studies of homicide and mass-shooting perpetrators show a range of ages (teens through middle adulthood) and do not indicate that most perpetrators are specifically 18–19 years old. Without a defined group and evidence, the blanket claim is not true.

claim: Property taxes "are now 18% higher than when (Mark Sharpe) first took office."
rationale: The statement is unverified as presented because it omits the jurisdiction, time span, and whether “property taxes” means tax rates, assessed values, or actual tax bills. Confirming an 18% increase requires comparing official tax-rate tables, assessment rolls, or average tax bills from the date Mark Sharpe first took office to today; no such data are provided. Without those specifics the numeric claim is unsubstantiated and should be treated as false pending evidence.

claim: As Massachusetts governor, Mitt Romney used a line-item veto to cut "millions of dollars for firefighting equipment," including firefighters' "coats, pants, helmets and boots."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and later fact-checks show that as Massachusetts governor Romney used his line-item veto authority to strike an appropriation for firefighters’ protective clothing that amounted to several million dollars. The vetoed item was described in budget language as funding for protective/turnout gear (commonly coats, pants, helmets and boots).

claim: "We've got 7.2 percent unemployment (in Ohio), but when you include the folks who have stopped looking for work, it's actually over 10 percent."
rationale: The statement gives no date, and Ohio unemployment rates fluctuate monthly. While the broader measure that adds discouraged and marginally attached workers (U-6-style measures) is typically higher than the headline U-3 rate, you cannot verify that a 7.2% headline rate in Ohio would correspond to 'over 10%' without a specific month and data. It may have been true at particular times, but as stated the claim is unverified and therefore treated as false.

claim: An email from Hillary Clinton to Donna Brazile Oct.17th, 2016 stated: "If that f-----’ bastard wins, we’re all going to hang from nooses! You better fix this s---!"
rationale: There is no credible record in the publicly released Clinton, Podesta, or DNC email archives of Hillary Clinton sending an email to Donna Brazile on Oct 17, 2016 containing that quoted threat. Such an inflammatory, memorable language would have been quickly reported and sourced from the leaked archives but no reputable source or primary email record supports the claim.

claim: We live in "a time of historically low violent crime rates and historically high gun ownership rates nationally."
rationale: The statement bundles two different claims; taken together they are inaccurate. While overall violent crime rates are much lower than the peaks of the early 1990s, homicide and some violent-crime measures rose in 2020–21 and remain elevated compared with the late 2010s. Meanwhile, surveys show the share of adults or households that own guns is not at an all-time high (it was higher in earlier decades), even though the total number of firearms and purchases spiked recently. Because the ownership-rate claim is misleading and the crime claim omits recent upticks, the combined assertion is false.

claim: Says "Rep. Jim Weidner proposed a bill taking away health care for 80,000 of Oregon's children."
rationale: I could not find authoritative evidence that Rep. Jim Weidner authored a bill that explicitly “takes away health care for 80,000 of Oregon’s children.” Such a large, specific action would be widely documented; the claim appears to conflate or exaggerate the effects of proposed budget or eligibility changes. Without a bill number or verifiable legislative text tying him to a measure that would directly terminate coverage for that exact cohort, the claim is not supported.

claim: The STAR Ohio fund "just received the highest possible credit rating one of these funds can receive."
rationale: The claim asserts a recent upgrade to "the highest possible credit rating," but STAR Ohio has long held top short-term ratings from some agencies (e.g., S&P's AAAm or similar short-term fund grades) rather than having just newly received them. Whether it is true depends on which rating agency and timeframe are meant; there is no unambiguous evidence that a new, singular "highest possible" rating was just awarded. Because the statement is vague about which scale/agency and presents timing as recent, it is not reliably true as stated.

claim: "We work longer hours than any people in the industrialized world, including the Japanese."
rationale: This is incorrect: international labor statistics (OECD/ILO) show the United States does not have the longest average annual working hours in the industrialized world. Countries such as Mexico and historically South Korea have had higher average hours, while Japan’s average annual hours are generally lower than the U.S. figure, so the blanket claim is overstated.

claim: "Today and every day, an estimated 14,000 Americans will lose their health insurance coverage."
rationale: This claim is misleading. There is no authoritative evidence that exactly 14,000 Americans lose health insurance every single day on an ongoing basis; such a figure is likely produced by dividing a particular annual estimate by 365 or by misinterpreting a short-term spike. Insurance loss (churn) varies by year, economic conditions, policy changes, and the definition of “lose coverage,” so the blanket statement “today and every day” is inaccurate.

claim: "Wisconsin is not as obese as the national average is. The national average, 35.7 percent of the population is obese. In Wisconsin, it's closer to 26 percent."
rationale: The specific numbers in the claim are inaccurate or misleading without a year/source. Recent CDC/BRFSS-based estimates show U.S. adult obesity prevalence well above 35.7% (around 40%+ in recent years), and Wisconsin’s adult obesity rate is lower than the national rate but is generally in the low 30s rather than as low as 26%.

claim: Says Jeff Foxworthy wrote a ‘fence test’ for Republicans and Democrats.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that comedian Jeff Foxworthy authored a formal "fence test" for Republicans and Democrats; the item appears to be an internet meme or misattribution. Foxworthy is primarily known for his "You might be a redneck" comedy routines, and reputable sources do not attribute a partisan "fence test" document to him.

claim: Georgia has saved $20 million through changes in criminal sentencing.
rationale: The claim is too vague and cannot be verified as stated: public reports about sentencing reforms in Georgia (U.S. state) have produced varying savings estimates depending on the reform, period, and accounting method, and I find no definitive, universally accepted figure of exactly $20 million without a cited timeframe or source. Because the statement gives a precise dollar amount but no context, it is not reliably supported by available general knowledge.

claim: There are "360,000 (deaths) a year from swimming pools. But we don’t shut the country down for that."
rationale: The asserted figure (360,000 annual deaths from swimming pools) is far higher than available data. WHO estimates roughly 200–300 thousand global drowning deaths per year (all locations) and only a fraction of those occur in swimming pools; U.S. pool drowning deaths are in the low thousands annually per CDC. There is no evidence that 360,000 deaths per year are attributable specifically to swimming pools.

claim: "Russia has more diversity in its governmental representation than we do in Texas."
rationale: The claim is false. Russia's national political elite and appointed officials are overwhelmingly ethnic Russian, male, and dominated by a centralized ruling party with limited political pluralism, whereas Texas—while imperfectly representative—elects a racially and gender-diverse set of officials (Hispanic, Black, Asian, women, etc.) across local and state offices. Overall, Russia does not demonstrate greater governmental diversity than Texas.

claim: Bill Nelson’s vote for the Affordable Care Act "cuts $500 billion from Medicare to pay for new government programs."
rationale: When the Affordable Care Act was scored, the Congressional Budget Office and other nonpartisan analyses found roughly $500 billion in net reductions to projected Medicare spending over the first decade, and those savings were used in part to offset the law’s new coverage and subsidy programs. The reductions came mainly from lower payments to providers and Medicare Advantage plans and changes to payment formulas rather than direct cuts to most beneficiaries’ guaranteed benefits, a nuance sometimes omitted in political claims.

claim: Federal spending is "the highest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years (and) revenue is the lowest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Federal outlays did spike during the COVID-era to levels not seen in many decades, but those levels were comparable to World War II-era peaks (well over 60 years ago), so phrasing it as "highest in 60 years" is inaccurate or at best imprecise; similarly, revenues fell sharply in 2020 but the long historical series includes other very low revenue years (e.g., 2009) and the exact ranking depends on the year and accounting conventions, so the blanket "lowest in 60 years" is not clearly supported.

claim: "As we watch the news from Colorado with horror and sympathy for the families, we should remember that each day more than 80 Americans are killed by gunfire, unnecessary tragedies."
rationale: Recent US mortality data show roughly 45,000–50,000 firearm deaths per year in recent years, which averages well above 80 deaths per day. Therefore the statement that more than 80 Americans are killed by gunfire each day is supported when counting all firearm deaths (homicides, suicides, accidents, legal intervention).

claim:
Says U.S. Sen Sherrod Brown "promised that the first stimulus bill would fund the
Brent Spence Bridge."
rationale: There is no clear contemporaneous evidence that Sen. Sherrod Brown promised the first COVID-era stimulus bill would fund the Brent Spence Bridge. Brown has repeatedly advocated for federal support for the Brent Spence Bridge and sought funding in subsequent infrastructure proposals, but the initial CARES Act and early relief packages were not structured to deliver a specific bridge construction appropriation. The claim appears to conflate his general advocacy with a specific promise about the first stimulus bill.

claim: Says Barack Obama "robbed Medicare (of) $716 billion to pay for ... Obamacare."
rationale: This is misleading. The Affordable Care Act included provisions that the CBO and Medicare actuaries estimated would reduce Medicare spending by about $716 billion over a decade, but those were projected spending reductions and payment changes (e.g., cuts to Medicare Advantage overpayments, provider payment adjustments, and fraud/waste reductions), not a literal "robbery" or a one-time seizure of Medicare funds or across-the-board benefit cuts.

claim: "Biden’s banking nominee demands all ‘private bank accounts’ be eliminated"
rationale: The claim misstates and exaggerates the nominee's position. Biden's controversial banking nominee (widely reported as Saule Omarova) has proposed expanding public payment and deposit options at the Federal Reserve and rethinking banks' exclusive control over deposit funds in academic work, but she did not explicitly call for eliminating all private bank accounts. Opponents have paraphrased her academic proposals in alarmist terms, producing the false headline presented.

claim: "Newspapers have framed this election as my fight against the Illinois mafia."
rationale: The claim asserts that newspapers broadly framed an election as the speaker’s “fight against the Illinois mafia,” but there is no clear evidence that major newspapers uniformly characterized any recent election in those terms. Media coverage typically varies and such a distinctive, charged phrase would be verifiable and attributable to specific outlets; absent named papers or examples, the statement is an overgeneralization and appears to be partisan rhetoric rather than a documented consensus.

claim: "There are no tax increases in this debt limit bill. Period."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement about an unspecified “debt limit bill” and cannot be validated without the specific bill text; absolute claims are rarely correct. Historically, debt-limit agreements and related legislation sometimes include offsets, fee changes, or revenue measures that can functionally raise revenue, so asserting “no tax increases. Period.” is misleading without checking the enacted language. Therefore I judge the blanket claim false pending examination of the specific bill.

claim: "In the last two years, super PACs raised more than $180 million -- with roughly half of it coming from fewer than 200 super-rich people and roughly 20 percent from corporations."
rationale: The claim is not reliably true as stated because it omits a clear time window and the cited breakdown does not match publicly available campaign‑finance patterns. In recent U.S. federal election cycles super PACs have raised well more than $180 million overall and analyses show large shares coming from a relatively small number of wealthy donors, but the precise figures (half from fewer than 200 people and ~20% from corporations) vary by cycle and generally do not match this exact formulation. Because the statement is specific but lacks a defined two‑year period, it cannot be verified as accurate.

claim: Between 40 and 50 percent of tax filers do not owe any income tax.
rationale: Recent analyses by IRS and independent tax researchers show that in multiple recent years roughly 40–50% of tax units/households had zero federal individual income tax liability after credits. The exact share varies by year and by whether one counts tax returns, tax units, or households and whether refundable credits and payroll taxes are included, but the claim matches commonly reported ranges for recent years.

claim: "Masks will kill quite a few people, it’s well known that they reduce blood oxygen levels and those with respiratory and cardiac disorders will die."
rationale: This claim is false. Multiple peer-reviewed studies and guidance from major public-health agencies show that cloth, surgical, and N95 masks do not meaningfully reduce blood oxygen levels or cause CO2 poisoning in the general public, and there is no evidence that mask use has caused large numbers of deaths. While people with severe respiratory distress may have individualized medical exemptions, the blanket assertion that masks will 'kill quite a few people' is unsupported.

claim: There are nanoparticles in the COVID-19 vaccine that will help people "locate you" via 5G networks.
rationale: This claim is false. Authorized COVID-19 vaccines do not contain metal microchips or radio transmitters — mRNA vaccines use lipid nanoparticles to deliver genetic material, but those particles are biological delivery vehicles, not electronic devices and cannot be interrogated or 'located' by 5G networks. 5G is a radio communication standard and cannot detect or track passive nanoparticles inside a body; locating a person via a network requires an active transmitter or a device with power and networking capability.

claim: Perpetrators of school shootings "have been drugged in many cases … many of these young boys have been on Ritalin since they were in kindergarten."
rationale: Systematic reviews and news fact-checks find no evidence that 'many' school shooters were chronically medicated with Ritalin from kindergarten. While a small number of perpetrators have had histories of psychiatric diagnoses or prescription drugs (of varying types), there is no consistent pattern showing most were on Ritalin long-term, and some high-profile shooters were never prescribed it. The blanket claim overstates and mischaracterizes the available evidence.

claim: Six states "decided to stop counting" votes as Donald Trump was "headed for a win" on election night.
rationale: This claim is false. No state officially “decided to stop counting” votes on election night to freeze a Trump lead; state and local election officials are required to process and count all legally cast ballots and in 2020 many jurisdictions continued counting into the next days because of mail and provisional ballots. What people sometimes point to were media projection pauses or slower overnight counting in some counties for procedural or security reasons, not six states halting counts to alter the outcome.

claim: "People were hopeless. Sixty percent of the population, 70 percent of the population wanted to live somewhere else. . . . By the time I left, 70 percent wanted to stay."
rationale: The claim presents specific large shifts in public opinion (60–70% wanting to leave, later 70% wanting to stay) but offers no source, context, dates, or location. Such concrete changes require verifiable polling or survey evidence; absent that, the statement is unverified and likely a misremembered or misrepresented quote rather than a factual report.

claim: "However, it took $19.5 million in Oregon Lottery funds for the Port of Newport to eventually land the new NOAA Marine Operations Center-Pacific."
rationale: The claim frames the NOAA Marine Operations Center–Pacific as having been secured solely by $19.5 million in Oregon Lottery funds to the Port of Newport, which is misleading. The NOAA facility was built with federal funding and local/state support; Oregon did authorize roughly $19.5 million in state economic development/bond-related assistance connected to the effort, but that funding was not a simple one-time direct 'Oregon Lottery' cash payment nor the only or decisive source. Saying it 'took $19.5 million in Oregon Lottery funds' overstates and misattributes the funding structure.

claim: In Sauk City, Wisconsin, "the ID office" that provides identification for voting "is only open on the fifth Wednesday of every month" -- a total of four days in 2016.
rationale: The claim is misleading. While 2016 did have four fifth Wednesdays, the Sauk City “ID office” was not only open on those days — voter ID services were available through regular municipal/ county offices and other DMV locations and hours, and local schedules and appointment options meant the service was not limited to four days. Fact-checks at the time found the statement exaggerated the actual availability of ID services.

claim: President Obama’s health care law says "when you sell your house now you have to pay a 3.8 percent tax."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did create a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax, but it is not a blanket tax on every home sale. The NIIT only applies to net investment income for taxpayers above income thresholds and can apply to capital gains on investment or second property sales; gains from a principal residence are generally excluded up to $250,000/$500,000, so most typical home sellers will not automatically owe a 3.8% tax.

claim: Says Amazon has removed "an educational game about Gettysburg."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream reporting that Amazon removed an identifiable "educational game about Gettysburg." The claim appears to stem from unverified social-media posts and lacks a named title, platform, or an official Amazon statement, so it is not supported by available information.

claim: Says Jennifer Aniston said, "Me and all the Trump supporter celebrities decide to make a company named ‘celebrities for Trump’"
rationale: There are no credible reports, recordings, or reputable news sources showing Jennifer Aniston ever said that line or announced a group called 'celebrities for Trump.' Aniston has generally been associated with Democratic-leaning public statements, and the quoted wording appears fabricated or misattributed.

claim: "BREAKING: Trump family donates $1 billion to wall fund."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or evidence that the Trump family donated $1 billion to any border wall fund. Public news coverage of wall fundraising and the Trump family's finances does not show a donation of that magnitude, and such a large gift would have been widely reported.

claim: "Obama admits he is not a citizen."
rationale: This claim is false. Barack Obama has repeatedly affirmed he is a U.S. citizen and in 2011 released his long-form birth certificate showing he was born in Honolulu, Hawaii; courts and state election officials have rejected challenges to his citizenship and eligibility. There is no credible evidence of Obama admitting he is not a citizen; the 'birther' assertions have been debunked.

claim: "Hillary Clinton leaves the country as Mueller indictment is announced."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous news reporting that former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton left the country at the time any Robert Mueller indictment was announced. Major indictments from the Mueller investigation were widely covered and would have reported unusual travel by a high-profile figure like Clinton; no such reports exist. The claim appears to be unsubstantiated and likely a rumor or misinterpretation of unrelated travel.

claim: "Despite what you may have heard about Wisconsin’s finances, Wisconsin is on track to have a budget surplus this year."
rationale: I cannot verify the claim as presented because it gives no specific year and my training data only goes through June 2024. State budget balances change with updated revenue collections and official forecasts; without a cited timeframe and the latest Legislative Fiscal Bureau or comptroller projections this statement is not verifiable. Given the ambiguity and potential for changed projections, the safe determination is that the claim is not established as factual.

claim: "They (Clinton and Obama) have never to my knowledge been involved in legislation nor hearings nor engagement on this issue (climate change)."
rationale: The claim is false. Barack Obama took major executive and policy actions on climate (e.g., Clean Power Plan, EPA rules, active U.S. role in the Paris Agreement) and Hillary Clinton, as a U.S. Senator and later Secretary of State, publicly supported climate legislation and participated in international climate negotiations and policy efforts. Both have been repeatedly engaged in legislation, hearings, and diplomatic efforts on climate change.

claim: Says former Clinton budget director Alice Rivlin said the stimulus bill "won't actually stimulate the economy."
rationale: I could not confirm that Alice Rivlin uttered the exact line “won't actually stimulate the economy.” Rivlin publicly supported fiscal stimulus in general while criticizing the composition or timing of specific measures, so attributions that she flatly said the entire stimulus “won't actually stimulate” appear to be mischaracterizations or paraphrases rather than a verbatim quote. Without a reliable primary source for that exact wording, the claim is not supported.

claim: "To children and the vast majority of young and middle-aged adults and the vast majority of teachers, (the coronavirus) poses virtually zero threat."
rationale: The claim is false because while children and many younger adults generally have lower risks of severe acute COVID-19 than older adults, risk is not zero. Documented outcomes include pediatric hospitalizations, deaths, multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), severe illness and deaths among young and middle-aged adults, and post‑COVID conditions (“long COVID”); teachers have also experienced infections and workplace outbreaks. Thus describing the threat as “virtually zero” is inaccurate and overstated.

claim: Brewpubs can't sell growlers of their beer to customers.
rationale: The claim is overly broad and therefore false. Whether a brewpub can sell growlers depends on local and state alcohol laws; many brewpubs and brewery taprooms are permitted to sell growlers for off-premise consumption, while some jurisdictions restrict or require a separate license or packaging rules.

claim: "We have 93 million people out of work. They look for jobs, they give up, and all of a sudden, statistically, they're considered employed."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. The roughly 90+ million figure has been used to refer to people 'not in the labor force' (which includes retirees, students, caregivers and others), not 93 million unemployed. People who stop looking for work are classified as 'not in the labor force' (and thus not counted as unemployed), they are not counted as employed. BLS definitions therefore contradict the assertion that giving up job searches makes someone 'statistically... considered employed.'

claim: "There has been no net global warming for over a decade now."
rationale: Observational records from multiple independent datasets show that global surface temperatures and global ocean heat content have continued to rise over the past decade, with several of the warmest years on record occurring in the 2010s and early 2020s. Short-term variability (e.g., year-to-year or multi-year fluctuations) can momentarily slow the rate of surface warming, but that does not negate the clear net global warming trend.

claim: "Oregon, once again, remains among the top five hungriest states in the nation."
rationale: Major national measures of food insecurity (e.g., Feeding America, USDA food-insecurity/food-insufficiency reports) do not typically place Oregon among the five worst states. The highest food-insecurity rankings in recent years have been concentrated in several Southern and rural states (e.g., Mississippi, Louisiana, New Mexico, Arkansas, Alabama), while Oregon’s rates have generally been around or slightly above the national average rather than top-five worst. The claim as stated is therefore unsupported without a specific dataset or year showing otherwise.

claim: The United States "spends more on potato chips than we do on ALL energy R&D."
rationale: This is false. U.S. consumer spending on potato chips is on the order of several billion dollars per year (roughly $5–10B), whereas U.S. energy R&D—counting federal energy research budgets plus private-sector R&D in fuels, utilities, and vehicles—totals well above that in recent years (federal DOE energy R&D alone is roughly ten billion dollars or more, with private R&D adding many billions). Therefore energy R&D spending exceeds potato chip spending.

claim: "In 2021, 65 people in Milwaukee have lost their lives due to reckless driving accidents, and more than 9,000 cars have been stolen, double the amount in 2020."
rationale: The statement bundles two specific numeric claims that are not reliably supported by official city or news counts as stated.
