claim: "Half of all hospitalized seniors are suffering from malnutrition so severe that it either caused their illness or it prevents them from getting better."
rationale: This statement overstates and mischaracterizes evidence. While many hospitalized older adults are malnourished or at risk (estimates vary widely by setting and screening tool), the proportion with "severe" malnutrition sufficient to have caused their admission or to definitively prevent recovery is much lower and causation is not established for half of patients. The claim therefore is not supported by typical epidemiological data and clinical literature.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "has been saying lately that she thinks that I am, 'not qualified to be president.' "
rationale: During the 2016 campaign Hillary Clinton publicly and repeatedly characterized Donald Trump as unqualified or unfit to be president in debates, speeches, and interviews. Saying she 'has been saying lately that she thinks that I am not qualified to be president' accurately reflects those public statements when the 'I' refers to Trump and the timeframe is the campaign period.

claim: "We had already issued several thousand Special Immigrant Visas .. to the (Afghan) translators, when I came into office."
rationale: I cannot verify that "several thousand" Special Immigrant Visas had been issued to Afghan translators by the time the speaker took office. Public reporting and official statistics show many SIV applications were pending and only a smaller number had been fully issued prior to January 2021, so the claim overstates what was completed. Without clear contemporaneous issuance figures to support "several thousand," the statement is not substantiated.

claim: Says Donald Trump "doesn't believe in equal pay."
rationale: There is no reliable public record of Donald Trump explicitly saying the sentence “I don't believe in equal pay.” While he has questioned the commonly cited gender pay gap statistics and emphasized market and qualification factors, those statements are not equivalent to an explicit rejection of the principle of equal pay for equal work. Thus the claim as a direct quotation is unsupported.

claim: Says health insurance premiums will rise under Obamacare.
rationale: The claim as a blanket statement is misleading. After the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare), premiums rose in some markets and years (notably parts of the individual market early on) but fell or grew slowly for many employer plans and were offset for most lower- and middle-income consumers by new premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions. Whether premiums "rise" depends on which market (individual vs. employer), which plans, geographic area, and whether one looks at gross premiums or net premiums after subsidies.

claim: A bill to eliminate Delta Air Lines’ jet fuel tax breaks "violates federal law and puts the state at risk of losing critical funding from the Federal Aviation Administration."
rationale: The statement overstates the legal consequences. Changing or eliminating a state tax exemption for jet fuel is not per se a violation of federal law nor an automatic trigger for loss of FAA grant funding; FAA concerns would depend on specific grant-assurance violations (for example, discriminatory use of airport revenue or access conditions) and on how the law is implemented. Without those specifics, the blanket claim that the bill "violates federal law and puts the state at risk of losing critical FAA funding" is inaccurate.

claim: "CA inmate pregnant after being forced to share prison with transgender ‘woman.’"
rationale: There is no verifiable, reputable evidence that a California prisoner was definitively impregnated as a result of being ‘‘forced’’ to share housing with a transgender woman. Media reports and public records include isolated allegations and lawsuits about housing and assaults but do not substantiate the broad causal claim as stated; the claim appears to be a circulating allegation lacking confirmed proof. Without specific corroborating details (facility, dates, medical or investigative confirmation), the claim is unproven and therefore treated as false.

claim: "No one visiting Disney can get in" because of protest.
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute—"no one" can enter Disney because of a protest—which is implausible and not supported by typical reporting. Protests can cause delays, lane or entrance closures, and occasional temporary park access disruptions, but they rarely prevent all visitors from entering an entire Disney property. Without specific time, location, or authoritative reports that an entire park was fully closed to all entrants, the universal statement is false.

claim: "A new poll shows 62 percent support the president's plan to reform health care. That means ... letting you choose between keeping the private insurance you have and a public health insurance plan."
rationale: The claim combines an unverified poll figure with a categorical description of the policy. Without a named poll, date, or president, the "62 percent" figure cannot be confirmed and support figures vary widely by question wording and timing. Also, not all presidential health‑care reform proposals mean "letting you choose between keeping private insurance and a public plan" — that describes a "public option," but other proposals (e.g., single‑payer) would not provide that choice.

claim: Photo shows a Chinese restaurant sign that says "F--- DeSantis."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific photo and there is no corroborating, reliable reporting or provenance provided for this claim. Viral images of storefront signs are frequently edited or miscaptioned, so absent independent verification (original image, source, or multiple trustworthy outlets), the claim should be treated as false. If the original unedited photo and context were available, the assessment could change.

claim: "With 320,000 net Ohio manufacturing jobs lost, (Sen. Rob) Portman calls NAFTA a ‘proven success’."
rationale: The claim mixes a contested numeric assertion with a separate quoted endorsement. Rob Portman has publicly praised NAFTA as beneficial, but the specific figure of “320,000 net Ohio manufacturing jobs lost” tied to NAFTA is misleading: Ohio did lose a large number of manufacturing jobs since the 1990s, but the 320,000 number, its timeframe, and direct attribution to NAFTA are disputed and not straightforwardly supported by official employment-series or academic analyses. Because the numeric/causal part is unclear/misleading, the combined claim is false as stated.

claim: The United States is "#1 in oil consumption" in the world.
rationale: Based on international energy statistics from agencies such as the U.S. EIA and the IEA, the United States consumes more oil than any other single country. Historically and through the 2010s–2020s the U.S. has been the largest national consumer, typically on the order of roughly 18–20 million barrels per day pre-pandemic, with China consuming fewer barrels per day.

claim: "$360 million of our tax dollars went straight to ... the Taliban."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that exactly $360 million of U.S. tax dollars was sent directly to the Taliban. U.S. officials froze roughly $7 billion in Afghan central-bank assets after the 2021 collapse and later negotiated settlements and humanitarian transfers, and while some U.S.-funded aid or assets ended up under Taliban control after the government fell, reporting does not support a verified, direct $360 million payment to the Taliban.

claim: There are fewer wars, there are fewer people dying in wars "now than there have been in quite some time."
rationale: Long-term empirical conflict data show that both the number of large-scale interstate and many civil wars and the annual number of battle-related deaths have fallen compared with mid-20th-century peaks (especially World War II and the Cold War era). That said, there are important exceptions and occasional large spikes in recent decades (e.g., Rwanda, Balkans, Syria, and the 2022 Russia–Ukraine war), so the statement is true as a broad long-term trend but not an absolute claim about every recent year or region.

claim: Under the Democratic health plan, families "will be forced to spend an additional $2,100 a year to keep their current health care."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not supported as a universal fact. No reputable, nonpartisan analysis showed that all families would be "forced" to pay an extra $2,100 per year to keep their current care; impacts of Democratic health proposals (such as the ACA) varied widely by household, income, employer offerings and subsidy eligibility, with many households projected to pay less or receive subsidies, while some could face higher costs under certain scenarios. The $2,100 figure appears to originate from partisan estimates or from narrow assumptions and does not represent a general, unavoidable increase for all families.

claim: "Already this calendar year, since January 1, we have had more than 20,000 people come across the border, apprehended, unauthorized."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous about the year and geographic scope (national vs. a single state or sector), so it cannot be verified as presented. Border apprehension totals are published by U.S. Customs and Border Protection and vary widely by time period and location; in many recent years the U.S. nationwide encounters have far exceeded 20,000 early in the calendar year, but that does not confirm the unspecified claim. Because key context is missing, I mark the claim as unverified/false as stated.

claim: "Our governor proposed initially a 5% cut across the board of state government."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks any identifying details (which governor, which state, which year). Budget proposals vary by administration and while some governors have proposed across-the-board cuts of particular percentages, there is no way to confirm this specific assertion without context. Therefore I mark it false due to insufficient information to substantiate the claim.

claim: The Buffalo Billion is "still breaking every job promise"
rationale: The statement that the Buffalo Billion is "still breaking every job promise" is an absolute claim that is not supported by the record. Independent audits and reporting show mixed results—some projects fell far short of promised jobs and faced clawbacks, but other funded projects did create jobs and met or approached targets. Therefore it is inaccurate to say the program is breaking every job promise.

claim: Says Mitt Romney is using "a million of his presidential campaign dollars to finance his Utah Senate race."
rationale: Contemporary news reports from 2018 state that Mitt Romney transferred roughly $1 million from a prior presidential campaign committee into his Utah Senate campaign to help finance it. Such transfers of leftover candidate funds to another federal campaign are legal and were widely reported at the time, matching the claim's core assertion.

claim: President Barack Obama’s health care reform "slashed $500 billion from Medicare."
rationale: While the Affordable Care Act was estimated by the CBO and Medicare actuaries to reduce projected Medicare spending by roughly $500 billion over about a decade, those were reductions in projected payments (largely to providers and Medicare Advantage plans) and slowing of future spending growth, not a one-time $500 billion cut to beneficiary benefits. Describing it as President Obama’s reform having 'slashed $500 billion from Medicare' is misleading without that context.

claim: "Lauren Boebert received a PPP loan for her restaurant."
rationale: Public PPP loan records and contemporary news reporting show that Shooter’s Grill, a restaurant co-owned by Lauren Boebert, received a Paycheck Protection Program loan in 2020. Boebert was associated with the business, so stating she received a PPP loan for her restaurant is accurate in ordinary usage (the loan was made to the business entity).

claim: In the U.S. Constitution, "there’s a little section in there that talks about life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness."
rationale: The exact phrase "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness" appears in the Declaration of Independence (1776), not in the U.S. Constitution. The Constitution (and its amendments) protects life and liberty through due process language (e.g., Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments reference "life, liberty, or property") but does not contain the wording "pursuit of happiness."

claim: Says that as president, Barack Obama has not gone to the Texas-Mexico border
rationale: The claim that Obama never went to the Texas–Mexico border as president is false. During his presidency he made official visits to the U.S.–Mexico border region, including trips to border cities and meetings with Border Patrol and local officials; presidential schedules and press reports document such visits. The claim likely conflates not visiting during a specific crisis with never having visited while in office.

claim: "How is a misogynist bigot of epic proportions (like U.S. Rep. Steven Smith) allowed to serve?"
rationale: The statement characterizes an individual as “a misogynist bigot of epic proportions,” which is a subjective value judgment rather than a verifiable factual claim. There is no clear, objective evidence in the claim itself to prove the absolute assertion, and the identity referenced (“U.S. Rep. Steven Smith”) is ambiguous or may be misidentified. Because it is opinionated and unverifiable as stated, it cannot be classified as a factual claim.

claim: Proposition 2 on November’s Texas ballot "does not cost state taxpayers any money."
rationale: The statement is unlikely to be strictly true as written because Texas ballot amendments are typically accompanied by a fiscal note from the Legislative Budget Board or Comptroller identifying any direct state costs, revenue impacts, or local government effects. Many ballot summaries say a measure would have "no fiscal effect to the state" while still creating administrative costs or revenue impacts for local governments or in practice; without a specific year or the official fiscal analysis it is not accurate to assert categorically that Proposition 2 "does not cost state taxpayers any money."

claim: "Middle-class income rose to a record level in 2017 as the strong economy lifted the fortunes of more Americans."
rationale: This is accurate in broad terms: the U.S. Census Bureau reported that real (inflation-adjusted) median household income reached a record high in 2017 (roughly $61,300). That rise occurred alongside broader improvements in the labor market in 2017, though gains were uneven across groups and locations.

claim: "Phony" ballots "were printed without my name on it."
rationale: The claim is unverified and provides no specifics about who “my” refers to, where or when the alleged ballots were printed, or any corroborating evidence. While printing or administrative errors with ballots can occur, there is no public, verifiable information provided to substantiate this particular assertion, so it cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: Says COVID-19 has killed more North Carolinians in a year than the flu has in 10 years.
rationale: This is true in the relevant sense: COVID-19 produced several thousand (and by some measures over ten thousand) deaths in North Carolina in a single pandemic year, a toll larger than what seasonal influenza typically causes in that state when CDC national flu-death ranges are scaled to North Carolina over a ten-year period. Flu death estimates are lower and vary by season, while COVID-19 produced an unusually large single-year mortality spike in NC. Therefore the comparative claim is supported by available mortality patterns.

claim: Amanda Murphy has "two vacation homes around the world."
rationale: There is no reliable, specific public evidence that an Amanda Murphy (the name is shared by multiple people) owns “two vacation homes around the world.” Claims about private property ownership require named identification and documentary sourcing; absent that, the statement is unverified and likely false. Because the name is common, the assertion could be true for some individual with that name but is not supported as a general fact.

claim: "In Rick Perry's Texas, the governor threatens to leave, to secede from the greatest country in the" world.
rationale: False. While Rick Perry made media comments around 2009–2011 saying he would not categorically rule out the idea of secession when pressed, he never formally threatened as governor to have Texas leave the United States nor took any legal or executive steps to do so. U.S. law and precedent (e.g., Texas v. White) hold that states cannot unilaterally secede, and Perry’s remarks were rhetorical rather than an actual secession threat.

claim: "Hydroxychloroquine cures this ‘virus.’ It just so happens this is the treatment used for radiation sickness!!"
rationale: The claim is false. Multiple randomized clinical trials (including large trials like RECOVERY and WHO Solidarity) and regulatory reviews found hydroxychloroquine does not cure COVID-19 and provides no mortality benefit, and its emergency use authorization was revoked due to lack of efficacy and safety concerns. Hydroxychloroquine is not a treatment for radiation sickness; standard treatments for radiation exposure are different (e.g., potassium iodide for radioactive iodine, Prussian blue for certain radionuclides, supportive care and colony-stimulating factors).

claim: "Ten percent of violent deaths in the U.S. each year are due to strangulation."
rationale: False. There is no authoritative national statistic showing that 10% of U.S. violent deaths annually are due to strangulation. Homicidal strangulation/ligature deaths are a small minority of homicides, and although hanging/suffocation is an important method among suicides, public health surveillance does not support a routinely cited 10% figure for ‘‘strangulation’’ across all violent deaths. The claim appears to conflate different causes/methods without a clear source or definition.

claim: Says Michael Kors said, "I’m tired of pretending I like blacks."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that fashion designer Michael Kors ever said “I’m tired of pretending I like blacks.” Such an inflammatory quote would have been widely reported and sourced; instead the phrase appears to circulate as an unverified/misattributed social-media meme or fake screenshot. Without a verifiable primary source (audio, video, or reputable news transcript), the attribution is not supported.

claim: "This is the only state in the country that bypassed the General Assembly to authorize [in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants]."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: multiple states have allowed in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants via administrative actions, university board/residency-rule changes, or executive orders rather than by passing new legislation. Because several states have used non-legislative routes at different times, it is not unique to a single state.

claim: Says Democratic Party created Planned Parenthood
rationale: Planned Parenthood traces to Margaret Sanger and early 20th‑century birth control activists (the American Birth Control League founded in 1921), later becoming Planned Parenthood in the 1940s. It was created as an independent nonprofit movement, not established by the Democratic Party. While many Democrats have supported or opposed it politically, the organization’s origins are activist and nonprofit, not a party creation.

claim: Heroin and prescription opioids are "the number one cause of accidental or preventable death in Wisconsin."
rationale: The statement is overly broad and lacks a time frame and definition of “preventable” or “accidental.” While opioid overdoses (including heroin and prescription opioids) have risen sharply and in some recent years surpassed motor vehicle crash deaths in Wisconsin, it is not clearly established that they are consistently the single top cause of all accidental or all preventable deaths statewide for all years. The claim as phrased is therefore not reliably supported without additional specification.

claim: "Iowa's Republican caucus stopped mattering years ago. It in no way determines the party nominee."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement but is inaccurate: Iowa does not by itself determine the Republican nominee, yet it still matters because early wins or losses shape media narratives, fundraising, and momentum. Recent cycles show mixed outcomes—winners in Iowa (e.g., Santorum in 2012, Cruz in 2016) did not become the nominee, but other times early Iowa strength helped frontrunners consolidate support. Saying it "in no way determines" the nominee overstates the case because the caucus remains an influential early test.

claim: "I became a Republican sooner in my life than" Ronald Reagan did in his.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because the speaker’s identity and the age or date when they became a Republican are not given. General knowledge indicates Ronald Reagan publicly switched to the Republican Party in the early 1960s when he was around 50–52, so without the speaker’s corresponding timing the comparative claim cannot be confirmed. Therefore I treat the unsupported comparative assertion as false.

claim: "Under the ruling of the Supreme Court, any lobbyist could go into any legislator and say, if you don't vote our way on this bill, we're going to run a million-dollar campaign against you in your district."
rationale: This claim overstates the effect of Supreme Court rulings. While decisions like Citizens United permit large independent political expenditures by corporations and groups, they do not authorize direct threats, bribery, extortion, or illegal coordination with a campaign. A lobbyist explicitly threatening a legislator with a paid campaign in exchange for a vote would likely violate criminal and ethics laws even after those rulings.

claim: "Congress files charges against Nancy Pelosi."
rationale: There is no record that Congress has filed criminal charges or articles of impeachment against Nancy Pelosi. The House would need to pass articles of impeachment to 'charge' a federal official and the Department of Justice brings criminal indictments; neither has occurred regarding Pelosi as of the current knowledge cutoff.

claim: Quotes Andy Borowitz as saying "stopping Hillary is a short-term solution. The long-term solution — and it will be more difficult — is fixing the educational system that has created so many people ignorant enough to vote for Hillary."
rationale: There is no reliable record or reputable source attributing that direct quote to Andy Borowitz. Borowitz is a satirist who publishes ironic commentary, and provocative lines are often taken out of context or misattributed online; absent corroboration, this specific quotation appears fabricated or misattributed.

claim: Under David Dewhurst’s leadership, the Texas "Senate passed an expansion of in-state tuition and free health care to illegal immigrants."
rationale: This is not accurate. The major Texas law allowing in-state tuition for certain undocumented students was enacted in 2001 (before David Dewhurst was Lt. Governor), and Texas does not provide general “free health care” to undocumented immigrants—only emergency care is required and most public programs (Medicaid/CHIP) exclude undocumented residents. While the Senate has debated immigration-related tuition and health measures at various times, there is no clear record that under Dewhurst the Texas Senate passed a bill creating expanded in‑state tuition plus free health care for undocumented immigrants that became law.

claim: President Barack Obama "is the first president to keep a dog-trainer on retainer for $102,000 a year at taxpayer expense."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Presidents have long had paid staff to care for presidential pets and the White House has animal-care personnel; the $102,000 figure appears to conflate a staff salary or position within White House support services rather than a unique, new ‘dog-trainer on retainer’ paid solely to train the Obamas’ dog and being the first of its kind. Fact-checks have found the statement overstated and lacking supporting payroll evidence that it was a sole-purpose retainer and the first ever.

claim: "You have 200,000 to 400,000 military veterans on the street in this country on any given day."
rationale: This greatly overstates known counts of veterans experiencing homelessness. Point-in-time counts by HUD and VA consistently find roughly 30,000–40,000 veterans homeless on a single night in recent years, and annual unduplicated counts remain far below 200,000–400,000. The claimant likely conflates different measures or uses an inflated estimate without defining timeframe or what “on the street” means.

claim: Hillary Clinton "has already said she's going to wipe out the Second Amendment. She doesn't believe in the First Amendment. And, she also believes in big government, which flies in the face of the 10th Amendment"
rationale: The statement is inaccurate and conflates policy positions with explicit declarations. Hillary Clinton has advocated stricter gun regulations (e.g., assault weapons ban, universal background checks) but has not said she will "wipe out" the Second Amendment; she has not repudiated the First Amendment; and while she supports an active federal role on issues like healthcare and education, calling that "big government" that violates the 10th Amendment is a political interpretation, not a factual claim she made. Overall the quoted assertions misrepresent her public record.

claim: A photo shows "brave women of the Red Cross" arriving in Normandy on D-Day to help injured troops.
rationale: This claim is false. Contemporary records and later debunking of circulating versions of this photograph show that female Red Cross volunteers did not accompany the initial assault on D-Day; military policy and operational practice kept civilian and most medical women out of the beach landings, with Red Cross staff serving from ships, hospitals, or arriving after the beachhead was secure. The image in circulation has been miscaptioned and comes from a different time/place rather than the June 6 Normandy assault.

claim: Former Gov. Pat McCrory appointed liberals to the North Carolina Textbook Commission, which "mandated textbooks" pushing critical race theory.
rationale: There is no evidence that Pat McCrory’s textbook appointments resulted in a commission mandate requiring K–12 textbooks to teach critical race theory. While governors appoint members to state textbook/adoption bodies, North Carolina’s process historically approves lists of textbooks and local districts select materials; it did not force CRT as a mandated curriculum and CRT is an academic legal theory not part of standard K–12 adopted textbooks. Characterizing appointees as “liberals” is subjective and unproven in this claim.

claim: "By registration fewer than 20 percent of Florida voters are Independents."
rationale: Florida’s official voter rolls categorize unaffiliated voters as “No Party Affiliation” (commonly equated with independents), and that category has been above 20% in recent official registration reports (in the low‑20s percent range). Therefore the statement that fewer than 20% of Florida voters are independents is inaccurate based on recent registration data.

claim: The 2020 election is in "recount territory" and "I’ve seen elections change as a result of" recounts.
rationale: Most key 2020 state margins were larger than typical automatic recount thresholds, and in the closest states (e.g., Georgia) recounts were conducted and confirmed the original result rather than reversing it. While recounts can and occasionally have changed outcomes in small, local races, they very rarely flip statewide or presidential results, so calling the overall 2020 election 'in recount territory' and implying recounts were likely to change the outcome is misleading.

claim: In Afghanistan, "over 100 billion dollars spent on military contracts."
rationale: Contemporary oversight reports and independent analyses show U.S. Department of Defense and other U.S. agency contract obligations tied to the Afghanistan campaign exceeded $100 billion over the course of the war. The figure covers large contracting outlays for logistics, base construction, private security, and services across many years of operations.

claim: David Beckham’s proposed soccer stadium at Miami’s Port "threatens the 207,000 jobs and $27 billion economic impact tied to the cargo and cruise industries."
rationale: The claim exaggerates impact: the 207,000 jobs and $27 billion figure refers to broad, regional economic impacts tied to the port complex and related industries, not jobs that would be directly displaced by a single stadium site. Public records and port officials indicated Beckham’s proposed site would not eliminate core cruise or major cargo operations and mitigation/lease terms were intended to avoid crippling port business. Therefore saying the stadium “threatens” that entire economic footprint is misleading.

claim: Officials "recommend that women who get one of these (COVID-19) shots should absolutely not get pregnant for at least the first two months after they’ve been injected."
rationale: Major public-health agencies (CDC, WHO, FDA and equivalent national bodies) did not issue a blanket recommendation that women must avoid pregnancy for two months after receiving COVID-19 vaccines. Official guidance allowed vaccination for women of childbearing age and did not require a two-month delay; some clinical trial protocols did ask participants to use contraception during the study period, but that is not the same as a public-health recommendation for the general population.

claim: The Keystone XL pipeline "doesn’t even have any oil for America."
rationale: This is false. The Keystone XL was designed to carry crude oil from Alberta to refineries on the U.S. Gulf Coast and would have delivered substantial volumes into the U.S. petroleum system, even though some refined products or crude could subsequently be exported.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We must block Trump from stopping the return of the heroic Alabama mother from ISIS. In many ways she is more of a hero then our veterans. Welcome home sister!"
rationale: There is no credible record or reliable news reporting that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez ever made this statement; the quote circulated as a viral social-media claim and appears to be a fabricated/misattributed meme. Public statements and her official accounts do not contain praise calling an alleged ISIS-linked returnee “more of a hero than our veterans.”

claim: Says Keanu Reeves gave a speech that began, "I cannot be part of a world where men dress their wives as prostitutes by showing everything that should be cherished ..."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or primary-source record (video, transcript, or reputable news report) showing Keanu Reeves gave a speech beginning with that line. The quotation circulates widely on social media and meme sites but has been debunked by fact-checkers as an unattributed or misattributed viral quote rather than something Reeves actually said.

claim: The people who want President Barack Obama impeached "are all white, they're all older, and guess what, they're in the far right wing of the Republican Party."
rationale: The claim uses an absolute universal (“are all”) which is false: proponents of impeaching President Obama were not exclusively white, not exclusively older, nor confined entirely to the far-right of the GOP. Support for impeachment included a range of Republican figures and activists across ages and some minority conservatives, and polling/elected-official positions showed variation rather than a perfect monolith.

claim: The minimum wage "in real terms right now is below where it was when Harry Truman was in office."
rationale: The federal minimum wage, when adjusted for inflation, had more purchasing power during Harry Truman’s presidency (late 1940s–early 1950s) than the current federal minimum of $7.25. For example, the federal minimum around 1950 was roughly $0.75/hour, which converts to about $9–10 in today’s dollars depending on the index used, so $7.25 is lower in real terms. Multiple historical wage series and CPI-adjusted comparisons show the same pattern.

claim: Says Texas high school graduates must pass Algebra II to be eligible for automatic admission to state's public universities.
rationale: This is not strictly true. Texas automatic admission is primarily tied to class rank (the state’s top-percent automatic-admission policy) and completion of a state‑approved high school curriculum, not a universal, standalone rule that every graduate must pass Algebra II. While many universities expect completion of the recommended core (which historically included a fourth math like Algebra II), requirements vary by institution and recent state curriculum changes allow alternative math pathways and endorsements.

claim: "Under Terry McAuliffe (there was a) record investment in education."
rationale: The statement is misleading: while Governor Terry McAuliffe did increase education funding and supported teacher pay raises and expanded pre-K during his term, calling it a “record investment” is not clearly supported without specifying the metric or timeframe. State budget records do show increases in certain years, but there is no unambiguous, verifiable claim that his administration made the largest-ever or absolute record investment in education overall. The phrase appears to be political spin rather than a precise fact.

claim: "Last year, 36 million Americans didn’t have a prescription filled because they couldn’t afford it."
rationale: National survey data in recent years (for example Kaiser Family Foundation health tracking polls) found about 14–16% of U.S. adults reported not filling a prescription in the past year because of cost, which converts to roughly 35–38 million people — consistent with the 36 million figure. The estimate hinges on survey wording and year but the headline number matches reputable survey-based estimates.

claim: "The average homeowner spends more than $2,000 each year on energy costs – more than on either real estate taxes or homeowners insurance."
rationale: National data indicate average annual residential energy spending is roughly in the low-to-mid thousands but typically does not exceed typical annual property tax bills for homeowners. Average U.S. property taxes are often above $2,000 (commonly $3,000+), while homeowners insurance premiums are generally lower (around $1,200–$1,500), so the claim that energy costs exceed both property taxes and insurance is not supported nationwide.

claim: "Trump’s daughter works at the White House. Her husband works at the White House. Rudy’s son works at the White House. Barr’s son-in-law works at the White House. Barr’s daughter works at Treasury. Trump’s sons do foreign business. Trump’s daughter is getting Chinese patents and Saudi grants."
rationale: The claim mixes true and false assertions. Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner did serve in the White House during the Trump administration and Andrew Giuliani held a White House role, and Trump’s children have had foreign business ties; however, specific claims about William Barr’s relatives working at the White House or Treasury lack evidence, and the statement that Ivanka is getting “Chinese patents” and “Saudi grants” is misleading (she pursued Chinese trademarks, not patents, and there is no verified record of Saudi government grants).

claim: "Amazing fact: Senate has already voted on more amendments in 2015 than Reid allowed ALL YEAR last year."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false because it provides no clear time cutoff and depends on how one counts "amendments voted" (full amendment roll-call votes vs. procedural or cloture votes). Senate voting records do not support a simple comparison without precise definitions, and contemporary fact-checking showed such one-line boasts were misleading. Without a sourced, precise tally, the statement cannot be accepted as true.

claim: "It's just outrageous that under President Bush, the National Institutes of Health have been basically decreased in funding."
rationale: This claim is false in the usual sense: the NIH budget did not fall under President George W. Bush in nominal dollars — funding rose in the early 2000s (continuing a multi-year increase that peaked around 2003) and was higher overall than at the start of his term. However, after those increases the budget largely plateaued and declined in inflation-adjusted (real) terms and grant success rates tightened, which may be the source of the speaker's impression.

claim: "When Marcy Kaptur brought home $42 million for new manufacturing jobs, Dennis Kucinich voted 'no'."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record that Dennis Kucinich cast a specific 'no' vote on a standalone measure that solely provided Marcy Kaptur $42 million for new manufacturing jobs. That kind of funding was typically embedded in larger appropriations or grant awards, and I found no reliable source tying a single roll-call 'no' by Kucinich to that exact $42 million item. Without a specific bill and date the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Estimated annual COVID-19 deaths in the U.S. totals 27,530, after you subtract those who died "with, not from" COVID-19, not in nursing homes and who didn't have four or more comorbidities.
rationale: The asserted total (27,530 annual U.S. COVID-19 deaths after those specific exclusions) is not supported by available national data or standard counting methods. CDC provisional and official counts across pandemic years show annual COVID-19 deaths far higher than 27,530 in most years, and the claim depends on arbitrary, nonstandard exclusions ('with, not from', excluding nursing home deaths, and excluding anyone without four or more comorbidities) that are not how mortality is routinely attributed. Because the methodology is unclear and the resulting number conflicts with publicly reported totals, the claim is false.

claim: "The Pentagon itself says that we could eliminate 20 percent of U.S. bases."
rationale: There is no clear, authoritative Pentagon statement explicitly saying ‘‘we could eliminate 20 percent of U.S. bases.’’ While Pentagon officials and outside analysts have at times discussed consolidating or reducing overseas posture and think‑tank studies have produced estimates of substantial cuts, those are not the same as an official Pentagon claim that 20% of U.S. bases could be eliminated. The original claim appears to conflate analyst estimates or political commentary with a formal Pentagon declaration.

claim: Says Trump ties are made "in China, not Colorado. Trump suits in Mexico, not Michigan. Trump furniture in Turkey, not Ohio. Trump picture frames in India, not Wisconsin."
rationale: The claim presents an absolute, single-country-for-each-item assertion, which is inaccurate. While reporting and product labels have shown many Trump‑branded ties, suits, furniture and frames have at times been manufactured overseas (including China, Mexico, Turkey, India), production sources vary by product, brand licensee, and time—so the blanket statement is false.

claim: Video footage from Georgia shows suitcases filled with ballots pulled from under a table and illegally counted after election observers were told to leave.
rationale: Multiple post‑election investigations and contemporaneous reporting found that the viral video shows election workers retrieving sealed containers/totes of ballots that had been stored out of the way, not suitcases of hidden ballots being illegally counted. Observers were asked to move back for processing and privacy protocols (and some left voluntarily), but there is no credible evidence that ballots were surreptitiously counted after observers were ordered to leave or that hidden suitcase ballots altered results.

claim: "Hillary Clinton invented ISIS with her stupid policies. She is responsible for ISIS."
rationale: The claim that Hillary Clinton "invented" ISIS is false. ISIS developed from al-Qaeda in Iraq (AQI) that emerged after the 2003 U.S. invasion, was shaped by Iraq's sectarian politics, the Syrian civil war, and local and regional actors; while some U.S. and allied policies (including decisions during and after Clinton's tenure as Secretary of State) are criticized for contributing to instability, responsibility is diffuse and not attributable to a single individual inventing the group.

claim: "Every four minutes, another American home or business goes solar."
rationale: The statement is a time‑dependent marketing statistic rather than an invariant fact. Industry groups sometimes report that “a home or business goes solar every X minutes” by dividing annual installation counts by minutes in a year, so the rate has varied by year and depends on definitions (systems vs. unique homes/businesses). Without a specific timeframe and source the absolute present‑tense claim is misleading and not reliably true at all times.

claim: A video shows an animal chip scanner detecting a microchip where a woman was vaccinated.
rationale: This is very unlikely: licensed human vaccines do not contain RFID or injectable microchips and such tags are far larger than vaccine needles allow. Animal chip scanners read implanted RFID transponders and can be triggered by metal, electronics, or the scanner being passed over conductive objects or phone components, so a beeping in a video does not prove a vaccine contained a microchip. Videos showing a scanner 'detecting' a chip at a vaccination site have been debunked as misinterpretations or demonstrations of scanner sensitivity to other materials.

claim: "Julia Roberts claims ‘Michelle Obama isn’t fit to clean Melania’s toilet’ "
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Julia Roberts ever said “Michelle Obama isn’t fit to clean Melania’s toilet.” The quote appears to be a fabricated, misattributed social-media rumor and contradicts the absence of such statements in verified interviews or reputable news coverage. Given the lack of sourcing and authoritative confirmation, the claim is false.

claim: Says "there have been some job gains in the McMansion State since Mr. Christie took office, but they have lagged gains both in the nation as a whole and in New York and Connecticut, the obvious points of comparison."
rationale: The statement is too indefinite to verify as presented. Chris Christie took office in January 2010, but whether New Jersey’s job gains “lagged” the nation, New York and Connecticut depends entirely on the end date and the employment measure used (payroll jobs vs. household survey, absolute vs. percent change). Labor‑market series (BLS and state reports) show periods when New Jersey trailed those comparators and other periods when it did not, so the blanket claim cannot be confirmed without a specified timeframe and metric.

claim: Quotes Anthony Fauci as writing, "I reject the notion that it’s ‘just a virus’ and we’ll all get it eventually. What a careless, lazy, heartless stance."
rationale: I could not find evidence that Anthony Fauci authored or publicly said that exact sentence. The line has circulated on social media but does not appear in his known speeches, op-eds, official statements, or verified tweets, and resembles a misattributed or paraphrased remark. Given the absence of a reliable primary source attributing the quote to Fauci, the claim is likely false.

claim: "On average, women make 77 cents for every dollar men make."
rationale: The "77 cents" figure is an outdated, context-free statistic that was widely cited in past years for the unadjusted U.S. gender pay gap. Recent U.S. data using common measures (median hourly or annual earnings for full-time workers) show women earn closer to about 80–83 cents on the dollar, and the exact gap varies by year and measurement method. The claim is misleading without specifying the year, country, and whether it refers to median vs. mean or full-time vs. all workers.

claim: "This election actually was not unusually close."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated because it does not identify which election is meant; whether an election is "unusually close" depends on its specific vote margin and historical or polling context. Without specifying jurisdiction, year, or the margin of victory, the statement cannot be confirmed and therefore is not factually supported. It might be true for some elections and false for others, but as an absolute assertion it is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Mitt Romney: ‘Trump has some very serious emotional problems, he must resign before we…’"
rationale: There is no reliable public record of Mitt Romney saying the exact quoted line — that “Trump has some very serious emotional problems, he must resign before we…”. Romney has publicly criticized Trump’s temperament and voted to convict after Jan. 6, but major reports and transcripts do not show this specific call for resignation in that wording. The claim appears to be a misquote or fabrication rather than a documented Romney statement.

claim: "Every day, 34 Americans are murdered with guns."
rationale: Federal data (CDC/FBI) show roughly 12,000–15,000 firearm homicides per year in recent years; dividing those annual totals by 365 yields about 33–41 gun homicides per day. The rounded statement "34 Americans are murdered with guns every day" matches commonly reported recent-year averages, though the exact daily count varies by year.

claim: "The same federal government that offers some money for a program is walking away from another health care program."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify as a factual claim: it makes a general observation without naming which federal government, which programs, or a timeframe. While it is common for a government to fund some initiatives while reducing or ending others, that general pattern does not make this specific sentence a verifiable fact. Without concrete details the claim is untestable and cannot be judged true as written.

claim: John McCain "voted against the tax cuts of 2001 and 2003, wrongly claiming they helped only the rich."
rationale: The statement bundles two assertions and is misleading: McCain did not categorically vote against both the 2001 and 2003 Bush tax cut bills, and whether his characterization that the cuts 'helped only the rich' is strictly wrong is debatable because the cuts produced benefits across income groups while larger dollar gains tended to go to higher-income households. Because the claim asserts both a precise voting record and an unambiguous factual error about distribution, it overstates the case.

claim: Tax rates were significantly higher "in the '40s, the '50s, and the '60s."
rationale: If referring to U.S. federal individual income tax rates, top marginal rates were much higher in mid‑20th century: they peaked around the WWII years (about 94%) and stayed near ~91% through the 1950s and into the early 1960s, substantially above rates in later decades. Thus the broad claim that tax rates were significantly higher in the '40s–'60s is accurate in that common sense.

claim: "Sixty percent of New Jersey doctors do not accept Medicaid patients."
rationale: This specific claim is not supported by available evidence: surveys and state-level data indicate that far fewer than 60% of New Jersey physicians categorically do not accept Medicaid. Acceptance rates vary by specialty and whether physicians are taking new Medicaid patients, but most estimates show a majority of providers in New Jersey do accept Medicaid in some form, so the 60% refusal figure is an overstatement and lacks context.

claim: Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp "mandates restaurants reopen"
rationale: This is misleading. In April 2020 Gov. Brian Kemp issued a state executive order that allowed restaurants to resume dine‑in service under safety conditions and preempted some local restrictions, but he did not force every restaurant to open or issue a blanket mandate requiring businesses to reopen. Individual restaurants could choose to stay closed and local governments retained limited public‑health authority in other areas.

claim: "Kelly Ayotte voted to give big oil more than $20 billion in tax breaks."
rationale: The claim overstates what can be directly attributed to a single Kelly Ayotte vote. Ayotte did vote for Republican tax legislation (notably the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act) that analysts say included provisions favorable to oil and gas, but authoritative estimates tying any one vote by Ayotte to 'more than $20 billion' for big oil are lacking and numbers vary by timeframe and method. The claim conflates aggregate industry benefits or disputed estimates with a single identifiable vote.

claim: "NYT is correcting their lies..Trump paid $1M in 2016 & $3.8M in 2017-18..THEY LIED..AGAIN. INFO ON TWITTER THIS AM."
rationale: The specific claim that the New York Times corrected earlier reporting to state Trump paid $1,000,000 in 2016 and $3.8 million in 2017–18 is not supported by the public record. The NYT's major tax reporting widely reported that Trump paid $750 in 2016 and 2017 and there is no documented NYT correction revising those years to the much larger amounts. Without a credible source for the alleged correction, the statement appears to be misinformation.

claim: Says Donald Trump warned outgoing Ghana President against last-minute job appointments.
rationale: There is no credible public record or reporting that former U.S. President Donald Trump warned an outgoing Ghanaian president about last-minute job appointments. Major news coverage of Ghanaian transitions (e.g., 2016) and Trump's public statements do not include such a remark, so the claim appears to be unsubstantiated or a misattribution.

claim: "Under the federal Controlled Substance Act, marijuana is listed in the same Schedule I as heroin," even though "marijuana is not a killer drug like heroin."
rationale: Under the federal Controlled Substances Act, cannabis (marijuana) is classified as a Schedule I substance and so is heroin, so they are placed in the same schedule at the federal level. Epidemiological and toxicological evidence shows heroin carries a substantial risk of fatal overdose, whereas marijuana has very low acute toxicity and is not associated with overdose deaths, so the characterization that marijuana is not a "killer drug like heroin" is broadly accurate.

claim: "After World War II, we tried, convicted, and, in some cases, executed Japanese soldiers for war crimes that included charges of waterboarding."
rationale: Allied military tribunals after World War II prosecuted many Japanese servicemen and officials for torture of POWs and civilians, and some defendants were convicted and executed. Trial records from Tokyo, Yokohama and numerous Philippine and regional trials include counts describing use of ‘‘water cure’’ or water torture (functionally similar to what is now called waterboarding) as one of the abuses. While contemporary documents often used terms like “water cure” rather than the modern term “waterboarding,” the substance of the allegation matches the claim.

claim: An independent payment advisory board created by the health care reform law "can ration care and deny certain Medicare treatments."
rationale: The Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB) created by the Affordable Care Act was statutorily barred from recommending measures that would ration care, restrict benefits or eligibility, or raise beneficiary cost‑sharing; its mandate was to propose payment and efficiency changes to reduce Medicare per‑capita spending. While its recommendations could become binding if Congress did not enact alternatives, the law explicitly prohibited recommendations that would deny specific treatments, so the claim that it "can ration care and deny certain Medicare treatments" is inaccurate.

claim: Says Jim Renacci ran against the Washington establishment in the election, but is now "hypocritically embracing it with big money, special interest fundraisers."
rationale: The claim mixes a plausible campaign positioning with an unverified accusation. Jim Renacci did run as a Republican outsider in at least some of his recent campaigns, but I have no specific, verifiable evidence that he has since 'hypocritically embraced' the Washington establishment by holding identifiable big‑money, special‑interest fundraisers. Without named events, dates, or documented fundraisers showing such ties, the accusatory second half is not supported.

claim: "Human meat found in McDonald’s meat factory"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that human meat was ever found in a McDonald’s meat factory; this is a recurring hoax circulated online. Major food-safety regulators, McDonald’s corporate communications, and independent fact-checkers have not reported any inspections, recalls, or prosecutions supporting the claim.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's Iran nuclear deal "lined the pockets of the world's number one state sponsor of terrorism with your money."
rationale: The Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) did provide sanctions relief that allowed Iran access to billions in previously frozen assets and increased oil revenues, but it did not send U.S. taxpayer money directly to Iran. The claim’s wording is rhetorical and misleading—it conflates sanctions relief and unfrozen Iranian funds with a direct transfer of “your money” and frames Iran as the unequivocal “number one” state sponsor, which is a politicized label.

claim: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve has "been mostly empty" for decades.
rationale: The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) has held substantial inventories for most of its existence since the 1970s and was not "mostly empty" for decades. The SPR built up to several hundred million barrels (peaking around the mid-2000s) and only saw large, deliberate drawdowns in 2022–2023, which reduced but did not leave it empty. The claim that it has been mostly empty for decades is therefore incorrect.

claim: Says Ted Budd "voted to gut protections for pre-existing conditions … letting insurance companies deny coverage for (necessary) treatment."
rationale: As a member of the House, Ted Budd voted for Republican repeal bills (notably the 2017 American Health Care Act) and backed other GOP efforts to overturn or weaken the ACA. Those measures would have allowed states and insurers greater ability to waive requirements such as essential health benefits and community rating, undermining ACA protections for people with pre-existing conditions and making it more likely insurers could deny or limit coverage for necessary treatments.

claim: U.S. Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison "voted to continue Roe v. Wade."
rationale: There is no single Senate roll-call vote that directly 'continues Roe v. Wade.' Preservation or overturning of Roe occurs via Supreme Court decisions, federal legislation, or confirmation of judges, not a direct Senate vote to 'continue' the precedent. Without a specific bill or amendment cited, the statement is misleading and cannot be substantiated as written for Sen. Hutchison's record.

claim: "Barron Trump was born in March 2006 and Melania wasn’t a legal citizen until July 2006. So under this executive order, his own son wouldn’t be an American citizen."
rationale: Barron Trump was born March 20, 2006 in New York City, and even if Melania was not yet a U.S. citizen in 2006, the 14th Amendment grants citizenship to virtually all persons born on U.S. soil. An executive order cannot override the Constitution, and the only typical exception is children of foreign diplomats — Melania was not serving as a diplomat, so Barron is a U.S. citizen.

claim: The United States has experienced "40 straight months of unemployment at 8 percent or higher."
rationale: Monthly U.S. unemployment (the standard BLS U-3 rate) rose above 8% during the 2009 recession but did not remain at or above 8% for 40 consecutive months. The rate peaked near 10% in 2009 and then declined, falling below 8% well before a 40-month continuous stretch would have elapsed.

claim: "State Rep. Kathleen Peters has a 100 percent pro-abortion voting record – even voting against a ban on sex-selection abortions."
rationale: The claim that Kathleen Peters has a "100 percent pro-abortion voting record" and specifically voted against a ban on sex-selection abortions overstates and mischaracterizes her record. Public roll-call histories and contemporary reporting do not indicate a flawless 100% "pro-abortion" score; Peters, a moderate Republican, has a mixed record on abortion-related measures, and the assertion about a specific sex-selection ban vote lacks clear, verifiable context (bill number/session). Without a precise bill and session, the absolute claim is not supported and is therefore false as stated.

claim: "Congressman Cicilline, when he was the mayor of Providence, espoused a sanctuary city."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Cicilline explicitly promoted or formally declared Providence to be a 'sanctuary city' while he was mayor. He did support immigrant-friendly measures during his 2003–2011 tenure, but the claim conflates general pro‑immigrant positions with an explicit endorsement or formal sanctuary-city designation.

claim: "Hate crimes against American Muslims and mosques have tripled after Paris and San Bernardino."
rationale: The broad claim that hate crimes against American Muslims and mosques “have tripled” after Paris and San Bernardino is misleading. Nationwide FBI statistics for 2015 showed a substantial increase in anti-Muslim incidents (roughly a two-thirds rise), and advocacy groups reported local or short-term spikes in mosque incidents after those attacks, but the data do not support a clear, sustained nationwide tripling across the board.

claim: Says a crisis actor played the parts of a shooting victim and the mothers of shooting victims in Las Vegas, Orlando and Thousand Oaks.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the same person acted as both a shooting victim and as mothers of victims in the Las Vegas, Orlando, and Thousand Oaks attacks. Major fact-checkers and news organizations have investigated and debunked recurring “crisis actor” allegations by verifying victims’ identities with families, law enforcement and public records; photographic and timeline evidence also show different people. The claim appears to rely on misidentification and conspiracy speculation rather than documented proof.

claim: Joe Biden "wants to get rid of something called ‘stepped up basis’" that reduces inheritance taxes.
rationale: This claim overstates and mischaracterizes Biden’s proposals. The Biden administration and campaign have proposed limiting or eliminating the step-up in basis only for very large inheritances (targeting unrealized gains above specified thresholds) rather than repealing it for all estates, and the rule affects capital gains tax treatment of inherited assets rather than the federal estate/inheritance tax itself. Saying he simply “wants to get rid of” it for everyone is inaccurate.

claim: Says the Security Against Foreign Enemies Act of 2015 would not "pause" the resettlement of Syrian refugees in the United States.
rationale: This is false. The Security Against Foreign Enemies (SAFE) Act introduced in 2015 would have imposed strict new vetting requirements and effectively suspended or paused refugee admissions from Syria (and in practice from parts of Iraq) until federal officials could certify enhanced security procedures, so it would have halted routine resettlement rather than leave it unchanged.

claim: Fifty-three percent of graduates from liberal arts colleges these days can’t find jobs.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 53% of liberal arts college graduates “can’t find jobs.” Official labour statistics and education data show unemployment among recent college graduates is far lower (single-digit percentages) and while underemployment or working outside one’s field can be substantial for some majors, it is not equivalent to 53% of liberal-arts graduates being jobless. The 53% figure likely arises from a misreading of surveys about underemployment, working outside one’s major, or a narrowly defined subgroup or time period.

claim: "Like every budget passed by the Senate since I have been lieutenant governor, Senate Bill 1 is within the spending limit set by the Texas Constitution."
rationale: The Texas Constitution requires appropriations not exceed certified revenue, and whether a Senate budget meets that limit is determined by the comptroller and subject to technical definitions (general revenue vs. all funds, use of one-time balances). Public reporting and fiscal analysts have disputed at least one Senate-passed budget during the current lieutenant governor’s tenure as exceeding the constitutional limit or relying on one‑time resources, so the blanket claim that every Senate budget since he took office has complied is inaccurate. The statement therefore overstates the record.

claim: By allowing brewpubs to sell beer, Georgia could become like Mexico with only a couple of manufacturers controlling all aspects of market.
rationale: The claim is unsupported and unlikely. Mexico’s beer market concentration arose from decades of mergers, acquisitions, and distribution practices by large conglomerates, not from allowing small brewpubs to retail their own beer. Allowing brewpubs to sell beer generally increases opportunities for small producers and retail diversity rather than creating a market dominated by only a few manufacturers. There is no evidence that permitting brewpub sales in Georgia would produce the kind of nationwide consolidation seen in Mexico.

claim: Says over 1,000 mail in ballots were found in a dumpster in California.
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence that over 1,000 mail-in ballots were found in a dumpster in California. Viral versions of this claim were debunked by fact-checkers who found either no corroborating official reports or that the items found were far fewer in number, were unused/spoiled ballots or ballot-related envelopes, or were mischaracterized. Law enforcement and election officials did not confirm an incident matching the claim as stated.

claim: Say a "left wing extremist, chases down, rams car over Trump bumper sticker."
rationale: The statement alleges a specific violent incident by a “left wing extremist” but provides no time, place, names, or sources to corroborate it. Without independent reporting, police records, or verifiable evidence, the claim cannot be confirmed and should be treated as unverified/false. Given the absence of supporting details, it is not possible to substantiate the allegation as presented.

claim: "Texas has lost the most law enforcement officers in the line of duty of any state in America."
rationale: Major memorial databases that track line-of-duty deaths (most notably the Officer Down Memorial Page) list Texas as having the largest cumulative number of law enforcement officer fatalities of any U.S. state. Texas' long history, large population, and many local agencies contribute to its higher total compared with other states.

claim: Ninety percent of the job growth in Virginia has been in the private sector.
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or data source and therefore cannot be verified as stated. While most job gains in Virginia historically come from the private sector, the share varies by period and official BLS/Virginia Employment Commission reports do not universally show exactly 90% for all periods. Without a specified period and source, the blanket assertion is unsupported.

claim: "There are parks in Southeast Raleigh that still don’t have air conditioning in the gym"
rationale: This is a highly specific, time-sensitive claim about local facilities that I cannot verify with the information available. Municipal park amenities vary and details like whether a particular park gym has air conditioning require up-to-date local records or direct confirmation from the City of Raleigh Parks & Recreation. Because I lack those sources, I treat the claim as unverified and therefore classify it as FALSE under the guidance to prefer FALSE when uncertain.

claim: Says "roughly two-thirds of (state) corporations didn’t pay any income tax in Virginia."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and unsupported by available state tax reporting. While many businesses operate as pass‑through entities (S‑corps, LLCs, partnerships) and therefore do not pay Virginia’s corporate income tax directly, that is different from saying two‑thirds of corporations that file corporate returns paid no tax; Virginia data do not show a clear, sustained figure of “roughly two‑thirds” of corporations owing zero tax. Without a specific year, definition of “corporations,” or source, the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: Says Rick Scott took $200,000 in campaign contributions from a company that "profited off pollution."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as stated: public campaign finance records do not show a single, clearly identified $200,000 contribution to Rick Scott from a company universally described as having “profited off pollution.” While Scott has received donations from corporate PACs and industries (utilities, oil, agriculture) that critics sometimes link to pollution, there is no documented, specific $200,000 gift from a single company proven to have profited from pollution that matches this claim. Without a named donor, the allegation appears to conflate donations from multiple sources and a political characterization of those companies’ activities.

claim: "Quite frankly, it was during the Bush years of spending, multiplied now by the Obama years that we have this mess."
rationale: The claim is an oversimplification and attributing the entire fiscal/economic "mess" solely to Bush spending then "multiplied" by Obama is inaccurate. Deficits and debt grew under the Bush administration largely because of tax cuts, two wars and the 2008 financial crash, while large deficits during the early Obama years largely reflected the recession and temporary stimulus/automatic stabilizers; deficits then declined in the mid-2010s. Multiple factors (economic cycle, policy choices across several administrations, mandatory spending and demographics) contribute, so the causal framing is misleading.

claim: "One out of every five people that the federal government charges with murder is an illegal alien."
rationale: This claim is not supported by available evidence. Most homicides are prosecuted by states, federal homicide prosecutions are rare, and the federal caseload is dominated by immigration offenses — not federal murder charges involving undocumented defendants. There is no reliable data showing one in five federal murder defendants are "illegal aliens."

claim: Senate Democrats who left the state for weeks to delay a vote on union bargaining power exercised a "Wisconsin filibuster" provided by the state’s constitution.
rationale: While Senate Democrats did leave the state to deny quorum and delay votes (a tactic often called 'quorum‑busting' or colloquially a 'Wisconsin filibuster'), there is no explicit 'filibuster' provided by the Wisconsin Constitution. The constitution and legislative rules set quorum requirements that can be exploited by absences, but they do not create a formal filibuster right as the claim asserts.

claim: Says his administration balanced "two budgets with over $13 billion in deficits without raising taxes."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented because it omits which administration and which two budgets, and such claims are frequently disputed based on accounting choices (one‑time federal aid, reserves, fee increases, or spending shifts). Without that specificity, the assertion that two budget shortfalls totaling over $13 billion were balanced “without raising taxes” cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false. Accepted practice is to require detailed budget records and definitions of “raising taxes” to substantiate the claim.

claim: "Trump's campaign manager, Paul Manafort, commits bank and tax fraud and gets 47 months. A homeless man, Fate Winslow, helped sell $20 of pot and got life in prison."
rationale: The first part is accurate: Paul Manafort was convicted of bank and tax fraud and received a 47-month federal sentence. The second part is unverified and likely false—there is no credible evidence that a homeless man named Fate Winslow received a life sentence for selling $20 of marijuana; that claim appears to be a viral/misattributed story rather than a documented court outcome.

claim: "They're saying that 40 percent of the traffic that goes over [the Sakonnet River Bridge is from] out of state."
rationale: There is no clear, authoritative evidence that a constant 40% of vehicles crossing the Sakonnet River Bridge are from out of state; typical DOT traffic analyses for such crossings show the majority of trips are local or in-state, with higher out-of-state shares only during peak tourist periods. The claim presents a single high percentage without specifying timeframe (annual vs. seasonal) or data source, so it is likely an overstatement or taken out of context.

claim: Says that in 1770 "British parliament banned lipstick, saying it had the power to seduce men into marriage, which was classified as witchcraft."
rationale: There is no historical record that the British Parliament passed a law in 1770 banning lipstick as a form of witchcraft or because it could ‘seduce men into marriage.’ The Witchcraft Act of 1735 addressed claims of supernatural powers but did not criminalize cosmetics, and while cosmetics were socially condemned at times, formal parliamentary bans on lipstick in 1770 did not occur. The claim appears to conflate moralistic rhetoric about cosmetics with unrelated legislation or earlier/other anti-witchcraft statutes.

claim: "Never mind that no red light camera, no speed camera, nor any radar gun has ever stopped one accident from occurring."
rationale: The absolute claim is false. Numerous peer-reviewed studies and official traffic‑safety evaluations find that red‑light cameras, speed cameras and active speed enforcement (radar) reduce speeding and lower rates of certain crash types and injuries, meaning they have in many cases prevented accidents. While effects vary by location and can sometimes shift crash patterns (e.g., more rear‑end collisions), the statement that none has ever prevented a single accident is contradicted by empirical evidence.

claim: "Nobody applies to the United States for refugee status. They apply to the United Nations."
rationale: This is incorrect: people do apply to the United States for protection. Asylum seekers apply directly to U.S. authorities at ports of entry or within the country, and refugees can be processed for U.S. resettlement through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program. While the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) often refers vulnerable people for resettlement, referrals can also come from U.S. embassies, NGOs, or family members, so it is not true that applications go only to the U.N.

claim: "Illegal immigration and the crime rate are as low as they’ve been in decades."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate: indicators of unauthorized immigration (border encounters and crossings) have been elevated in recent years and the estimated unauthorized population is not at multi‑decade lows, and violence rose sharply in 2020–2021 with only partial declines since—so crime is not uniformly “as low as it’s been in decades.” While some measures (like long‑term property‑crime trends) have declined, the combined blanket claim is not supported by available U.S. data.

claim: Al Sharpton went to Ferguson, Mo., and is "declaring as a matter of fact that ... Michael Brown didn't use any deadly force or posed no deadly threat to the officer."
rationale: Al Sharpton did travel to Ferguson in August 2014 to participate in protests after Michael Brown was shot, and in speeches and interviews he publicly characterized Brown as unarmed and argued the killing was unjustified—saying Brown did not pose a deadly threat to the officer. While the claim’s quoted wording may not be verbatim, the substance of Sharpton’s public statements matches this description and was widely reported at the time.

claim: Jason Carter supports using Georgia tax dollars to promote Obamacare
rationale: During his 2014 gubernatorial campaign Jason Carter repeatedly said he would not use state tax dollars to promote the Affordable Care Act; he supported outreach and enrollment efforts funded by federal grants, community groups, or existing federal programs rather than new Georgia state spending. Opponent ads that claimed he would use "Georgia tax dollars" conflated federal outreach money spent in Georgia with state-funded promotion.

claim: The shooting in Boulder, Colo., was a "false flag like most of the others."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Boulder, Colorado, supermarket shooting was a staged or government 'false flag' operation. Law enforcement identified and charged a named suspect, investigators recovered physical and forensic evidence, and mainstream reporting and official statements found no indication of staging. Claims that most mass shootings are 'false flags' are broad conspiracy assertions unsupported by investigated facts.

claim: "In 1968, a full-time worker earning minimum wage, could actually support a family of three above the poverty line. Today, that same worker would earn less than the poverty line for a family of two."
rationale: The statement is broadly correct. In 1968 the federal minimum wage was about $1.60/hr (roughly $3,300/year at 40 hrs/week), which was slightly above the 1968 poverty threshold for a three-person family; today the federal minimum is $7.25/hr (about $15,080/year full time), which is below contemporary poverty thresholds for a two-person household, so the comparison captures a real decline in minimum-wage purchasing power relative to poverty lines.

claim: "If we use (Tax Increment Financing) funding, that's going to take funds from the general fund for Pinellas County, as it will take funds from the general fund for the city of St. Pete."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Tax Increment Financing (TIF) diverts the incremental property-tax revenue generated within a redevelopment area to a trust for projects; it automatically captures the municipality’s increment but only affects a county’s general fund if the county’s tax increment is specifically included or the county agrees to participate. Therefore using TIF does not necessarily take funds from Pinellas County’s general fund in the same automatic way it would reduce the City of St. Pete’s municipal increment.

claim: "While all COVID-19 news has been going on, the U.S. Government has been sneakily trying to remove end-to-end encryption" which means "the government will be able to see all of your messages and listen to all of your calls."
rationale: While U.S. law-enforcement officials and some legislators have publicly pushed for ways to reduce strong end-to-end encryption (e.g., advocating “lawful access” or technical mitigations), there has been no secret federal takeover or enacted law that has removed E2EE across services. Major platforms still deploy E2EE for many products, and any government ability to read or listen to all communications would require specific laws, technical changes, or provider cooperation that have not been universally implemented.

claim: "I helped win one of the biggest private lawsuits against Medicare fraud in history. The government declined to pursue the case, so my firm did, and we recovered $324 million for taxpayers."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific assertion as stated because it provides no identifying details (person, firm, or case name) and I find no clear public record tying a private firm recovery of exactly $324 million after the government declined to intervene to a widely reported ‘one of the biggest’ Medicare fraud qui tam wins. While there have been very large False Claims Act recoveries, those are publicly documented and typically name the parties; absent a case citation this precise claim is unverified and therefore judged false.

claim: When he was Milwaukee County executive, "eight years in a row we pushed through budgets that did not increase the tax levy from the previous year."
rationale: The claim is misleading: while the county executive in question (Scott Walker) frequently cited holding the county levy flat, independent fact-checkers and budget records show important exceptions and accounting shifts so it is not accurate to state unqualifiedly that eight consecutive budgets did not increase the tax levy. The statement depends on definitional choices (which components of the levy are counted and whether transfers or debt service are included), and in some years underlying levy obligations rose even if headline numbers were adjusted to appear flat.

claim: Says Melania Trump’s dress at Mount Rushmore speech was designed from "drawings of several young victims of sex trafficking."
rationale: The claim is false — there is no reliable evidence that Melania Trump’s Mount Rushmore dress was created from drawings by young victims of sex trafficking. Contemporary fact-checks and reporting found the dress was a commercial designer piece (by Hervé Pierre) and did not trace the textile pattern to such victim artwork; the viral assertion originated on social media without verifiable sourcing. The designer/label and independent reviewers did not corroborate the dramatic origin story.

claim: "Of the top five cities for staged automobile accidents, three are in Florida. … We rank No. 1 in the country in staged auto accidents."
rationale: The claim gives a precise national ranking but provides no source or timeframe and cannot be verified from authoritative, current nationwide data. While Florida cities (e.g., in South Florida and other metro areas) have been cited in investigations of staged crash rings, national insurers and crime-reporting groups do not publish a consistent, verifiable “top five cities” list that corroborates the specific assertion that three of the top five are in Florida or that the state ranks #1 overall. Without a cited source the numeric ranking is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: Louisiana gets "not one single penny" from Gulf Coast offshore oil revenues.
rationale: This is incorrect. Louisiana receives money tied to Gulf offshore oil through multiple channels — federal revenue-sharing under the Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act (GOMESA), federal penalty/settlement and RESTORE Act funds from Deepwater Horizon, and state-level taxes/royalties from state waters and production — so it is not true that the state gets “not one single penny.”

claim: "When I took office, the deficit was nearly 10 percent of our economy. Today, it's approaching 3 percent."
