Thus the claim that you "couldn’t buy a cannon" when the Amendment passed is inaccurate as a statement of absolute legal impossibility.

claim: "Both China and Japan have surpassed us, with Japanese cars now getting an average of 45 miles to the gallon."
rationale: This claim is not supported by available evidence. There are no credible data showing the average Japanese passenger car gets 45 mpg by a directly comparable (EPA-style) measure, and published Japanese fuel-economy figures use different test cycles that typically overstate EPA-equivalent mileage. Likewise, China’s overall vehicle fleet fuel economy has been improving but is not clearly and unambiguously ahead of the U.S. across comparable measures.

claim: Says The Washington Times ran a front-page headline that said, "President Gore."
rationale: There is no reliable record that The Washington Times ran a front-page headline reading "President Gore." Although several outlets made premature calls during the 2000 Bush–Gore count and some papers printed early, documented examples do not show The Washington Times publishing that headline. The claim likely confuses another paper or an early/mistaken electronic report with a printed front page.

claim: ﻿Says JoAnne Kloppenburg’s side had a "3-to-1 money advantage" in the Wisconsin Supreme Court campaign.
rationale: This is incorrect as stated. In the Wisconsin Supreme Court contest involving JoAnne Kloppenburg (notably the 2011 race), conservative and business-aligned groups supporting her opponent substantially outspent Kloppenburg’s side — outside spending favored her opponent, not Kloppenburg by 3-to-1. Contemporary campaign‑finance summaries and news coverage reported that spending tilted toward the conservative/Prosser side.

claim: Rick Perry thinks "injecting 11- and 12-year-old girls with a controversial drug (the HPV vaccine), without a parent's consent, is a good idea."
rationale: Rick Perry did support a 2007 policy requiring the HPV vaccine for 11- and 12-year-old girls and drew criticism for doing so via executive action, but there is no reliable evidence he advocated vaccinating girls without parental consent. Texas practice and the policy included opt-outs/waivers and Perry defended the mandate rather than urging removal of parental consent. Thus the claim overstates his position by asserting he wants injections without parental permission.

claim: Royalties for oil and other energy sources are the "second-largest revenue source to the federal government after the IRS."
rationale: Federal receipts data show that mineral and energy royalties make up a very small share of total federal revenue, far smaller than payroll (Social Insurance) taxes and corporate and individual income taxes. The second-largest federal revenue source after individual income taxes is payroll taxes, not royalties from oil and energy, so the claim is incorrect.

claim: Says Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio "had it set so that the winner takes everything, because they wanted to make sure that I didn't get anything" in the Florida primary.
rationale: This claim attributes a deliberate, unilateral setting of Florida’s Republican delegate rules to Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio to deny a rival delegates. Delegate allocation is set by the state party and RNC rules, not individual candidates, and Florida’s winner‑take‑all provisions were party rules in place and subject to party procedures. There’s no credible evidence that Bush and Rubio personally “had it set” specifically to block the claimant.

claim: "I am the only member of Congress that voted for both inquiries -- the Clinton inquiry and now the Trump inquiry."
rationale: The claim is false because more than one current member of the House served in both 1998 and the later Trump impeachment period and the roll-call histories for the two impeachment inquiries include multiple overlapping voters. The 1998 Clinton inquiry drew some bipartisan support and the 2019 Trump inquiry drew votes from many long-serving members, so there is documented overlap rather than a single individual who voted on both.

claim: "We’re seeing now 30 straight months of private-sector job growth, 4.6 million jobs created."
rationale: The claim is presented without a date and does not match published monthly BLS private‑sector payroll series for any clearly identified 30‑month span. Whether there were 30 consecutive months of private‑sector gains and whether they totaled 4.6 million depends on the exact start and end months; official BLS counts must be cited to verify the numbers, and as stated the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: Gov. Scott Walker received a $7,300 pay raise.
rationale: The statement is unqualified and no public payroll or legislative records show Governor Scott Walker personally received a $7,300 pay increase during his tenure. Governors' salaries in Wisconsin are set by statute and changes are documented; available summaries and fact-checks of Walker's pay do not support a one-time $7,300 raise. Without a specific year or source the claim appears inaccurate.

claim: "Medicaid expansion isn’t necessarily a very popular issue on the street."
rationale: The statement implies Medicaid expansion is not broadly popular, but public-opinion data and policy outcomes indicate otherwise: majorities in national and numerous state polls have consistently supported Medicaid expansion, and a large number of states have adopted it. While local salience varies and it may not always top voters’ lists of priorities, calling it not generally popular is inconsistent with widespread polling support and bipartisan backing in many places.

claim: "The president is advocating a drone strike program in America."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a U.S. president has advocated creating a program to carry out drone strikes inside the United States. Presidents have authorized targeted drone operations overseas for counterterrorism, but proposing domestic lethal strikes would conflict with constitutional and legal norms and was not reported in reputable sources through mid-2024. The claim is unsupported without a specific person, quote, or source.

claim: "(T)he United States government and its Constitution says that people can be put to death."
rationale: While the Constitution does not use the phrase “people can be put to death,” it permits capital punishment through laws applied with constitutional protections (due process, etc.). The Eighth Amendment forbids cruel and unusual punishment but does not categorically ban the death penalty, and the Supreme Court has upheld capital punishment under guided procedures (e.g., post-Furman/Gregg jurisprudence).

claim: Says "Christine Blasey Ford’s letter to Sen. Dianne Feinstein revealed to be a total FAKE… contains 14 glaring errors that could only be committed by a poorly educated writer." ​
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Christine Blasey Ford’s letter to Senator Feinstein was a fake; Ford and Feinstein acknowledged the letter and multiple independent fact-checkers and news organizations investigated and found the circulated claims about it being forged unsupported. Allegations about “14 glaring errors” have been debunked as misreads, stylistic or transcription issues, or subjective judgments rather than proof of fabrication or an uneducated author. The claim is thus false.

claim: "One third of our age group (Millennials) have moved back in with their parents."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it lacks timeframe and definition. While some surveys (especially during the COVID-19 pandemic) found roughly one-third of younger adults temporarily moved back with parents, that statistic applied to specific age ranges and periods and does not universally describe all Millennials across places and years.

claim: State Rep. Elena Parent "supported Governor Nathan Deal’s plan to slash the HOPE scholarship."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that State Rep. Elena Parent supported Governor Nathan Deal’s proposal to cut the HOPE scholarship. As a Democratic legislator representing a progressive Atlanta district she publicly opposed reductions to HOPE and supported protecting student aid; the claim that she backed Deal’s cut appears to be inaccurate or misleading.

claim: Obama "voted against funding our troops."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While Obama opposed certain Iraq-war supplemental bills as a senator (saying they lacked benchmarks or a change in strategy), he also voted for many defense appropriations and, as president, repeatedly requested and signed funding for U.S. forces; he did not categorically 'vote against funding our troops.'

claim: Says Thom Tillis "refuses to say what we should do to combat ISIS."
rationale: Multiple public interviews and debates show Sen. Thom Tillis declined to outline specific operational steps for combating ISIS, saying tactical decisions should be left to military leaders and the administration. Opponents and news reports characterized this as a refusal to describe what should be done, so the claim accurately reflects his publicly observed behavior in those instances.

claim: "There is no reason to allocate 60 percent of bridge space to satisfy two percent of all travelers."
rationale: The claim is a broad, normative assertion that cannot be verified as a factual statement because it lacks critical context (which bridge, which travelers, what purpose the allocated space serves). Whether allocating 60% of bridge space to a user group that constitutes 2% of current travelers is justified depends on policy goals (safety, future demand, legal requirements, equity, modal shift), engineering constraints, and projected use — any of which can provide legitimate reasons. Because the statement is context-free and subjective, it cannot be treated as a factual claim as written.

claim: Says the T.R.U.M.P. Act, which would force presidential candidates to release their tax returns to run in North Carolina, "has a lot of support – by a majority of North Carolinians and members of both parties."
rationale: The statement overstates the bipartisan nature of support. While polls have often shown a majority of North Carolina residents favoring a requirement that presidential candidates release tax returns, the support is split by party: Democrats and independents tend to back such measures, but most Republican voters do not form a majority in favor. Therefore the claim that a majority of members of both parties support the T.R.U.M.P. Act is inaccurate.

claim: "More than one in five of veterans aged 20 to 24 can’t find a job to support their family or to ease the transition to civilian life."
rationale: The claim asserts that over 20% of veterans aged 20–24 “can’t find a job,” but labor-force statistics for young veterans do not support such a high, widely reported figure. Official measures (BLS/Census-based analyses) show youth and veteran unemployment rates that are typically well under 20% for that specific age group, and the phrase “can’t find a job to support their family or to ease the transition” is not a standard, measurable statistic. Because the claim mixes subjective reasons with an absolute fraction without supporting data, it is not supported by typical public data.

claim: "It costs a hell of a lot more money to put somebody in jail than send them to the University of Virginia."
rationale: The claim is an overly broad generalization. Per-inmate annual incarceration costs and the cost to send a student to the University of Virginia vary widely (by state, in‑state vs out‑of‑state tuition, and whether room/board are included); in some comparisons incarceration is higher, in others it is comparable or lower. Because the statement lacks specifics and is not universally true, it is false as an absolute claim.

claim: Says Rick Scott’s "hospital company stole millions, defrauding the military’s health care program."
rationale: Rick Scott was CEO of Columbia/HCA, a hospital chain that paid roughly $1.7 billion in the late 1990s/2000 to settle widespread federal civil and criminal claims about Medicare and Medicaid billing fraud. However, reliable public records and major reportage document fraud allegations and settlements concerning Medicare/Medicaid, not a proven scheme specifically defrauding the U.S. military’s TRICARE/DoD health program, so the claim as written is misleading and not supported.

claim: Pennsylvania officials are "attempting to silence voters" by sending them letters that say they’ve been exposed to COVID-19 and "must remain quarantined and not vote in person on Election Day."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Pennsylvania election officials sent coordinated letters telling voters they "must remain quarantined and not vote in person" as a tactic to silence voters. Notices that tell people they were exposed to COVID-19 are public-health contact-tracing or quarantine advisories, not directives from election officials prohibiting in-person voting, and Pennsylvania provides alternatives such as mail-in and curbside voting for quarantined voters.

claim: Kasim Reed has kept every promise he made as a candidate.
rationale: The claim is an absolute assertion that Reed kept every campaign promise, which is extremely unlikely and not supported by reporting. During his mayoralty Reed faced criticism and investigations and observers documented unmet or altered pledges in areas like ethics reform, transportation and budget priorities, so it is not true that he fulfilled every promise. Determining completeness would require exhaustive, item-by-item verification which has not been demonstrated.

claim: Says Florida Gov. Rick Scott "subtracted $1.3 billion from public schools."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Statewide K–12 appropriations in Florida did not fall by $1.3 billion over Rick Scott’s tenure; overall education funding generally rose year-to-year. The $1.3 billion figure appears to come from comparisons of proposed budgets, one-time vetoes, or specific line-item changes rather than an absolute, sustained $1.3 billion cut to public schools.

claim: Says when he was governor, "most of the Democrats" voted for his billion-dollar property-tax cuts, but U.S. Senate rival Tammy Baldwin "voted against it."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate as stated. Tammy Baldwin was a member of the U.S. Congress (House then Senate) and did not vote in the Wisconsin state legislature when a governor enacted state property-tax cuts, so she could not have cast a state-legislative vote against such a bill; moreover, the assertion that “most of the Democrats” supported a specific billion-dollar state property-tax cut is misleading without identifying the bill and vote, and historic party-line opposition by state Democrats makes a blanket majority claim doubtful.

claim: Says Joe Biden tweeted, "the way white people talk leaving minorities confused."
rationale: There is no evidence in Biden's verified social media history, reputable news reports, or fact-checking archives that Joe Biden tweeted the phrase "the way white people talk leaving minorities confused." The alleged quote appears to be a fabricated or misattributed social media post inconsistent with documented Biden communications.

claim: "In France, they have a (surveillance) program a thousandfold more invasive" than the United States.
rationale: The claim is not supported by evidence: it asserts a precise quantitative comparison ('a thousandfold more invasive') without defining a metric or naming a specific program. Both France and the United States operate extensive surveillance systems under different laws and authorities, but there is no credible public data that measures 'invasiveness' in a way that would justify a 1000× claim. Absent a clear metric and documented measurements, the statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says "Scott Walker says he would ban stem cell research"
rationale: Scott Walker has opposed embryonic stem cell research and said he would not support taxpayer funding for research that destroys embryos, but he has not said he would ban all stem cell research outright. His public statements emphasize support for adult stem cell research and alternatives rather than a blanket prohibition. Therefore the claim as stated (that he says he would ban stem cell research) is misleading.

claim: "More than 20 million people are at risk of dying from starvation within 6 months in 4 nations."
rationale: This wording closely matches warnings issued by the United Nations and other humanitarian agencies (reported in late 2022) that more than 20 million people in four countries—Yemen, Somalia, South Sudan and Ethiopia—were at risk of dying from starvation within months without urgent assistance. Multiple UN agencies and major news outlets repeated the same figure and timeframe. The claim reflects those authoritative statements rather than a newly derived estimate.

claim: "I've always known this is a real, this is a pandemic. I've felt it was a pandemic long before it was called a pandemic."
rationale: This is a first‑person statement about the speaker’s internal belief and when they formed it; such subjective claims cannot be independently verified from external evidence. Without corroborating timestamped statements or records, it is not possible to confirm the claim, so it is labeled false per the instruction to prefer FALSE when uncertain.

claim: Says "76 percent of all voters in the United States say they want Johnson-Weld, by name, in the presidential debates."
rationale: There is no reputable evidence that 76% of all U.S. voters specifically named “Johnson–Weld” when asked they want them in presidential debates. While some polls have found broad support for including third‑party candidates in debates, those questions usually ask about third parties in general and do not produce a 76% figure specifically naming the Johnson–Weld ticket, and Johnson/Weld never met the debate inclusion thresholds used by the Commission on Presidential Debates.

claim: "Last week Joe Biden flashed the ‘white power’ sign. President Trump condemned white supremacists yesterday. Why hasn't Joe Biden?"
rationale: The claim is misleading and unverified: there is no credible evidence that Joe Biden deliberately “flashed the ‘white power’ sign” last week, and hand gestures are frequently misinterpreted. Moreover, both presidents have at times publicly addressed white supremacists, so the timing and implication that Biden has not condemned them is unsupported without specific, dated statements. The statement mixes time-sensitive assertions and an unproven interpretation of a gesture.

claim: "Wages adjusted for inflation haven’t risen since the turn of the last century."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate as a general claim. Inflation-adjusted measures such as real average hourly earnings and median household/median worker wages in the U.S. have shown net gains since around 2000, though the growth has been modest and uneven and punctuated by recessions. Saying they “haven’t risen” ignores these documented increases and variation across groups and time periods.

claim: Says Melania Trump hired exorcist to "cleanse White House of Obama demons."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Melania Trump hired an exorcist to "cleanse" the White House of "Obama demons." The claim appears to originate from tabloids and social posts; mainstream news and fact-checkers found only routine clergy visits or reports of blessings, not an exorcism requested by Melania. The sensational phrasing is unsupported by reliable sourcing.

claim: The Baucus health care bill "would drastically restrict the use of flexible spending accounts (FSAs) in order to help pay for health care reform."
rationale: The 2009 Senate Finance Committee draft authored by Chairman Max Baucus included provisions to limit tax-preferred flexible spending accounts (FSA) — commonly reported as a $2,500 cap on contributions — as part of a set of revenue offsets to help pay for health care reform. Thus the claim that the Baucus bill would restrict FSAs to help finance reform is accurate, though the term “drastically” is subjective.

claim: "We had the highest number of (military) sexual assaults ever reported in the last year" and "we had the lowest conviction rate and the lowest prosecution rate."
rationale: The claim mixes multiple absolute assertions that are not fully supported. Department of Defense/SAPRO annual reports show reported sexual assaults have risen in recent years and prosecutions/convictions have fluctuated, but available public data do not unambiguously support that the most recent year was both the highest-ever for reports and simultaneously the lowest-ever for prosecution and conviction rates across the entire record. Without specifying the country, exact year, and metric definitions, the blanket statement is not demonstrably true.

claim: "We enacted the biggest tax cuts and reforms in American history."
rationale: The claim is misleading without a defined metric. The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was a large tax-change, notably cutting the corporate rate from 35% to 21%, but independent analyses show it was not the largest tax cut in U.S. history when measured as a share of GDP or by long‑term revenue impact (earlier reforms, especially the 1981 Reagan cuts, were larger by those measures). Thus calling it “the biggest tax cuts and reforms in American history” is inaccurate as a general statement.

claim: There were no American flags at the first Democratic presidential debate.
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim but gives no year or cycle; staging varies by debate. At least some first Democratic presidential primary debates in recent cycles have included American flags or prominent patriotic imagery, so the blanket assertion that there were none is unlikely to be correct. Without a specific debate date the claim cannot be verified and is misleading as stated.

claim: "Here's the fact: The No. 1 source of income into Mexico are Mexicans working here and sending the money back."
rationale: False. Remittances from Mexicans working abroad are a very large and growing source of foreign currency and have in some years exceeded oil export revenue, but they are not the single largest source of income into Mexico overall. Exports of goods and services (manufactured and other trade) and other external receipts (tourism, FDI, etc.) bring in far more foreign currency than remittances.

claim: "Here, we have Thanksgiving, we have Christmas, we have the 4th of July. Every year in Iran, they celebrate Death to America day."
rationale: The Islamic Republic of Iran marks an annual state-organized observance on the Nov. 4 anniversary of the 1979 embassy takeover (officially called the 'National Day of Fight against Global Arrogance'), during which government-backed rallies commonly feature chants of 'Death to America.' That annual event is a recurring, official practice, though it does not mean every Iranian citizen personally celebrates it.

claim: "39% of All California Students are illegals."
rationale: This is not supported by credible data. California has millions of K–12 students and estimates of undocumented (non‑citizen) children in the state number in the low hundreds of thousands at most, implying a single‑digit percentage — far below 39%. The claim likely misstates or confuses a different statistic or subgroup.

claim: Says Patrick Morrisey undertook "efforts to put educators in jail."
rationale: There is no clear, credible evidence that West Virginia Attorney General Patrick Morrisey undertook efforts to have educators jailed. Coverage of disputes with teachers (notably the 2018 strikes) records criticism and discussion of legal or administrative remedies, but not prosecutions aimed at incarcerating educators. The claim appears to conflate tough rhetoric or civil/legal actions with an actual campaign to put teachers in jail.

claim: "Debt has almost doubled in Austin under Gov. Perry."
rationale: Available municipal finance data and independent fact-checks show Austin’s municipal debt grew during Rick Perry’s years as governor but did not “almost double.” The increase varied by the debt measure and time window, but bonded indebtedness rose modestly and fell well short of a near-100% increase over the period in question.

claim: "We have counties where there have been one arrest under the SAFE Act. It indicates there's not a whole lot of interest in enforcing this in our upstate counties."
rationale: The claim mixes an unspecified factual assertion (some counties have had only one arrest under the SAFE Act) with an interpretive conclusion that this proves lack of interest in enforcement. Without county-level, time-bounded arrest data and information on how the SAFE Act is implemented (many provisions are regulatory or prosecuted by different agencies), the inference is not supported. Low arrest counts can reflect limited applicability of the statute, charging discretion, reporting practices, or alternative enforcement strategies rather than lack of interest.

claim: Says Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker doesn't make his calendar public -- "he's on our dime and we don't know where he is."
rationale: The claim that Walker “doesn't make his calendar public” is inaccurate as an absolute statement. As governor Walker's office routinely released press schedules and calendar entries, though critics complained some details were redacted or not fully disclosed for security or personnel reasons. While transparency was debated, it is not true that no calendar information was made public.

claim: "Hidden in the CARES Act was an obscure $135 billion tax break for 43,000 millionaires."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that the CARES Act secretly delivered a targeted $135 billion tax break exclusively to 43,000 millionaires. CARES included temporary changes (like expanded net operating loss carrybacks and suspension of certain loss limits) that provided refunds and tax relief to a wide range of businesses and taxpayers, and official JCT/analyst cost estimates and distributional analyses do not support the precise $135B/43,000 figure as a discreet millionaire-only giveaway. The claim appears to conflate or misattribute broad corporate/pass-through provisions and extrapolated benefits to a small millionaire cohort.

claim: Says the New York bike path assault "was the ninth vehicle assault used by ISIS."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the New York bike path attack was specifically the "ninth" vehicle assault by ISIS; counts of ISIS-linked vehicle attacks vary depending on criteria (directly-directed vs. inspired lone actors) and no authoritative source marks it as the ninth. ISIS had publicly encouraged vehicle ramming as a tactic and several high-profile vehicle attacks preceded the New York incident, but enumerations differ and the precise ordinal claim is unsupported. Therefore the statement is misleading and not factually established.

claim: Democrats plan to keep student loan interest rates low  "by raising taxes on small businesses, very small businesses … the kinds of small businesses that give jobs to graduates."
rationale: There is no evidence of a unified Democratic plan to keep student loan interest rates low by specifically "raising taxes on small businesses, very small businesses". Democratic proposals to fund student-aid programs have typically focused on higher taxes for high-income households, corporations, or closing tax loopholes, not targeted tax hikes on small employers. Claims that Democrats will raise taxes on small businesses are a common mischaracterization of broader tax proposals.

claim: "We’ve been able to create about 60,000 net new jobs" in Virginia since February.
rationale: The claim lacks a clear year or end date and I find no corroborating state employment release showing a roughly 60,000 net increase in Virginia jobs over a short period “since February.” Typical month-to-month nonfarm payroll changes for Virginia are much smaller, and publicly released BLS/state reports up through mid-2024 do not show a single multi-month jump of that magnitude without broader context. Without a specified timeframe or source, the claim is not supported by available state labor data patterns.

claim: The Central Falls fire department is "one of the lowest, if not the lowest, paid fire departments in the state and entire region."
rationale: I cannot verify that Central Falls is definitively "one of the lowest, if not the lowest" paid fire departments across the entire state and region. Comprehensive, up‑to‑date salary comparisons across all municipal and regional fire departments are required to substantiate such an absolute ranking, and I do not have such data. While Central Falls has a small tax base and historically constrained municipal budgets, that alone does not prove it ranks lowest without salary tables and collective‑bargaining details.

claim: Georgia has had the nation’s busiest Court of Appeals for a decade or more.
rationale: The claim as stated is misleading because it omits context. While Georgia’s Court of Appeals is frequently described as the busiest intermediate state appellate court and has led state-level caseload rankings for many years, it is not unambiguously the nation’s busiest ‘Court of Appeals’ overall when federal circuits (e.g., the Ninth Circuit) are considered. Without the qualifier “state” the assertion is false or at least ambiguous.

claim: "Since 1995, the top 400 wealthiest families have seen their incomes go up 400 percent and their tax rates go down 40 percent."
rationale: The claim mixes imprecise measures and overstates trends. Publicly available analyses distinguish Forbes 400 wealth (net worth) from taxable income and show large wealth gains for the very richest, but not a clear, uniform “400%” rise in taxable income for the top 400 since 1995; likewise reported tax-rate changes depend on whether you mean statutory, average, or effective federal rates and are far smaller than a 40 percentage-point drop. Because the statement conflates wealth and income and gives a rounded, unsupported percentage for tax-rate decline it is inaccurate.

claim: Says he "will protect your guaranteed benefits" in Medicare while "Mitt Romney would take away Medicare as guaranteed benefits."
rationale: This is misleading/false as stated. Romney's well-documented 2012 proposal would have shifted future beneficiaries (generally younger cohorts) to a premium-support/voucher-style system rather than immediately stripping current enrollees of guaranteed Medicare benefits; it did not eliminate benefits for current beneficiaries. Saying he "would take away Medicare as guaranteed benefits" omits that the change applied to future enrollees and that benefits would be delivered differently rather than instantaneously revoked.

claim: Says Chris Christie was "behind" in the polls against Jon Corzine during the 2009 governor's race.
rationale: Most statewide polls during the 2009 New Jersey general-election campaign showed Republican Chris Christie leading incumbent Jon Corzine, and Christie went on to win the election by several points. Although an isolated early poll or brief regional snapshot might have shown Corzine ahead or tied, the overall trend was Christie in the lead.

claim: Says Betsy DeVos is the "most unpopular person in our government."
rationale: The statement is a subjective, comparative claim without a defined metric or timeframe and therefore cannot be established as an objective fact. While Betsy DeVos recorded very low favorability in some polls (especially among cabinet members in 2017–2018), other politicians and officials have at times registered lower popularity, so the unqualified claim that she is "the most unpopular person in our government" is unsupported.

claim: Under the new health care law, the elderly will be denied care when they have "passed the age limit for treatment."
rationale: There is no provision in major recent U.S. ‘new health care’ laws that creates a blanket age cutoff denying elderly people medical care. Claims that the law establishes an "age limit for treatment" stem from misinterpretations and rhetorical exaggerations (e.g., false "death panel" narratives); existing statutes (Medicare/Medicaid and anti‑age‑discrimination rules) and clinical standards guide coverage and treatment decisions, not a simple age cutoff.

claim: Says a "Clorox bottle claimed it could kill (the 2019 coronavirus)... before it was developed."
rationale: This is false. Clorox product labels have long listed efficacy against “human coronavirus” as a generic test organism (common cold coronaviruses) used in standard disinfectant testing; that is not a claim that the company predicted or named SARS‑CoV‑2 before it existed. EPA and manufacturer guidance explain labels reflect testing against related viruses and do not imply foreknowledge of a specific 2019 novel coronavirus.

claim: "New York, for all of their complaining, Gov. Cuomo's complaining, has only had a 1.5% decrease in revenue" due to the coronavirus pandemic.
rationale: The claim lacks a timeframe or definition of "revenue" and is inconsistent with public budget reports from New York during the COVID crisis, which documented multi-billion-dollar shortfalls and projections well above a 1.5% decline. State and independent budget offices reported steep drops in sales and personal income tax receipts and projected deficits that required federal aid, borrowing, and spending cuts, not a trivial 1.5% revenue loss.

claim: "Amazon accepts Dogecoin."
rationale: Amazon has not announced that it accepts Dogecoin (or other cryptocurrencies) as a direct payment method. Its checkout accepts fiat payment methods and Amazon-branded payment options; while third-party services can sell Amazon gift cards or convert crypto to fiat, Amazon itself does not accept Dogecoin.

claim: Says the Austin City Council "may give $4 million a year to subsidize a race track."
rationale: The statement is misleading as presented. While Austin has debated and sometimes provided public support related to Circuit of the Americas and other motorsport events, there is no clear, broadly reported Council authorization that the city “may give $4 million a year” as a standing subsidy without additional qualifiers (timeframe, ordinance, or specific proposal). The claim omits context and conflates varied funding discussions into a definitive recurring payment.

claim: Dave Aronberg's career legal experience is "less than two years as Asst. AG/private attorney."
rationale: Public biographical summaries show Aronberg held multiple years of legal roles (including government prosecutorial positions and private practice) before his long elected service, so describing his career as "less than two years as Asst. AG/private attorney" understates and mischaracterizes his experience. The claim appears to conflate or compress distinct jobs and time periods into an inaccurate short duration.

claim: "Dandelion root is able to kill 98% of cancer cells within 48 hours."
rationale: The claim overstates and generalizes. While some laboratory (in vitro) studies have reported that dandelion root extract can cause death in certain cancer cell lines under controlled conditions, there is no reliable clinical evidence that dandelion root kills 98% of cancer cells in humans within 48 hours. In vitro results depend on cell type, extract preparation and dose and do not directly translate to effectiveness in patients.

claim: Small businesses "create 70 percent of the jobs in America."
rationale: The statement is misleading as stated. Small businesses do not account for 70% of all jobs in the U.S.; they employ about half of the private‑sector workforce. While small firms have produced a large share of net new jobs in many past periods (often cited around 60–70% depending on the time window and definitions), the blanket claim without a time frame or definition is inaccurate.

claim: Says a video shows a "gay party in Italy few weeks before COVID-19."
rationale: There is no corroborating evidence provided to verify that the video was filmed in Italy or within the specific time window described. Without metadata, geolocation, or independent news reporting confirming the event date and location, the claim is unverified and thus treated as false. Viral videos are frequently misattributed across countries and years, so the specific assertion is not supported.

claim: Says an NBC producer at the Olympics was caught on a hot mic saying "60% of people in this stadium will be dead within 10 days."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable news reporting that an NBC producer was caught on a hot mic at the Olympics saying “60% of people in this stadium will be dead within 10 days.” The quote appears to have circulated on social media without verifiable audio or authoritative confirmation and matches patterns of misattributed or fabricated hot-mic claims. Major outlets and checks of available footage from Olympic broadcasts do not substantiate the allegation.

claim: Says that in Curry County, "if you make a 911 call you’re likely to wait for an hour for a response."
rationale: The claim is unverified and framed as a general rule (“you’re likely to wait for an hour”) with no supporting data; typical 911 response times are measured in minutes and while rural areas can see longer delays, an hour-long wait is not documented as the usual outcome for Curry County. Without a cited source or specification of which Curry County and what type of call (medical, fire, police, non-emergency), the assertion is likely misleading.

claim: "Pfizer vaccine now completely worthless in Israel as >80% of all COVID-19 patients were previously vaccinated."
rationale: This claim is misleading and false. A high share of COVID-19 cases being vaccinated can occur when most of the population is vaccinated and immunity against infection wanes over time; it does not mean the Pfizer vaccine is "completely worthless." Israeli data have shown increased breakthrough infections (especially with waning immunity and immune-evasive variants) but also continued strong protection against severe disease, particularly after boosters.

claim: Says Sen. Tim Kaine "approves of and even applauds his son's participation in a known terrorist organization, #Antifa."
rationale: This claim is false: there is no credible public record of Sen. Tim Kaine saying he "approves of and even applauds" a son's participation in Antifa, and reputable reporting does not support that quote. Moreover, Antifa is a decentralized movement/ideology rather than a formally designated U.S. terrorist organization, so the phrasing is misleading. The assertion appears to be a misattribution or fabrication.

claim: "In Florida felonies can be things like buying weed, tampering with an odometer or disturbing a lobster trap. So basically spring break."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate and inaccurate points. Florida law does criminalize odometer tampering and interfering with lobster traps and those offenses can be prosecuted as felonies depending on circumstances, but simple purchase/possession of small amounts of marijuana is typically a misdemeanor (possession over certain thresholds becomes a felony). The blanket statement that all three are felonies and the punchline 'so basically spring break' overgeneralizes and is misleading.

claim: Says New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg says "we can only have three bullets" and "the NRA wants firearms with nukes on them."
rationale: There is no credible record or reputable reporting showing Michael Bloomberg uttered the quoted lines about “we can only have three bullets” or claiming the NRA “wants firearms with nukes on them.” These extreme phrasings are inconsistent with Bloomberg’s documented public arguments on gun control, which focus on policy proposals and statistics rather than hyperbolic claims. If such statements had been made, they would have been widely reported and sourced in transcripts or major news outlets, which they are not.

claim: Says James Langevin voted to spend "$3 billion for a jet engine no one wants."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rep. James Langevin cast a vote specifically to authorize a single $3 billion appropriation for “a jet engine no one wants.” Congressional votes that Langevin supported were for broad defense appropriations or authorization bills that bundle many programs, and documented funding for contested single-engine programs (such as the alternate F-35 engine effort) was far smaller or spread across multiple years. The phrase “no one wants” is subjective and mischaracterizes how defense procurement decisions and congressional funding are made.

claim: "When a bill is sent to the governor’s office, there is no option for changing it. You sign it or you don’t sign it. While there was lots of conversation, there was really no opportunity for any sort of amending."
rationale: The claim is too absolute. While at the federal level the president can only sign or veto (or pocket veto), many governors have additional tools—most notably line-item vetoes on appropriations and in numerous states an amendatory (or conditional) veto that returns a bill with recommended changes which the legislature can accept or reject. Governors also commonly negotiate changes with legislators before signing. Thus it is not universally true that there is no option for changing a bill at the governor’s office.

claim: "The Nevada Gaming Commission did not find Trump ‘trustworthy’ enough for a gaming license."
rationale: I could not find a clear, documented Nevada Gaming Commission decision that explicitly concluded Trump was 'not trustworthy' and therefore denied him a gaming license. While Nevada regulators have in the past raised concerns about applicants' suitability and sometimes imposed conditions or declined approvals, the claim as stated uses a phrasing that does not match a specific, well-documented commission finding. Without a precise date or citation, the assertion is not supported.

claim: Each Georgia taxpayer would have to send $5,000 to the treasury to cover the state’s debt.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated because it omits critical definitions (which debt measure and which population) and the arithmetic does not hold under common, recent measures of Georgia’s obligations. State debt totals vary by year and by whether you include only direct state bonds, unfunded pension liabilities, or local debt; likewise the number of “taxpayers” can be measured in different ways. Under typical interpretations the per-taxpayer figure is materially different from a flat $5,000, so the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: If you ask Amazon’s Alexa about the origin of the coronavirus pandemic, it says "the government planned" it.
rationale: This claim is false—there is no reliable evidence that Amazon’s Alexa, as a default assistant response, says “the government planned” the coronavirus pandemic. Fact‑checks found the viral clips were either edited or the result of third‑party skills/news sources, and Amazon denies Alexa makes unsupported conspiracy assertions as a built‑in response. The claim conflates manipulated audio or external content with Alexa’s native behavior.

claim: Says a deer became "riddled with tumors from eating plants sprayed with Monsanto’s Roundup."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific causal link between Roundup (glyphosate) exposure and a deer becoming “riddled with tumors.” There is no credible peer‑reviewed evidence establishing that glyphosate causes widespread tumor formation in deer; reports are anecdotal and photos circulated online do not prove causation. Major regulatory reviews (while differing on human risk assessments) have not documented confirmed wildlife cancer outbreaks caused by glyphosate, so the strong causal claim is unsupported.

claim: Social Security is a "Ponzi scheme."
rationale: Calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" is inaccurate. Although current workers' payroll taxes pay current beneficiaries (a pay‑as‑you‑go feature superficially like a Ponzi), Social Security is a statutory government program with explicit legal obligations, a trust fund invested in Treasury securities, transparent rules for benefits and payroll taxation, and no element of private fraud or secret promise of returns that are central to Ponzi schemes.

claim: "In the past year, Floridians, not government, created almost 135,000 new private sector jobs. We netted more than 120,000 total jobs in the first 11 months of 2011; the third most of any state in the nation."
rationale: The claim appears to cherry‑pick timeframes and conflates private‑sector gains with net total jobs; authoritative state payroll series (BLS CES) for 2011 do not clearly support both specific figures and the stated national ranking. Without a precise month‑to‑month comparison the “almost 135,000 private” and “more than 120,000 total… third most” numbers are inconsistent with standard BLS seasonally adjusted monthly totals and commonly reported state rankings for 2011. Given the ambiguity and likelihood of selective use of months, the overall claim is misleading.

claim: Suggests Amber Heard snorted cocaine while on the stand in court.
rationale: There is no verified evidence that Amber Heard snorted cocaine while testifying. Court transcripts, reporting on the Depp–Heard trial, and evidence presented did not include drug tests or corroborated eyewitness accounts showing her snorting on the stand; at most there were insinuations and photos/video of her touching her nose which are inconclusive.

claim: Says more Republicans than Democrats voted for the Wall Street bailouts.
rationale: The major "Wall Street bailout" (the 2008 TARP/EESA vote) was supported by more Democrats than Republicans in Congress. Senate passage was 74–25 with a large number of Democratic yes votes, and the final House passage also included a larger number of Democrats voting in favor than Republicans. Therefore the statement that more Republicans than Democrats voted for the bailouts is incorrect.

claim: About 800 people refused to get a drug screening because they are "out there on drugs."
rationale: The statement is unverified and lacks crucial context (who, where, when) and there are no corroborating sources establishing that exactly ‘about 800 people’ refused a drug screening for the explicit reason that they are 'out there on drugs.' Because the claim provides a precise number and motive without attribution and cannot be substantiated, it is likely false or misleading as presented.

claim: "Joe Biden just confirmed that he is running for president in 2020 and it has America applauding!"
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: Joe Biden announced his 2020 presidential campaign in April 2019, so he did not "just" confirm a 2020 run now. Additionally, the assertion that "it has America applauding" is a sweeping, subjective claim not supported by universally positive public reaction—responses were mixed.

claim: Arnold Schwarzenegger slept on the ground in front of a bronze statue of himself because he had been turned away from a hotel.
rationale: There are no credible contemporary reports or reliable biographies that corroborate the specific story that Schwarzenegger slept on the ground in front of a bronze statue of himself after being turned away from a hotel. While Arnold has recounted hardship early in his career (sleeping on gym floors or struggling financially), this particular image appears to be a distorted or fabricated anecdote conflating different events. Without independent sourcing, the claim is not supported.

claim: Says "John James supported Betsy DeVos’ agenda to cut public school funding and put it into wealthy private schools instead."
rationale: John James publicly supported Betsy DeVos’s nomination and has consistently backed ‘‘school choice’’ policies (vouchers, tax-credit scholarships and expanded charter options) that divert public education dollars to private providers. Those positions align with DeVos’s agenda and have been criticized as effectively reducing funding for traditional public schools in favor of private schooling.

claim: Says Clint Eastwood is dead.
rationale: There were no credible reports or official announcements that Clint Eastwood had died up to my knowledge cutoff in June 2024, so the claim that he is dead is unverified and treated as false. I cannot confirm events after that date, so I err on the side of falsehood absent reliable, recent evidence.

claim: Because of union rules, cooks helpers moved into DMV jobs they were not trained for
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as presented: it provides no jurisdiction, timeframe, or supporting evidence. Union rules differ widely and generally govern job classifications and transfers, but DMV positions are typically filled through formal hiring or civil service procedures that require training or certification; there is no general rule that would cause untrained cook helpers to be placed into DMV jobs. Without a specific documented incident or source, the assertion cannot be verified.

claim: A person’s immune system "tanks" after their second COVID-19 vaccine dose.
rationale: This claim is false. Clinical trials and extensive real-world data show COVID-19 vaccines stimulate strong antibody and T‑cell responses rather than causing the immune system to ‘‘tank’’; common post‑vaccine symptoms are transient reactogenicity, not lasting immune suppression. While brief laboratory changes (e.g., transient lymphocyte count drops) and very rare immune-mediated adverse events have been reported, they do not amount to generalized, durable immune collapse after a second dose.

claim: "We have more coal reserves in the United States than they have oil reserves in Saudi Arabia."
rationale: U.S. proven recoverable coal reserves (on the order of a few hundred billion short tons) contain more total energy than Saudi Arabia’s proven crude oil reserves (roughly 260–300 billion barrels). Converting coal’s heat content to barrels-of-oil-equivalent yields on the order of ~800–900 billion barrels equivalent versus ~266 billion barrels in Saudi Arabia, so the statement is true when comparing total energy contained.

claim: Says "Morgan Carroll opposed requiring convicted sex offenders to register their online profiles, making it harder to track online sex offenders and child predators."
rationale: I could not find clear, reliable evidence that Morgan Carroll categorically opposed a law requiring convicted sex offenders to register their online profiles; the available information suggests the claim is a misleading summary of legislative debate or a specific vote and lacks necessary context. Without documentation of a direct vote or public statement matching that characterization, the assertion as stated appears inaccurate.

claim: "Biden’s Air Force One is not the same as Trump’s Air Force One," which indicates Biden is not the real president.
rationale: The claim is false because which specific airframe or livery is used does not determine who is legally president. "Air Force One" is the radio call sign for any U.S. Air Force aircraft carrying the sitting president, and administrations routinely use different physical planes, paint schemes, or tail numbers for logistical and ceremonial reasons. Therefore a difference between Biden's and Trump's aircraft says nothing about Biden's legitimacy as president.

claim: "The current (agriculture) commissioner allowed tainted beef to be sent to school cafeterias."
rationale: The claim is vague (no named commissioner, jurisdiction, or time) and there is no clear, publicly documented evidence that a current agriculture commissioner knowingly allowed tainted beef into school cafeterias. Food‑safety incidents and distribution of contaminated meat are normally traced, recalled, and reported by inspection agencies; an allegation of deliberate allowance would require concrete investigative or official findings. In absence of specific, verifiable facts, the claim is unproven and treated as false.

claim: "Speaker Gingrich for 20 years supported a federal individual mandate" for health insurance.
rationale: Newt Gingrich publicly endorsed the idea of requiring individuals to obtain health insurance for many years prior to opposing the ACA mandate, advocating individual responsibility and a national requirement in Republican policy proposals and his public statements dating back to the late 1980s/1990s. Multiple contemporaneous GOP plans and Gingrich’s own speeches and writings over roughly two decades endorsed an individual mandate as a conservative market-based approach before he broke with the ACA version.

claim: "We’ve been down this road before—blanket protectionism is a big part of why America had a Great Depression."
rationale: Most economic historians and economists view U.S. protectionism—most famously the 1930 Smoot–Hawley Tariff and subsequent retaliatory tariffs—as an important contributor that deepened and spread the downturn by collapsing international trade. It was not the sole cause of the Great Depression, but calling blanket protectionism a big part of why America experienced a worse depression is consistent with mainstream scholarship.

claim: After Fahrenheit 9/11 came out, "Bush's approval rating never was better, it only got worse."
rationale: False. National polling after Fahrenheit 9/11 (released June 2004) shows Bush’s approval rating fluctuated rather than monotonically declining — there were upticks (notably around the 2004 election and into early 2005) before later drops (e.g., after Hurricane Katrina). The statement ignores these variations and depends on which poll and exact dates are used.

claim: The DeWine campaign is "receiving money from so many more people. (Cordray's) money is coming almost exclusively from the party, labor unions, and special counsel that he has given business to."
rationale: This is an overstatement. Public campaign finance reports from the 2018 Ohio governor race show both DeWine and Cordray received contributions from a mix of individuals, party committees, unions, and outside groups; Cordray did not receive funds "almost exclusively" from the party, labor unions, and a special counsel. While Cordray had notable support from Democratic committees and labor, he also raised money from many individual donors and outside PACs, and DeWine likewise received party and large-donor support in addition to many small donors.

claim: The Orlando shooter used "a weapon of war."
rationale: Investigations of the 2016 Orlando (Pulse) shooting found the attacker used legally purchased semi-automatic firearms (a handgun and an AR-style semi-automatic rifle) and high-capacity magazines; there is no evidence he used military automatic weapons. Calling those civilian semi-automatic firearms a literal "weapon of war" is a rhetorical characterization, not an accurate technical description based on reported facts.

claim: In Wisconsin, Foxconn has "4,000 jobs, people making $53,000 a year."
rationale: False — Foxconn did not actually have 4,000 Wisconsin employees earning $53,000 a year. State audits and contemporary news reporting show the workforce on the Wisconsin campus was well below the 4,000 mark and that the $53k figure was a projected/targeted average (or included benefits), not the realized typical annual pay for current employees.

claim: President Obama has "the worst ratings of any president at the end of his first year."
rationale: This statement is incorrect as an absolute claim. National approval-tracking (e.g., Gallup) shows that several presidents registered lower job-approval numbers at the end of their first year than Barack Obama did; exact ranks vary by poll and specific end-date. The claim also omits which poll and which exact date define "end of his first year," which changes comparisons.

claim: Between 2000 and 2006,  "health insurance company profits quadrupled."
rationale: Available historical industry financial data and analyst summaries do not support a fourfold increase in overall health insurance company profits from 2000 to 2006. While insurer revenues and some firms' earnings rose in that period, aggregate net income increased by a much smaller factor and the claim appears to conflate different measures (revenues, premiums, or select companies) to exaggerate growth.

claim: "The Parole Board operates with Mark Herring’s advice and consent."
rationale: The phrase “advice and consent” is a legislative confirmation power, not something an attorney general performs. Mark Herring served as Virginia Attorney General and can provide legal opinions, but he does not personally give “advice and consent” for Parole Board appointments or operation. Parole board members are typically appointed by a governor and confirmed by the legislature or follow statutory appointment processes, not by an attorney general’s consent.

claim: Says in the governor’s proposed budget "the use of that, what is called one-shots, is a 500 percent increase over the last Corzine budget."
rationale: I cannot verify the quoted 500% increase from available information and the claim omits which governor and which fiscal years are being compared. Establishing a 500% change in 'one-shots' requires specific dollar figures from the named governor's proposed budget and Corzine's last budget; without those figures the assertion is unsubstantiated and likely misleading.

claim: Georgia ranks 49th for women serving in elected state and federal offices.
rationale: The claim is not correct as stated — recent trackers of women’s representation (e.g., by CAWP and similar outlets) do not place Georgia at 49th overall for women in elected state and federal offices. Georgia has women serving in its congressional delegation and a non-last share of seats in its state legislature, and published rankings vary by year and by whether the metric combines state and federal offices. Without a specific year or source the blanket assertion that Georgia ranks 49th is misleading.

claim: Gov. Kitzhaber oversaw creation of the Oregon driver card law "behind closed doors without allowing any input from citizens who represent the public interest."
rationale: The Oregon driver card was established through the normal legislative process—bills, committee hearings, public debate and advocacy—and was signed into law by Gov. Kitzhaber rather than unilaterally imposed in secret. Stakeholders on both sides, including immigrant‑rights groups and opponents, participated publicly, so it is inaccurate to say it was created behind closed doors without input from public‑interest representatives.

claim: Republicans "created a trillion dollar prescription drug entitlement program without paying for it."
rationale: The claim refers to the creation of Medicare Part D, the prescription drug benefit enacted in 2003 under a Republican Congress and President Bush; it created a large new entitlement program whose projected costs were substantial and were not fully offset by dedicated financing. CBO and other budget analysts at the time estimated large multi‑year costs (and long‑term liabilities that exceed $1 trillion under many scenarios), and the law relied on general revenues and beneficiary premiums rather than one‑time offsets to “pay for” those costs.

claim: Says "the mandate is 71 times that a child’s body will be injected with a disease" for immunizations.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. Vaccines do not inject a disease into a child’s body in the sense of causing the illness; they deliver antigens, inactivated/attenuated organisms, or genetic material to stimulate immunity. There is no credible mandate that requires children to be injected with a disease “71 times” — that number appears to be a mistaken or misleading interpretation of vaccine doses, antigens, or schedule items.

claim: "Republicans want to restore #gunrights to felons"
rationale: The statement overgeneralizes. While many Republican officials and parts of the GOP emphasize Second Amendment rights and some Republican lawmakers have proposed restoring firearm rights for certain ex-felons (often nonviolent offenders or after sentence completion), the party does not uniformly support blanket restoration for all felons and positions vary by lawmaker and state.

claim: Says New Jersey has "the highest unemployment rate in the region" and "stagnant job growth."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because it gives no timeframe or definition of “the region,” and New Jersey has not consistently had the highest unemployment or uniformly “stagnant” job growth compared with its neighbors. State unemployment and job-growth rankings change monthly/quarterly; while New Jersey has had periods of weakness, it is not reliably or continuously at the top of regional unemployment nor universally stagnant.

claim: "Schools that are consistently implementing COVID-19 mitigation strategies remain among the safest places for our students."
rationale: Multiple public-health analyses and peer-reviewed studies have found that layered COVID-19 mitigation measures in K–12 settings (masking, ventilation, cohorting, testing, vaccination where eligible) substantially reduce in-school transmission and outbreaks. When such strategies are consistently applied, schools have generally been documented as lower-risk environments for students compared with many uncontrolled community settings. However, effectiveness is contingent on the specific measures, adherence, and prevailing community transmission/variant conditions.

claim: "There's only four senators senior to me ... there's still 44 older than me."
rationale: The statement gives specific counts but provides no speaker or date, so it cannot be verified. Whether exactly four senators are more senior and 44 are older depends on which senator and the composition and ages of the Senate at a specific time; those facts change over time. Without identifying information or a timestamp the claim is unprovable here, so I label it FALSE.

claim: Georgia is the second-fastest growing state for international tourists.
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or source and cannot be confirmed as a standing fact. Year-to-year rankings of U.S. states by growth in international visitors vary and available national tourism data does not consistently place Georgia (the U.S. state) as the second-fastest growing for international tourists. Without a specific year and source the statement is not verifiable and is therefore treated as false.

claim: With voting by mail, "you get thousands and thousands of people sitting in somebody's living room, signing ballots all over the place."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization and not supported by evidence. While isolated cases of improper handling or fraud have occurred, research and official records show mail-vote fraud is rare and there is no basis for the claim that mail voting routinely produces 'thousands and thousands' of people signing ballots in living rooms. Mail ballots are normally completed by individual voters and returned under state-prescribed procedures and safeguards.

claim: "This Is Real: Biden Waves To An Empty Field."
rationale: The claim presents a specific visual event but gives no sourcing, and I cannot verify a credible, contemporaneous source that confirms President Biden waved at an entirely empty field. Such clips are often cropped or taken from angles that hide off-camera crowds, or are miscaptioned or edited. Without original video, timestamp, and location, the claim is unverified and thus classified as false by default.

claim: Says Vice President Kamala Harris called the unvaccinated "dirty Trump people."
rationale: There is no credible record or reliable news source showing Vice President Kamala Harris used the phrase "dirty Trump people" to describe the unvaccinated. The claim appears to be a misquote or a misleading paraphrase of remarks about vaccine reluctance among some supporters of former President Trump; fact-checkers have found no evidence she uttered that exact phrase.

claim: Says that Olive Garden is "funding" President Trump's 2020 re-election campaign.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Olive Garden as a company directly funded President Trump's 2020 re-election. U.S. law prohibits direct corporate contributions to federal candidates; any political donations would come from Darden Restaurants' PAC or individual employees/executives, which is not the same as the restaurant chain itself 'funding' the campaign.

claim: Republicans "went out of the way to praise (Eric) Holder's nomination. ... Not a single Republican senator opposed Eric Holder's nomination."
rationale: The Senate confirmed Eric Holder as attorney general by a 75–21 vote, and the opposition votes included multiple Republican senators, so it is incorrect to say not a single Republican opposed his nomination. While several Republican senators did offer praise or voted in favor, support was not unanimous among GOP senators.

claim: Says Jeb Bush tweeted "Ok boomer" at Donald Trump.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or record that Jeb Bush tweeted “Ok boomer” at Donald Trump; the claim appears to originate from doctored screenshots and social-media memes. Major news outlets and archives of Bush’s verified account do not show such a tweet, and fact-checkers flagged similar posts as fabricated.

claim: "Private prison systems are calculating how many new beds (they will need) based on the ... number of third graders."
rationale: There is no credible public evidence that private prison companies literally base bed-capacity projections on the headcount of current third graders. While research does show third-grade reading proficiency correlates with later high-school outcomes and incarceration risk, private prison capacity planning is typically driven by demographic/crime trends, sentencing laws, and contract forecasts rather than a simple count of third-graders. The claim conflates a statistical risk factor with an explicit industry planning metric.

claim: The "stand your ground" law caused the shooting death of Trayvon Martin.
rationale: The immediate cause of Trayvon Martin's death was the gunshot fired by George Zimmerman during their altercation in Sanford in 2012. Florida's 'stand your ground' statute did not physically cause the shooting; at most it has been discussed as influencing perceptions of legal protection for use of force or shaping prosecutorial decisions after the fact. Assigning legal causation to the statute over the person who pulled the trigger misstates direct responsibility.

claim: "I’m proud to say that under my administration, as you just heard, we will be building the first new heavy icebreakers the United States has seen in over 40 years."
rationale: The U.S. last commissioned heavy polar icebreakers (USCGC Polar Star and Polar Sea) in the 1970s, more than 40 years ago, and no new heavy-class polar icebreaker has been completed since. The administration initiated and funded the Polar Security Cutter program to build new heavy icebreakers, which would be the first new U.S. heavy polar icebreakers in over four decades if built as planned.

claim: The CDC said it "made a mistake" and reduced its count of Florida COVID-19 cases from 90,000 to 11,000.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the CDC said it “made a mistake” and cut Florida’s COVID-19 case total from 90,000 to 11,000. CDC data are periodically revised and states sometimes correct their own totals, but fact-checks and official CDC communications do not support the dramatic reduction or that wording attributed to the agency. The claim appears to conflate different datasets/revisions or misquote officials.

claim: "27 U.S. Air Force pilots resign over COVID-19 vaccination mandate."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official U.S. Air Force/DoD confirmation that exactly 27 Air Force pilots resigned specifically over the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. Fact-checkers and public DoD data showed only a small number of service members sought separation or were processed related to vaccine refusals, and social-media posts inflated or misattributed figures. The specific claim of '27 pilots' is unverified and appears to be misinformation.

claim: "Historically," Senate ratification of arms control treaties "has been bipartisan."
rationale: The statement overgeneralizes. While many major arms-control accords that were ratified (e.g., NPT, ABM Treaty, INF Treaty, CWC, New START) received bipartisan Senate support, key cases contradict the claim—SALT II was never ratified and the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty was rejected by the Senate in 1999 largely along partisan lines. Thus ratification has often been bipartisan but not uniformly so historically.

claim: "$3 billion over the next five years will be taken out of our public schools and be put into vouchers."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and unsubstantiated as presented: it gives no jurisdiction, bill, or authoritative source and there is no widely reported federal or nationwide plan to divert $3 billion from public schools into vouchers over five years. School funding is primarily controlled by states and local districts and voucher programs and their budgetary effects vary by state; some proposals could reallocate funds but the blanket $3 billion claim cannot be verified as a general fact.

claim: "If the FAA is worried about what the 5G deployment will do to the planes, what do you think it will do to our bodies?"
rationale: This claim implies FAA concern about 5G and aircraft means 5G will harm human bodies. The FAA's documented concerns were about radio-frequency interference with aircraft radar altimeters and flight safety, not evidence of biological harm. Major health agencies (WHO, FCC, FDA) say there is no established health risk from 5G radio frequencies at regulatory exposure limits.

claim: In 2011, "the average annual compensation for a teacher in the Milwaukee Public Schools system will exceed $100,000."
rationale: Contemporary salary and budget data for Milwaukee Public Schools in 2011 show average teacher salaries in the range of tens of thousands of dollars (roughly $40k–$60k), and even when employer-paid benefits and pension contributions are added, average total compensation did not approach $100,000. The claim that the average teacher in MPS would exceed $100,000 in 2011 is inconsistent with published payroll and state educator salary reports from that period.

claim: "Reporters rehearse questions with White House press (secretary)."
rationale: The statement as written is inaccurate: reporters do not routinely "rehearse" their questions with the White House press secretary. The press secretary fields questions at briefings and White House communications staff sometimes hold on- or off-the-record pre-briefings that preview topics or provide background, but that is not the same as reporters rehearsing their questions with the press secretary. Routine rehearsal by reporters with the official who will be answering would conflict with standard press-independence practices.

claim: Says science shows the physiological effects of wearing masks include hypoxemia, hypercapnia, shortness of breath, toxicity and increased muscle tension.
rationale: The claim is not supported by the scientific evidence: multiple clinical studies and public-health reviews find that cloth, surgical, and typical N95 masks do not cause clinically significant hypoxemia or hypercapnia in healthy wearers, and allegations of general “toxicity” from mask use are unfounded. While some people report subjective shortness of breath or increased breathing effort (and N95s can slightly increase work of breathing), objective measurements of blood oxygen and carbon dioxide generally remain normal.

claim: Says a mall Santa beat up a child molester.
rationale: The statement is presented without any identifying details (who, where, when) and I find no corroborating, reliable reporting for a specific incident in which a mall Santa beat up a child molester. Viral anecdotes about vigilante actions by Santas frequently circulate but are often unverified or mischaracterized; absent verifiable evidence this claim should be treated as false.

claim: "Hillary Clinton surged the trade deficit with China 40% as Secretary of State, costing Americans millions of jobs."
rationale: The claim wrongly attributes a roughly 40% rise in the U.S.–China trade deficit and “millions” of lost jobs to Hillary Clinton’s actions as Secretary of State. The Secretary of State does not set trade policy (that is led by the U.S. Trade Representative, Commerce, Treasury and Congress), and changes in the China trade balance during 2009–2013 are better explained by the post‑recession economic recovery, global demand, exchange rates and long‑term trade trends. There is no credible evidence tying a discrete 40% increase or ‘millions’ of job losses causally to Clinton’s tenure or direct actions.

claim: Most voters prefer zombies to the current U.S. Congress.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a majority of voters would literally prefer zombies to the current U.S. Congress. While congressional approval ratings are often very low, low approval does not mean most people prefer an implausible alternative like 'zombies'; the claim appears hyperbolic and unsupported by reputable polls. Any isolated humorous or satirical surveys do not establish that 'most voters' hold that view.

claim: "Biden impeachment in progress."
rationale: The claim is presented as a current definitive fact but is ambiguous. As of my last comprehensive knowledge (June 2024) the House Republican leadership had authorized an impeachment inquiry into President Biden (Sept 2023) and investigations were ongoing, but the House had not completed an impeachment and there had been no Senate trial, so saying simply 'Biden impeachment in progress' is misleading without a timeframe or clarification.

claim: "More than 90 percent of the gains have gone to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The statement is too broad and missing key context (what kind of "gains", and over what time period). Empirical studies show the share of gains captured by the top 1% varies substantially by whether you measure income or wealth and by the specific period; very high shares have been reported for some short periods but the blanket claim that "more than 90% of the gains have gone to the top 1%" is not universally true. Without a defined metric and timeframe the claim cannot be verified.

claim: "I finished" the controversy about where President Barack Obama was born.
rationale: The claim is false because no single person definitively "finished" the birth-location controversy; it was effectively resolved when President Obama’s birth records (short-form in 2008 and the long-form certificate in April 2011) and confirmations from Hawaii state officials established he was born in Honolulu. Even after those releases some conspiracy adherents continued to dispute the facts, so someone claiming sole credit for ending the controversy is inaccurate.

claim: Says Michael Bennet wants to close Guantanamo Bay prison and bring terrorists "right here to Colorado."
rationale: Michael Bennet has expressed support for closing the Guantanamo Bay detention facility and has supported transferring detainees to facilities in the U.S. for trial or detention, but there is no reliable evidence he said he wanted to "bring terrorists right here to Colorado" or advocated specifically moving detainees to Colorado. The claim appears to be a misleading paraphrase used in political attack messaging rather than an accurate quote of Bennet's position.

claim: "Beachgoers trash Florida beaches with 13,000 pounds of litter after beaches reopen."
rationale: The claim as stated is not verifiable and is likely misleading: there is no single, authoritative statewide report confirming that beachgoers left exactly 13,000 pounds of litter 'after beaches reopen.' Local cleanups have reported thousands of pounds of debris in specific areas and timeframes, but the claim bundles a precise figure and broad geographic scope without sourcing. Without a cited official tally, the statement overstates what can be confirmed.

claim: On financial reform, there is "a million dollars being spent, per congressman, in lobbying expenses on this issue. (The) industry has four lobbyists per member of the House and Senate working on this."
rationale: The specific claim is not supported by available evidence: dividing plausible totals for financial‑sector lobbying on financial reform by the 535 members of Congress does not yield $1,000,000 per member, and independent counts of registered lobbyists do not show a sustained ratio of four lobbyists assigned to each member for this issue. Financial firms did spend heavily and hired many lobbyists during financial‑reform debates, but the per‑member dollar and lobbyist‑per‑member figures are exaggerated.

claim: "Inspections of abortion centers around Virginia have found multiple violations of parental consent laws … but Gov. Terry McAuliffe and his administration have done nothing."
rationale: There is no credible public record that statewide inspections of Virginia abortion clinics documented multiple violations of parental-consent laws and that the McAuliffe administration simply ignored them. Media reporting and official inspection records do not support a pattern of such findings, and enforcement of parental-consent rules is typically handled through prosecutors and courts rather than direct unilateral action by a governor. The claim therefore misstates or exaggerates the available evidence.

claim: In the past three years, state legislatures have "enacted more of these restrictions (on abortion) than in the previous 10 years combined."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false because it is a sweeping, source-dependent comparison. Available public tracking (e.g., by research groups that catalog state abortion laws) shows a surge in restrictive laws after the 2022 Dobbs decision, but whether those restrictions in a specific recent three-year span exceed the total enacted in the prior ten years depends on the exact definitions and window used and is not supported as a general fact without a cited data source. Prior years (especially early 2010s) also saw substantial state-level restrictive activity, so a blanket "more than the previous 10 years combined" statement is not reliably true.

claim: "The Books Sarah Palin tried to have banned."
rationale: The statement as written is an unsubstantiated categorical claim and lacks specifics (no titles, dates, or actions named). There is no clear, reliable evidence that Sarah Palin personally attempted to ban a particular list of books; while she has been involved in local school and municipal controversies, documented instances of her formally trying to ban specific books are not established. Without concrete examples or sources the claim cannot be verified and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "Bryce Reeves chaired a group bankrolled by a New York billionaire who fired hundreds of Virginia workers and sent their jobs to China."
rationale: There is no credible reporting that Bryce Reeves chaired a group funded by a specific New York billionaire who then fired hundreds of Virginia workers and moved their jobs to China. Reeves has chaired or led local political groups and coalitions, but I find no reliable link tying him to a donor who engaged in that mass layoff/outsourcing described in the claim.
